en: Pramāṇavārttika, First Chapter:
Establishment of the Means of Valid Cognition (Pramāṇasiddhi)
Homage to Samantabhadra, whose form is profound and vast, who has shaken off the web of conceptual construction, and whose radiance pervades everywhere. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.1)
Generally, people are attached to the vulgar and possess unrefined intellect;
they not only fail to benefit from well-spoken words, but even come to hate them, being defiled by envy.

Therefore, we have no thought that this [work] is for the benefit of others; rather, our mind has long been bound by a longing for it, as our passion for the practice of eloquent sayings has increased. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.2)
Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge; non-contradiction consists in the stability of purposeful action.
This applies even to verbal cognition, because it communicates the speaker’s intention.

The object that appears in the intellect as the domain of the speaker’s activity—that is where the word has its authority; it does not depend on the actual nature of the thing itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.4)
Because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, a conventional [cognition] is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
for activity regarding things to be avoided or adopted is primarily dependent upon that [conventional cognition]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.5)

And because there is a difference in the apprehension of the cognition due to the difference in the form of the object, its existence follows from that very [apprehension]; thus, its own nature is understood by itself.
Validity is established by worldly convention; scripture is for the cessation of delusion;
or else, it is the illumination of an unknown object, subsequent to the apprehension of its own nature. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.7)

The cognition of a universal is attained when the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) has not been cognized; this is said with the intention that [it is] a cognition [arising] from the investigation of the particular characteristic. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.8)
In the same way, the Blessed One is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of turning away from what is non-existent;
since his speech is that of one who has realized reality, it depends upon the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and thus his status as a *pramāṇa* is logical.

There is no eternal means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because the attainment of the reality of an object depends upon its validity; and since that [validity] is impermanent due to the impermanence of the objects of knowledge, it cannot endure among those things that arise sequentially.

Because there is no production from that which is eternal, because dependence is impossible, and because it cannot be assisted in any way, even in the case of what is non-eternal, there is a lack of validity. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.11)

If [the opponent argues that] the non-occurrence [of a thing] while remaining [in its state] is due to specific configurations, purposeful action, and so forth, then there is either the proof of what is already accepted, a lack of proof, or else doubt regarding the example. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.12)

Whatever established arrangement and so forth follows the presence or absence of a presiding agent, that [arrangement] is joined with it; therefore, that [agent] is inferred from it. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.13)

When there is a difference between actual entities, it is not proper to infer a non-difference based on the identity of a word, as one would not infer fire from a white substance [simply because they share the same name]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.14)
Otherwise, because a potter produces some modification of clay such as a jar and so forth, it would follow that even an anthill is his creation. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.15)

When an effect is used as a probans, even though it is accompanied by the property to be proven in a general sense, the fault of asserting a distinction based on the difference of its correlates is considered to be the "equal-to-the-effect" (kāryasama) sophistry. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.16)

Because one observes a commonality of the word [“cow”] applied to things established as belonging to different classes, it is not logical to prove that speech and so forth possess horns, on the grounds of their being "cows. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.17)

Since words are dependent upon the speaker's intention, they do not exist anywhere [inherently]. However, if the object were established by the mere presence of those words, then everything would be established for everyone. Pramāṇavārttika 1.18.

By this, the lack of consciousness and other [qualities] in the followers of Kapila and others has been examined; likewise, the consciousness [of trees] is refuted by their impermanence and so forth, and by the removal of the bark due to death. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.19)

When the nature of the entity is established, this logical principle applies: "The qualification is not a subverter [of the thesis], even if it is unestablished, just as sound has space as its locus. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.20)
Even when the word itself is unestablished, it succeeds in establishing the established entity,
just as the proof of corporeality and so forth was stated by a Buddhist against the follower of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣika).

Even when there is deviation and so forth on the part of that [object], the means of proof should be known as defective even if the word itself is non-deviant, because the establishment of a real entity depends upon the real entity. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.22)
Just as that thing is a cause, so too is it a non-cause;
when it is a cause, by what [reason] is it considered such, and why is it not accepted as a non-cause? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.23)
When Caitra’s wound heals due to his connection with a weapon and medicine, why is the unrelated post not also imagined to be the cause? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.24)
Without a difference in intrinsic nature, even causal activity is not tenable;
because that which is eternal lacks differentiation, its capacity is difficult to establish.
When something necessarily exists given certain conditions, if one imagines something else as its cause, there would be an infinite regress of causes in every case. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.26)

The earth and other elements are the cause for the production of a sprout through a transformation of their own nature, because a specific quality [of the sprout] is observed when they have been prepared. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.27)

If it is argued that, just as the aggregate of object and sense-faculty is the cause of cognition even without a specific [quality], so too is this [the case here]— it is not so, because even in that instance there is a specific [quality].

If things that are individually incapable lack any excellence in their intrinsic nature, they would likewise lack capacity even when combined; therefore, an excellence [of nature] is established. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.29)

Therefore, those things which are individually incapable but in whose combination a quality is possible possess causality through their union; this does not apply to [theories such as] Īśvara and the like, because they lack such differentiation.

Some declare that because there is no means of accomplishing the knowledge of an imperceptible object, there can be no performance [of religious acts]; thus, they deny its validity. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.31)
Someone possessing knowledge is sought out in order to practice what he has taught, by those who suspect deception when an ignorant person provides instruction. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.32)
Therefore, let his knowledge regarding what is to be practiced be investigated;
of what use to us is his thorough knowledge of the number of insects? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.33)

He who makes known the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means [for doing so], is accepted as a valid authority (pramāṇa), but not one who merely makes everything known. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.34)
Whether it sees far or not, let it see the desired reality;
if one who sees afar is the authority, then let us worship vultures! (Pramāṇavārttika 1.35)
The accomplishment [of compassion] results from the practice of compassion; that [practice] depends upon the body and the intellect.
If it is argued that practice cannot be established [without a stable basis], we say no, because the [notion of a permanent] substratum is refuted. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.36)

In the acquisition of birth, the arising of the vital breaths (prāṇa), the downward breath (apāna), the sense faculties, and the intellect does not proceed from the body alone, independently of their own kind. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.37)
If it were seen as possessing the power of reconnection, why was that which does not exist later absent from it previously, such that it would not possess reconnection? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.38)
There is no part of the earth or other elements where beings born from moisture and so forth do not arise; therefore, everything has the nature of a seed.

If the sense organs and so forth were to arise independently of their own homogeneous causes (*sajāti*), then, just as there would be transformation for one, it would likewise occur for all without distinction. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.40)
Even when each of the sense faculties is impaired, there is no impairment of the mental consciousness;
yet, when this [mental consciousness] is destroyed, their destruction is observed.
Therefore, that which is the support for the persistence of cognition, being itself dependent upon cognition alone, is the cause of the sense-faculties;
hence, the sense-faculties exist by virtue of cognition.
Just as it was previously [the case that the mind] was projected [by the body], so let it remain so even later;
because it is assisted by the cognitions of that [body], it is said that the mind is dependent upon the body. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.43)
Although cognition does not exist without the sense-faculties, nor do they exist without it,
nevertheless, because they are mutual causes, they are both mutually caused.
A sequential entity does not arise from a non-sequential cause, nor does it arise from that which lacks a specific dependence;
since cognition arises sequentially from the body, this [fact] indicates that the body itself possesses sequence.
Since each preceding moment would be the cause of every subsequent moment that arises at every instant,
let it be observed that this very [preceding] cause exists at all times.
What contradiction is there in the connection of a subsequent mind with the final consciousness? Likewise, why is the connection of the Arhat’s mind not accepted? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.47)
If the thesis has not yet been established by means of a valid cognition, why is it followed?
If you say it is because of a deficiency in the reason, then why was that very [deficiency] not pointed out here?
For, since its apprehension occurs as if it were an object, mental cognition does not arise from the sense organ;
nor does it arise from the [organ] in its entirety, because there is a difference in the capacity for producing cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.49)
Because it is insentient, there is no coexistence [of the body] with anything else due to a lack of difference in cause;
rather, its modification occurs through the medium of objects, as in the case of the sense organs or like color and taste. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.50)
That which always assists [the effect] through its constant connection is the cause; therefore, it is expressed by the seventh case (locative) and also as "from the arising" (*utpādāt*).
Or perhaps it may sometimes be a benefactor to the mental continuum;
yet, by that much alone, there is no cessation [of the continuum], just as fire and the like do not cease because of a jar and the like.

Furthermore, as long as the body persists, there would be the undesirable consequence that the mind does not cease [its activity], because its existence depends on that [body] and because it is subject to it; therefore, the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) are not that [the cause of death]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.53)

How could there be impelling and attracting by the wind without effort? For those two [impelling and attracting] would result in decrease and increase, due to the decrease and increase of that [effort]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.54)

The same consequence applies to those two as well; however, they are not equal regarding the cause of the mind, because another cause is accepted for the maintenance and projection [of the continuum].

If the body, being impaired by the humors, were the cause [of cognition] like a wick and so forth, then there would be a return to life once the humor has been pacified upon death. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.56)
If it is argued that [the defect] does not cease because, even when the fire has been extinguished, the transformation of the wood does not cease—
this is not so, because of the application of medical treatment.
In some cases, due to the impossibility of recurrence, a certain transformation is produced in something;
in other cases, it is the opposite, as in the case of fire acting upon wood or gold. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.58)

Even a slight modification of the first [type] is irreversible; however, that which has been produced can be restored to its original state, just as gold returns to its natural condition after being altered into a necklace. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.59)

Because a healer is difficult to find, some [diseases] are said to be incurable; or [they may be incurable] due to the exhaustion of the lifespan. However, when there is only a [physical] disorder (*doṣa*), there is no incurability. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.60)

If, upon death, [the person] does not breathe again because the cause of the transformation has been removed—either by the administration of an antidote to poison or by the cutting off of the ten vital points (marmans)—then how much less so [would they breathe] otherwise? Pramāṇavārttika 1.61.

Without a modification in the material cause, no modification of the effect can be produced, just as a pot or similar object cannot be made from clay without a change in the clay itself. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.62.

For that substance which is modified without itself being modified cannot logically be the material cause (*upādāna*) of that modification, just as a cow is not the cause of a gavaya. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.63)
In this way, because the arising of the effect occurs from that cause through the cooperation of mind and body, they exist together, like the fluidity of copper when in contact with fire.
Since neither the existent nor the non-existent can serve as a basis, there is no basis that acts as a cause for persistence.
If it were a basis for the existent, it could not be distinct from the persisting entity itself.

Even if [destruction] were distinct [from the entity], what would that cause of destruction do for the entity? If it is argued that this [distinction] is held to avoid the consequence of the entity's non-destruction, [the response follows].
The same consequence applies there as well; what then is the use of a cause for stability?
If it is argued that its persistence lasts until the arrival of a cause of destruction, then that would be the very nature of things.
If it is argued that this destruction is sublated by reality, so what is the need for a cause of its persistence?
If you say it is like water having a container as its support, then the same applies here as well.
For since entities perish at every moment, it is because the continuum of those entities arises in such a manner that it possesses a cause; otherwise, a substratum would be untenable.
A substratum may exist for things such as water because it prevents their movement; but what need is there for substrata for qualities, universals, and motions, which are themselves devoid of motion?
By this, the inherence [relation] and the inherent cause, as well as the fixed status of universals and so forth, are refuted, because they lack a substratum. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.71)
If the destruction of entities occurs due to something else, what is the use of a cause for their persistence?
It would perish even without other factors; thus, causes of persistence are powerless.
Every substratum is stable, and everything that arises has a substratum;
therefore, no entity whatsoever ever undergoes destruction.
If its nature is inherently perishable, what other [agent] could establish it? If its nature is not inherently perishable, what other [agent] could establish it? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.74)
Even the decrease and increase of wisdom and other qualities occur through the differentiation of mental activity, even without the decrease and increase of the body. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.75)
This [dependence] does not exist for things such as the light of a lamp that depend upon it;
even if there were some distinction from that [lamp], it would not apply to the mind, which provides no assistance [to the self].

The increase of passion and so forth arises from nourishment and the like, which sometimes produce pleasure or pain; and these two [pleasure and pain] arise from the proximity of internal objects such as the equilibrium of the bodily humors (*dhātu*). (Pramāṇavārttika 1.77)

By this, the loss of memory resulting from the derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*) and so forth is also explained; for it is the mind alone that undergoes modification when produced by specific internal objects. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.78)

In certain cases, when there is an intensification of the mental continuum through [the consumption of] tiger blood and the like, delusion and other such states arise simply from hearing or seeing them, just as [in the case of those who have heard or seen the teachings]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.79)
Therefore, consciousness invariably follows its own own latent impression (saṃskāra);
since it is inseparable from that, consciousness is dependent upon consciousness.
Just as the cultivation of learning and so forth, performed in each successive moment of mind,
becomes manifest over time due to its non-differentiation, so too would there be a quality [of memory] in the body.

The assumption of a lowly state by one who possesses self-attachment—being led by no other being—is due to the desire for the abandonment of suffering and the attainment of pleasure. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.82)
Regarding suffering, distorted cognition and craving are the causes of bondage.
He for whom these two do not exist among those subject to birth does not undergo birth.

If it is argued that the coming and going [of the senses] are not perceived because of their lack of acuity—just as smoke, though present, is not seen by one with weak eyesight—then [the following applies]. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.84.

However, because of its subtlety, even a material entity may lack the capacity to act in certain places, like water [in a vessel] or mercury in gold; it is not as if it were non-existent due to being unperceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.85)

If [the whole] were to tremble when the hand or another part trembles, it would follow that everything undergoes trembling; since a single action is impossible for [a whole] that is opposed [to such a consequence], otherwise there would be a separate establishment [of the parts]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.86)

If one [atom] were obstructed, all would be obstructed; if one were unobstructed, all would be seen. Furthermore, if one [atom] were colored, all would appear colored; or else, there would be no perception of the uncolored. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.87)
Therefore, there is no single composite [entity], even if there were multiplicity, as in the previous case.
If it is argued that movement is not established because there is no distinction [between parts] and because of their atomicity, [the answer is: it is not so. Pramāṇavārttika 1.88.
Since there is no distinction [in their nature], the sense-faculties are not atomic;
by this, the absence of obstruction and other such qualities is also refuted. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.89)

Or how could [the senses] perceive things mixed with mercury, gold, and so forth, or heated stones and the like? For those [senses] that are individually incapable, what is the means of apprehension? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.90)
If it is argued that [the cognition] arises from conjunction, then the same consequence applies here to gold and the thread.
If it is argued that the conjunction is perceptible, how can there be a cognition [of it] when its substrata are imperceptible? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.91)

If it is claimed that conjunction (saṃyoga) is metaphorically designated as the connection with taste, form, and so forth, then let there be a distinction in cognition; but how could there be such cognitions as "a row" or "long"? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.92)
In the same way, the nature of number, conjunction, action, and so forth does not appear to the cognition as distinct either by its own form or through verbal expression. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.93)
In the cognition of a word, by means of a conceptual construction that follows after the distinction between real entities—
as in the case of qualities and so forth, or as with things destroyed or not yet born— the object is merely imagined.

If it is held that there is a metaphorical designation (upacāra) here, then why is that very basis upon which it depends not accepted as the cause for both [the cognition and the designation] in all entities? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.95)

If figurative usage does not apply everywhere because the qualifiers are distinct, then from what [source] is it derived that the primary sense applies only where there is no distinction? For how can there be a difference in meaning when there is no difference [in the object]? Pramāṇavārttika 1.96.
Even if they are causes for no distinct object, words such as "white" and so forth are not synonyms;
for if even in those cases there were a distinct object associated with number and the like, [they would be synonyms]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.97)
There would be no distinction between a quality (*guṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*), even though they are different due to a difference in their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*);
this would be the case even if they do not have different referents, just as in the case of the words "non-action" (*akarma*) and "non-substance" (*adravya*). (Pramāṇavārttika 1.98)

Furthermore, when words denoting an entity express [a property] as if it were distinct [from the entity], such as number and so forth, they differentiate that [entity] from other properties inherent in it. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.99)

In some cases, scripture—intended for one who desires to know only that [specific object] and not implying all other things—teaches as if it were a distinct property, saying, "The yoga is by means of the finger. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.100)
The term *yuktāṅgulī* (joined fingers) denotes the substratum (*dharmin*) because it implies all [the fingers] through a collective reference;
likewise, even when expressing a single well-known object, the established form [of the compound] is prescribed in that same manner. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.101.

The word "jar" functions without implying the specific distinctions between the potencies of form and so forth; rather, it excludes those causes that do not produce an effect identical to its own. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.102)
Therefore, there is no co-referential expression such as "the pot is form. Such a distinction exists between [words] that denote a genus and those that denote a collection. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.103)

"Color and so forth belong to the jar"—in this way, the various powers of that [jar] are made known as being subordinate to its general property. Other [referents] may also be expressed by this same method. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.104)
And if they were causes as a whole, there would be no [result] even when a single factor is deficient;
yet if each were individually capable, there would be the simultaneous production of many [results]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.105)
Nor can inhalation and exhalation be the regulators [of cognition], because multiplicity is equally applicable;
even if [the self] were a single entity, there would be a plurality of manifestations due to the constant presence of their cause.

If it is argued that there is no single cause [for the simultaneous perception of multiple objects], we say no, because there is no distinction [in the conditions]; for even in a single moment of consciousness, there is the apprehension of multiple objects, and therefore there is no fixed rule [regarding their sequence]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.107)

If it is argued that multiple cognitions arise from a single [cause] all at once because there is no contradiction, let them not arise even sequentially, since there would be no difference [in the cause]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.108)
If many momentary vital breaths, which do not belong to the same class [as the mind], are postulated as the cause of such minds, [then there would be no restriction]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.109)
How could they possess a sequence without a cause that possesses a sequence?
If their own preceding members were the cause, there would be no possibility of a first member.
There is no such cause for that [simultaneity], or if there were, there would certainly be multiplicity;
because the vital breaths occupy different locations, cognitions therefore arise simultaneously. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.111)

If multiple [sensory objects], though occurring at the same time, were the cause of a single consciousness, then even when one of them is deficient—as in the case of faint breathing and so forth—[consciousness] would still arise. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.112)
Now, if the cause [of cognition] is as it actually exists, there would likewise be a distinction in the cognition;
for that which does not differ despite the difference of its [cause] cannot be its effect.
Consciousness is the cause of a single [subsequent consciousness] due to the restriction of its capacity;
for when the cognition is impaired by attachment to another object, there is no apprehension of a different object. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.114)
Cognition, once arisen from the body, is restricted by its own kind;
if it were [to continue] due to something else, why would there be a cessation of the capable body? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.115)
If it is argued that the mind might remain alone even when the body has ceased because it lacks a support, [we reply:
there must be a cause for the persistence of the mental continuum. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.116)

If the cause for the production of another body—the fivefold sense-base belonging to this life—does not become a factor [for rebirth] because it fails to obtain the activity that is its cause, [then there would be no rebirth]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.117)

Non-perception, when used to negate the state of being a cause that is a constituent part [of another], has been declared to be non-conclusive; this applies even to the sense faculties and so forth, as they are also "residual" (śeṣavat) reasons. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.118)
Furthermore, an attachment of the preceding sense-faculties to their own respective species is observed;
and because transformation is seen, rebirth after rebirth is established. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.119)
If its birth were from the body, the same consequence as before would follow;
if it were from the mind, then let the birth of another body arise from that very [mind] as well. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.120)
Therefore, it is not due to a deficiency in the cause that there is no reconnection for all final moments of consciousness;
thus, such a proof is considered to be *śeṣavat*.

If it is argued that even with excellence through practice, there should be no transgression of one's inherent nature—just as in the cases of jumping or heating water—if that [nature] has been established [as such]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.122)
Furthermore, it would require further effort if it were to have a non-abiding substratum;
otherwise, no excellence would ever increase, and its nature would not be such [as to allow for change]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.123)

In that regard, because the means of proof lack the capacity to bring about further specificities once their power has been exhausted, and because [the self] never abides without a substratum, [it cannot be established]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.124)

Since a particularity has no intrinsic nature, when it has been produced even by an increase [of effort], it would not require further effort; otherwise, that further effort would have to be the producer of another particularity. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.125)

Just as [the transformation of] wood, mercury, gold, and so forth occurs through fire and other means, compassion and the like arise spontaneously in the mind through the power of repeated practice. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.126)
Therefore, that nature which has arisen in them becomes a quality;
each subsequent effort brings about a further distinction. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.127)

And since the cognitions of compassion and so forth increase from seeds of a similar kind that preceded them, how could there be a cessation of them when they have been practiced? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.128)

And it is not the case that jumping arises solely from a prior jump; rather, because the capacity of its causes—strength and effort—is established, the nature of jumping remains constant. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.129)
At first, due to a physical impairment, there is a failure to leap as far as one can;
later, once that impairment has been gradually removed through effort, one remains established in one's own natural strength. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.130)
Compassion arises from its own seed; if it is not obstructed by opposing factors arising from their own seeds within the mind, it attains the state of being an ultimate nature.

For thus, each preceding practice is the root for each subsequent one, in order to bring about the proficiency of mental qualities such as compassion, dispassion, and awakening. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.132)
The nature of compassion arises from practice, overcoming aversion, dispassion, and attachment;
once perfected, this excellence of compassion is impelled by an inability to endure the suffering of others. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.133)
The compassionate one applies himself to the means for the sake of eliminating suffering;
for it is indeed difficult to explain that which is beyond perception—the goal and its cause. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.134)

Investigating through both reasoning and scripture, one examines the cause of suffering, as well as its impermanent nature and other characteristics that qualify suffering itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.135)

Since one perceives that as long as the cause remains in such a state, there is no cessation [of the effect], one examines its opposite in order to abandon that cause of the effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.136)

Its opposite is established by understanding the nature of that cause: attachment, which has conditioned phenomena as its object, is produced by the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.137.
The cause of its opposition is the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*), which subverts it through many means in many ways over a long period of time. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.138)
As one practices therein, the virtues and faults become manifest;
and due to the proficiency of the intellect, the latent predispositions (vāsanā) are abandoned. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.139)
This is the distinction of the Great Sage from those who act for the sake of others by means of swords and the like:
this very practice of skillful means is considered the teaching because it has that [benefit of others] as its purpose. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.140)

Because it exists prior to the accomplishment [of the result], these two are called causes; the abandonment of the cause possesses three qualities, and Sugata-hood consists in the absence of dependence. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.149.
It is taught that suffering [ceases] through the view of selflessness, or else by means of reasoning;
furthermore, when "return" is mentioned, it refers to the arising of birth and defects.
Through the abandonment of the seed of the view of a self, there is no further return;
because that [self] is distinct from the elements, the remainder is free from afflictions and feverish distress.

Deficiencies of body, speech, and intellect, or even lack of skill in explaining the path—all these are eliminated through practice; by means of such instruction and so forth, there is the exhaustion of faults.
"No," say some, "for its negative concomitance is doubtful due to deviation; moreover, the defects are inexhaustible because they are eternal and thus lack a means of removal. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.145)

Or one might imagine [the opposite] due to a lack of understanding of the means, because of the presence of a contradictory cause, or because of the destruction [of that cause] through repeated practice. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.146)
Through the knowledge of the nature of causes, that [reliability] is also established:
"Salvation is the teaching of the path seen by oneself; because it would be fruitless, one does not speak untruth. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.147)

Because he is compassionate and because of his application to all undertakings for the sake of others, therefore either he is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or his teaching of the Four Noble Truths is the means of valid cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.148)

The aggregates of those in cyclic existence are suffering, because we observe the intensification of passion and so forth; this occurs through habituation, not by chance, nor without a cause, as that would contradict the nature of birth. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.149)
If it is argued that there is no fault because the property [of being produced] is not a property of air and so forth due to deviation and the confusion of natures,
then why is another such property not also observed to belong to it?
It does not follow that all dharmas possess equal passion for everyone;
if it is argued that there is no fault because they are like visible forms and so forth, then the same objection applies to that case as well.

If there were no predominance of specific karmas in that regard, then even when there is a distinction [in the results], [the cause] would be unestablished because the defects [of the causes] remain undifferentiated. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.152)
It is not the case that [an effect] arises from a modification [of its cause] through another modification, nor do all [effects] arise from everything;
furthermore, it is illogical for an effect to diminish when its cause is increasing.
Just as in the case of heat and so forth, there is also a transformation of passion and the like arising from pleasure and so forth;
[but] if it is argued that passion does not arise because of the suffering produced by disharmony.
It must be explained by whom [the mind] arises; from that equilibrium comes the increase of passion, and from that, the god of love.
For one who is impassioned is seen even when the humors are in disequilibrium, yet another is not seen even when they are in equilibrium. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.155)

If it is argued: "Even though blood and semen are diminished by [sexual] discharge, intoxication is not restricted to a single woman; therefore, O dear one, it would not be intense toward one woman alone, because of factors such as beauty and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.156)
It would not be non-conclusive for all [cases], nor would it be unrestricted;
for even one who perceives no qualities might possess that perception of quality as a factor [of valid cognition]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.157)
If everyone were to grasp only virtues because there is no distinction in the cause,
then a person who is considered to be full of passion in a certain state would likewise not be one who feels aversion.
Because those two are of an identical nature, no fixed rule is observed here;
for their activities are restricted by the distinctions of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) belonging to their own respective classes.
For one who possesses passion and the like, these faults do not follow as a consequence;
by this, both their status as properties of the elements and their dependence upon a substratum are refuted.
Because of the negation, white and other qualities do not reside in earth and so forth;
furthermore, the word "derived from that" (tadupādāya) has the sense of a reason, and [the quality] resides in its own substrate. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.161)

Alternatively, because it exists inseparably from form and so forth, it may also be their substratum, just like the power of intoxication and the like; however, there is no such separability for a real entity.

If power (*śakti*) were a distinct entity, it would perish while its substratum remains unimpaired; yet it does not perish. If you argue that it departs [to another substratum], that is not so, because there is no difference [between the two cases]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.163)
Because the perception of the elements and consciousness appears as distinct,
and because the body remains unchanging, the mind would have to be of a uniform nature.

Like form and so forth, what dependence on an external object could conceptual construction possibly have, when it arises from the awakening of latent predispositions (vāsanā) without depending upon a body? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.165)
Someone might have some knowledge from something; therefore, [the object] is not [known] by that [knowledge].
Furthermore, it is established because there is no cognition of what is not cognized, due to the lack of appropriation [of that object] by cognition.
If it is claimed that every entity is connected to the power of consciousness, who else but this Sāṃkhya beast would venture to say such a thing without shame? (167)
"There are a hundred elephants on the tip of a blade of grass, though never seen before"—that form which has now come into the range of vision was not seen previously. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.168)

Even if the cause were dispersed in a hundred ways, how could that [effect] exist? Furthermore, it would follow that there would be no restriction regarding passion and so forth in the manifestation of what was previously non-existent. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.169)

If everyone who possesses passion and so forth has not transcended their elemental nature, then everyone would have equal passion; unless, that is, there is a distinction due to the excellence of the elements.

Even though there is no difference in the vitalizing function (*prāṇatā*) of living beings, that basis upon which this [perceptual] difference depends—being subject to decrease and increase—would cause those [vital functions] to diminish as that [basis] comes to an end. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.171)
If, despite their difference, there were no exhaustion of the similar nature that causes passion and so forth,
then passion would be identical everywhere, because its cause is of a similar nature.

For there is nowhere any gradation in the cognition of a cow that arises from a common essence, whether in the case of earth and so forth, or here in the case of being a living being and so on. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.173)

If it is argued that just as fire is never non-hot despite variations in the degree of its heat, so it is here as well, we say no; for there is no denial of the difference between fire and its heat. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.174)

The qualities of another existing entity that are experienced in varying degrees are sometimes obstructed when there is a difference in that [entity], just like white and other colors. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.175)
There is no such restriction for those [mental factors] as there is for form and so forth, because they are inseparable from the primary elements.
If it is argued that this is the same [for mental factors], it is not so, because it would entail the consequence that desire and the rest arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, because they are objects of conceptual construction, objects themselves are not determinants [of cognition].
Alternatively, due to the absence of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), there would be no restriction regarding passion and the like.
The arising of all cognitions at all times must depend upon the presence of their causes;
since they are only occasionally perceived and because they rely on [causes] that are subject to defects, they are impermanent.
Suffering exists because it is subject to causes; it is neither the self nor presided over by one.
There can be no presider without a cause, and how could that which is eternal be a cause? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.179)

Therefore, a plurality [of effects] does not arise from a single [cause] at a different time, because the effect is not produced even when other causes are present in conjunction. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.180)

There would be an inference based on a different reason, but this does not apply to eternal things; for the fact that this suffering has a cause is established by its occasional nature. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.181.
A thing must be either eternally existent or non-existent, because it does not depend on external causes;
just as there is no cause for the sharpness and other qualities found in thorns and the like. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.182)
Some declare that this [definition] would be the cause:
"That in the presence of which something arises, or in the modification of which there is a modification [of the effect]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.183)
They say that this is its cause, and it exists for those [senses] as well;
because touch is the cause of form, it possesses the status of a causal sign (nimitta) in the act of seeing.
Since eternal entities and [theories] such as God are refuted, they are not possible;
therefore, the cause is the grasping of the desire for existence, because of its incapacity [to produce otherwise]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.185)

Because that [activity] of humans toward a specific place is produced by the hope of attaining it, such activity would occur for one who desires both attainment and non-attainment of pleasure and pain. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.186)
Furthermore, since living beings desire the power of sensual pleasures,
that [desire] arises everywhere because it has self-attachment as its cause.
"Because craving is the basis for existence for one who perceives pleasure in what is not pleasure, the Teachers declare that dispassion is not seen in those who are born. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.188)
Since attachment is not observed in the absence of a body, attachment arises from the body;
while the presence of a cause is thus accepted, the [body as] a material cause (*upādāna*) is nevertheless rejected. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.189)
But one who seeks this reasoning contradicts his own position by himself:
"If there were coexistence with birth, because passion is seen in those already born. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.190)
Although it is established that [craving] is the cause for the arising of similar [moments], it was not mentioned [previously];
rather, ignorance was stated [as the cause], because craving alone impels the continuum toward existence. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.191)
And because of its immediacy, even karma [is not absolute], for while that [defilement] exists, [the result] is impossible;
it is therefore non-absolute because of the possibility of obstacles to the cause and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.192)

There would be no liberation because of being subject to cyclic existence; nor is this [liberation] desired, nor is it established. As long as there is no loss of love for the self, one will continue to suffer.
Having projected [the notion of a self] upon what is so afflicted, one does not remain at ease;
therefore, effort is exerted for the sake of abandoning false superimposition, even though there is no liberator.

The state of those free from passion [is maintained] either through compassion or through karma; for, since they do not desire to turn back once [the momentum] has been projected, it is sufficient that the auxiliary conditions have perished. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.195)
For those who have transcended the thirst for existence, no further karma can be projected;
[their stream] carries on the previous formations, being non-contradictory to the knowledge of suffering.
The arising of compassion is a property of the object itself; it does not depend upon sentient beings.
Attachment toward an object that lacks that nature arises from the superimposition of another self. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.197.
In this way, compassion arises merely through contact with the continuum of suffering;
and delusion is the root of the defects, yet that [delusion] exists without the grasping at a sentient being.
Therefore, there is neither hatred nor fault in the absence of a cause for rebirth; hence, compassion is considered appropriate.
There is no non-liberation [of the Buddha], because when previous latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted, there is no further linking to a new birth.
Those whose latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*) possess undiminished power remain faultless;
yet, due to the dullness of their compassion, they do not exert great effort in [the task of] establishing [others]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.200)
But those for whom there is great compassion remain indeed dependent on others;
through the disappearance of the view of a real self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), their very first state would be non-becoming (abhava). (Pramāṇavārttika 1.201)
If [the self] were on the path, there would be no loss of its innate nature; or if it were not lost, how could there be cyclic existence?
For one who thirsts with the thought, "May I be happy, may I not suffer," [there is rebirth]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.202)
The very cognition "I am" is itself the innate perception of a self;
for no one feels affection toward themselves without perceiving "I. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.203)
Moreover, one who desires happiness does not rush toward [an object] without love for the self.
Since bondage consists in being the cause of the arising of suffering, how could that apply to something eternal? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.204)
Liberation is the state of being a cause for the non-arising of suffering; how could that belong to something eternal?
For that which is inexpressible as impermanent cannot be the cause of anything at all. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.205)
Even bondage and liberation are in no way applicable to that which is inexpressible;
the wise call that "eternal" whose intrinsic nature does not perish. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.206)
Having abandoned this shameful [view] because it has been seen to be so, let that [self] be called impermanent.
The path has been taught; through its cultivation, the basis (the continuum) undergoes transformation.
If it is argued that even when [the sense organ] is habituated, there is still the presence of defects—just as in the case of the [wrong] path—we say no, because of its lack of omnipresence.
For the apprehension of objects is the very nature of consciousness, just as it exists.
"He is apprehended as its producer by means of his existing self"—this is its natural state; however, it falters due to other causes. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.209)
The cessation [of afflictions] depends on conditions and is not firm, like the cognition of a snake [in a rope];
this mind is luminous by nature, while the stains are adventitious. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.210.
If they were incapable even before, how could there be capacity later for those things consisting of that [nature]?
They are not able to sprout at all, like fire on wet ground. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.211)

Even when an object is capable [of being negated], because it possesses within itself the capacity for the arising of a sublater, its nature—which is a real entity free from affliction—cannot be overturned by contrary cognitions. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.212)

Even when an effort is made, there is no sublation [of the false view], because cognition has a partiality toward that [view], because it originates from the single source of grasping at a self, and because of the relationship between cause and effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.213)
Even when passion and aversion are distinct, they do not obstruct one another;
because of their non-opposition to delusion, there is no absolute suppression of the defects through loving-kindness and the like.

All impurities have that as their root, and that [root] is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because it is the opposite of true knowledge (*vidyā*) and because it is perceived as a mental factor (*caitta*). (Pramāṇavārttika 1.215)
Ignorance is false apprehension; by logic, anything other than that is irrational.
Herein, whatever contradiction exists must be explained, and because of that contradiction, [the same applies] to those things composed of it. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.216)
The contradiction with the faults of sentient beings is established for one who holds the view of emptiness;
[the Buddha] is not subject to exhaustion because he possesses the nature of a vow, and because [exhaustion] is unestablished, just like form and so forth. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.217.
Furthermore, because no abandonment of the counteragent is observed when there is a connection [with the object], there is no arising again of the fault that opposes it, as in the case of hardness;
for it would not be eliminated due to having become one's own nature (*sātmatva*), and because [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), like ashes. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.218)

For one who perceives a self, there arises therein a permanent attachment characterized by "I am this. Due to that attachment, one craves pleasures; craving, in turn, conceals the faults [of those pleasures]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.219)
Seeing qualities and craving for them, one grasps at the means to achieve them, thinking "this is mine";
as long as there is this adherence to a self, so long does one remain in saṃsāra. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.220)
When there is a self, there is the notion of "other"; from the division of self and other arise attachment and aversion. Bound up with these two, all defects are produced. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.221)
Necessarily, one who feels affection for the self does not become dispassionate toward what belongs to it.

And there is no cause for the removal of affection toward a self that is free from defects. If it is argued that affection is itself defective, what follows from that? Why should it be abandoned? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.223)
When its object has not been found faulty, it is impossible for that [cognition] to be abandoned,
because [the cognition] is connected with qualities and defects such as desire, aversion, and so forth.

The sequence by which there is no perception of those two [the self and the mind] with respect to an object, but there is perception of external things, does not arise from the quality of affection; rather, it arises from the perception of the qualities of the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.225)
When that cause is unimpaired, by what could the effect be prevented?
Or what fault has been observed in affection, other than its being the basis of suffering?
Nevertheless, there is no detachment here [toward the body] because one perceives it as "mine," just as there is none toward the self;
for if the self is the cause of suffering without those [senses], then those [senses] are likewise [the cause of suffering without the self].

Thus, both [theories] are faultless because of detachment from duality; therefore, there is no [need for] duality. If it is argued that [detachment] arises through the cultivation of the perception of suffering, like the abandonment of a limb bitten by a snake, [it is not so]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.228)
In this context, renunciation occurs through the abandonment of the notion of "mine," but not otherwise;
for [renunciation does not occur] regarding the sense faculties and so forth when they are grasped as the basis for experience. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.229)
By whom could the cognition of ownership be prevented? How, then, could there be detachment toward it?
For everyone, [the sense of ownership] regarding hair and so forth [separated] from the body is indeed perceptible. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.230)
A mind of aversion arises toward those who have passed away, while a mind of longing arises toward others;
for in that case, one's own cognition is produced by relations such as inherence (samavāya) and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.231)
"It remains exactly as it was" means that even when a fault is perceived, it does not lose its nature;
for even in the absence of inherence (*samavāya*) and the like, there exists a capacity to assist in all cases. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.232)

If one thinks that because it involves suffering it is not beneficial—just as with a finger—it is not so, for that [pleasure] is not exclusively suffering; rather, for the most part, it is like food mixed with poison.
From attachment to a distinguished pleasure, there may arise detachment toward its opposite;
one might renounce some pleasure out of a thirst for a more distinguished pleasure. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.234)
But regarding those who lack a sense of self, [sexual desire] proceeds according to what is obtained out of attachment to the self;
when it is not obtained, as seen among animals, even a drunken woman is desired. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.235)
How could one who holds the self dear desire its destruction—that which is the locus of all qualities, experiences, and worldly activities that have ceased? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.236)
How could one desire love, for such is not the nature of love? In every respect, the grasping at a self sufficiently strengthens affection toward the self. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.237)
However, the seed of affection for "mine" remains established in that very state;
even with effort, detachment from "mine" occurs only by relying on some slight quality [of the object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.238)
One who possesses [right] conduct obstructs those faults and conceals them;
if there were detachment even toward oneself, then one would now become detached. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.239)
Just as he abandons himself [through such meditation], the cultivation of suffering is therefore futile;
for even by cultivating the idea of suffering, he would only bring about further suffering. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.240)
Even though that [object] was previously perceived directly, one nevertheless does not become dispassionate;
for even if the mind is momentarily shaken by a fault in one instance, [it does not follow that it will remain so]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.241)

One who is dispassionate is not attached even to that [object], just as one who is lustful is not attached to another woman; for attachment is that which arises solely toward the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.242)
It is the seed for the successive arising of all powers;
it is affection toward a faultless object, and it is itself faultless along with its means of accomplishment. *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.243.
And if the world is only this much, where could he now become dispassionate?
Even if there were defectiveness in it, that would be the same in respect to the self as well. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.244)
In that case, one who is not yet dispassionate toward it—how could he now become dispassionate toward its defects?
For one who perceives defects cannot subvert the affection born from perceiving qualities. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.245)
And that [reliability] does not reside in the sense faculties and so forth, because it is possible even for infants and others;
furthermore, it exists even when there are defects, and it is absent even when there are qualities. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.246)

Furthermore, because [the notion of "mine"] has been abandoned even with respect to the past and so forth, which are other than what belongs to the self, for that very reason there is no perception of qualities in the cognition of "mine" either. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.247)
That [affection] also diminishes because of its cause; therefore, it does not [diminish] from seeing faults.
Furthermore, the attribution of non-existent virtues is indeed seen there due to affection.
Therefore, how can an injunction that does not subvert its own cause subvert that [perception]?
Because there is the cognition of destruction and arising from the pursuit of what is prior and posterior.
People perceive the self as distinct from the sense faculties and so forth;
therefore, even through the view of their oneness, one who feels affection does not feel it for the self. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.250)
One is naturally attached to internal objects of perception;
however, that aversion which arises toward present suffering is of this [same] nature.
Even then, there is no dispassion for him, because he still seeks other states;
since hatred is born of suffering, his state lasts only so long as that [suffering] persists. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.252)
When that [cognition] has ceased, it returns once more to its own very nature;
for indifference prevails everywhere due to the abandonment of both rejection and acceptance. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.253)

Detachment is said to belong to those who regard an axe and sandalwood as equal; it is called the cultivation of suffering after one has realized the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). (Pramāṇavārttika 1.254)
And that production of our cognition has its basis in the vision of selflessness;
liberation, however, arises from the vision of emptiness, and all other meditations are for that purpose.
From that very [fact of] impermanence, he taught suffering; from suffering, selflessness. And one who is not dispassionate possesses craving and relies upon all undertakings. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.256)
Such a person, not yet liberated from afflictions and karma, is called a transmigrator;
for one who does not even desire what belongs to a self, there exists no enjoyer of it either.
At that time, even the self does not exist for him, for its defining characteristic consists in action and experience;
therefore, [the stream of consciousness] has as its seed a homogeneous series that is beginningless.
O you who desire liberation, uproot the view of a self-entity, for you do not perceive any basis for the existence of such a thing in scripture. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.259)

One who speaks of liberation as occurring merely through [the performance of] rituals does not provide satisfaction; for a procedure perfected by means of seeds and the like is not sufficient for the non-arising of human beings. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.260)
Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that liberation could result even from oil massages, fire-burns, and the like;
furthermore, since one is heavy before and light after [the act], it follows that no removal of sin has been accomplished. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.261)
Let it not be that for this [being] there is only weightiness and no sin, because sin is formless;
rather, [sin exists] by virtue of false cognition, the thirst arising from it, and volition. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.262)
From that, birth occurs as a transition to an inferior state; for once that [inferiority] is severed, [superior birth] arises.
Indeed, the causal capacity for those two [inferiority and superiority] exists only at the moment of birth, because they exist solely in that [birth].
These volitions themselves are the action, the indivisible cause of birth;
they are the instruments for movement and perception, and their substrata exist through the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
Because the unseen [force] perishes, there is no movement; its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is not consciousness.
This is because the capacity for the production of an instrument follows the presence or absence of that [unseen force]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.265)

These [qualities] are seen in the Buddha and not in anyone else; how could they lead [others], since sustaining, impelling, agitating, and restraining are under the control of volition? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.266)
If they were incapable [of functioning], those [defilements] would not exist immediately after his initiation;
moreover, since the cognition does not exist at that time, they would not exist, for it is [the cognition] that is conjoined with the impurities. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.267)
If they were incapable, then even while living, they would be unable to act against them;
for there would be a decrease in the opposing side and an increase in their own side through the process of nourishment. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.268)
Defects, being part of the continuum of their own seeds, are not prevented even in one who has been initiated;
furthermore, because an eternal entity is independent, its successive production is contradicted. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.269)

In both action and non-action, there is a unity of the two actions because they possess a similar nature; likewise, there is a distinction between cause and effect, and consequently, a distinction between those two.
There would be the loss of being an agent and an enjoyer, and causal capacity would not be established;
furthermore, the undesirable consequences of [the self] remembering or experiencing what belongs to another do not constitute valid objections.

Because there is no memory of anything that has not been experienced, the arising of memory occurs with respect to the four truths—such as "this is stable," "this is happiness," "this is mine," and "this is I. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.272)
Having superimposed sixteen unreal aspects, one becomes intensely thirsty;
yet, it is precisely there that [the cognition] conforms to the aspects of the reality that is the opposite of those [unreal aspects]. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.273)
Right view, when well-cultivated, destroys craving along with its attendants;
thus, there is no arising from the three causes even when karma and the body persist. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.274)
Just as there is no arising of a sprout without a seed due to the absence of that one [cause], so too,
because an opposing factor is impossible, there can be no destruction of karma and the body.
Furthermore, because it is impossible [to eliminate karma] while craving remains— since [karma] arises again—
and because effort toward the destruction of both would be futile, labor for the sake of exhausting karma is useless.
Moreover, because a variety of fruits is observed, a diversity of potencies is inferred for actions;
therefore, their destruction does not occur through asceticism, since that is of a single uniform nature.
The fruit produced by that [action] might somehow be small, but it cannot be of a different genus;
nevertheless, through the power of asceticism (tapas), there may be a confusion, an increase, or a destruction of those potencies. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.278)
If one were to abandon everything entirely due to some affliction, provided that no trace of affliction remains,
then if another desired goal arises from that affliction, that austerity is indeed nothing but affliction itself.
Therefore, because that is the fruit of karma, there is no confusion of powers and so forth;
for even those [factors] which are contrary to defects serve to eliminate the defects arising from birth. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.280)
They would be capable of performing that very action; how then could there be a failure of the act?
Faults do not belong to the action itself; it is the agent who acts defectively, not because of a reversal in the nature of the action.
Without false conceptualization, there is no desire even for pleasure;
therefore, that [conceptualization] is the means for attaining the stable and complete knowledge of all particulars.
Because the root *gam* signifies "attaining enlightenment," he is superior to those outside [the fold] as well as to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Therefore, there is the accomplishment of the knowledge for the sake of others; therefore, that is his teaching. // Pramāṇavārttika 1.283 //

Compassion consists in being dependent on the welfare of others; because one whose goal is accomplished does not cease [from activity], through compassion he teaches what is beneficial, and through knowledge, the truth along with its means. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.284)

Since one who is diligent in application is able to state that [truth], therefore its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the fact that the teaching is such [as it is]; for there is praise [of the Buddha] based on his having given that teaching. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.285)
Because [the reason] is not excluded even in inference for the sake of establishing the reality of the means of valid cognition,
or because its application is observed— as in the case of "whatever has an origin by nature" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.286)— [it is a valid reason].

"All that has the nature of cessation," and so forth—in these various ways, the logical mark (liṅga) which is the basis of inference is characterized by invariable concomitance (avinābhāva). And that [concomitance] is clearly stated by means of the reason (hetu) through the demonstration of pervasion (vyāpti) with the probandum (sādhya). Pramāṇavārttika 1.287.
The second chapter:

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*māna*) is of two kinds, because of the twofold nature of its objects, according to their capacity or incapacity [to produce a cognition].
In the case of purposeful action, hair and the like are not the object, because they are resolved upon as non-objects.

And because of similarity and dissimilarity, and because of being an object and not being an object; and because of the presence or absence of cognition when other causes for verbal expression are present. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.2)
That which is capable of causal efficiency is here said to be ultimately real;
the other is called conventionally real. These two are your particular and universal characteristics.
If it is argued that everything is incapable [of causal efficiency], [we reply: the capacity of seeds and the like toward sprouts and the like is observed;
if that [capacity] is held to exist conventionally, let it be so, however that may be.
If it is argued that [the universal] exists everywhere, [we reply:
no, because the intellect does not perceive it through positive and negative concomitance, just as in the case of the cognition of color and so forth by the eye. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.5)

By this [same principle], cognitions regarding the lifting of a jar, universals, numbers, and so forth, are explained through internal factors such as convention and mental application. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.6)
Hair and the like are not universals because they lack adherence to [external] objects;
since they are apprehended as objects of knowledge, no fault follows regarding non-existent things.

Since there is no refutation of their being likewise [illusory], the appearance of clarity arises; for, because they have the nature of cognition, they are not external objects. Furthermore, the notion that "these are hairs" and so forth [is merely a mental construction].
If the appearance of hair is considered to be an object because it has the nature of cognition, then it would follow that even a universal is an object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.9)

Thus, because it is accepted as such, there is no fault; there is equality by virtue of having the nature of the object, since it is of an identical form in all cases due to its reliance on the exclusion of that [object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.10)
That [name] is not the thing itself, because it is not something to be differentiated [from it], and because the collection of sense faculties is effective [only with respect to the thing];
for when a name and so forth are uttered, they are connected to the speaker, the hearer, and the object denoted. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.11)

If it is argued that the application [of a word] to an object occurs through error due to similarity when the name and so forth are unrelated to that object, then such application would not occur at all times. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.12)

And there is no confusion regarding the object in cognition, because the arising of such a cognition occurs only from that [object] and not from anything else; for cognition does not arise otherwise. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.13)

Alternatively, there is no validity regarding the means for the appearance of external objects, because the existence of anything distinct from consciousness is not established. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.14)

If it is argued that [the mind] possesses all objects of knowledge because it perceives them otherwise in dreams and so forth, this is incorrect; for blue and other such appearances arise from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.15)
Because it is not obstructed by blue and other objects, that [cognition] is not [perceived] by those situated in suitable locations;
since it is known by itself even while unknown [to others], by this [argument] names and so forth have been explained. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.16)
Why is it that cognition through the eyes and other senses is considered to possess its desired object?
If it is because the capacity of the object is perceived, then [cognition] arising from anything else would necessarily be devoid of an object.

If linguistic activity were to occur even in the absence of a relation [between word and object], as if there were a relation with the object, then the past and the future could not be denoted, because those have perished and do not exist. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.18)
If it is argued that there is no such over-extension [of the term] because the word [denotes] the apprehension of the universal, that is not so;
for either the universal is not apprehended alone, or even if it were apprehended, [the fault remains]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.19)
Because its manifestation is not identical to that [object], there would be a constant perception of it;
and if manifestation were the cause of perceptibility, then because of its permanence, [the object] would be constantly perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.20)
That which is capable of producing cognition in relation to itself is indeed always capable;
however, if it were ever incapable, it would be incapable at all times. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.21)
Whether its capacity or incapacity exists by way of its own nature, since it is eternal, what could possibly diminish it? Who is capable of exhausting it? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.22)
And while conforming to that general cognition, that slight trace of the form of blue and so forth which is perceived—by whom was it produced within it? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.23)

If it is argued that the sense organs are not useless because they serve the purpose of producing direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then from what cause does that single cognition arise with diverse appearances from sound and other objects which possess a single form? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.24)
A universal is not of the nature of an individual possessing that universal such that it would depend on another;
for if it were established as distinct, its being an effect is what is designated as "dependence."

An effect, even though independent of anything else for its production because it arises from its own causes, is connected [to those causes] by conceptual construction; how could that which is not an effect ever be so connected?
If they were different, it would be unconnected to that [entity], and thus its lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) is established.
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of the existence of a universal (jāti) in a non-entity; for those two, there can be no dependence, as there is an absence of such [causal] relation.
Therefore, although formless, the universal (jāti) is conceptualized as depending upon forms;
it is manifested by words whose purpose is to penetrate its specific distinctions.

The appearance of form within that [consciousness], or the apprehension of an object as being real, is an error produced by the habitual practice of perception since beginningless time. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.29)
That which is the generality of objects, characterized by the exclusion of others—that upon which these words are based has no form whatsoever. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.30)

Since it is not perceived as having a form in the universal-cognition which itself lacks form, that cognition is also accepted as an error regarding the object; for that [cognition] too is a superimposition of a universal.
Because it does not exist as a real entity in the form of an object, it is not possessed of form;
and because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is considered inexpressible by any statement whatsoever. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.32)

If, in some way, the ineffability of things regarding a given object [is asserted], it is not at all ineffable, because difference is metaphorically attributed due to the difference in their material causes (*upādāna*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.33)

Even regarding objects past and future, verbal cognitions (*śruti*) function by being based on general characteristics (*sāmānya*); how then could there be a distinction between existent and non-existent properties? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.34)

If it is argued that this [designation] is accepted as a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), then what proximity does a present jar have to its own non-existence, which is not found in the case of a cloth or other objects? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.35)
The unerring function of the intellect always pertains to both the primary and the superimposed meanings;
likewise, there is even a worldly convention regarding the lion and the boy. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.36)

Wherever a word has been applied by people through conventional usage even to an unreal object, it is primary (mukhya) in that context; elsewhere, due to its similarity to that [primary sense], it is secondary (gauṇa), its application being faltering.

Just as people might apply the designation "non-existence" even to that which exists, or apply it according to their own conceptualization, so too they might apply the term "Pradhāna" and the like to that which is either incapable or capable. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.38.

Just as a cognition arising from words is observed to be the same whether [the object] has perished or not, such is the case for cognitions of real objects; this is not so for the cognitions of the ear and other senses.
Because both cognitions apprehend only the universal,
the prior apprehension of that universal in its isolation has already been refuted.
How could that which is undifferentiated belong to things that are mutually distinct?
Or, if it possesses two forms, how could that entity be one? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.41)

If their form were identical, then that [form] would have to be something other than those two; thus, the relation "of those two" would not hold. However, there is no fault in the case of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Pramāṇavārttika 2.42.
Therefore, in this context of the *sāman*, it is precisely this similarity that constitutes the characteristic of being a non-entity (*avastu*).
If it were an effect, it would be manifold; nor is it accepted as something momentary.
Because destruction is invariably concomitant with the mere entity itself, there is no permanence;
and because universals (jāti) are not effects, they lack any [real] form and thus have no connection [with the entity]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.44)
And that cognition which arises from the power of the real object does not depend on convention; this is clearly understood in the case of cognitions of universals. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.45.
When two things are perceived, there may arise some cognition that follows their difference;
even without a linguistic convention, that cognition is based on the proximity of the objects. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.46)

Just as proximity is desired [as the cause] for the effects that are cognitions in the case of the eyes and so forth even without a universal (jāti), or just as a universal follows [its instances] through differentiation; Pramāṇavārttika 2.47.
If the sense organs were the seer, their form would appear [in cognition]; however, that form does not appear even in some cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.48)
Because they possess form, universals are not perceived in isolation; furthermore, when an individual is apprehended, nothing other than its own specific form is seen. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.49)
For that very reason, it is incapable even of performing the function of being an object of mere cognition;
by virtue of that incapacity, it is formless, for that indeed is the characteristic of non-entities.
That which is the opposite of what has been stated is held to be the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
That universal (sāmānya), moreover, is of three kinds, based on existence, non-existence, and both.

If cognition were based on an entity because it is invariably concomitant with an entity, that is not so; for the answer has already been stated, and because [cognition] is observed otherwise in the case of the past and so forth.

If it is argued that there would be a loss of its being a property of an existent (bhāvadharmatva) because that cognition is preceded by the apprehension of an existent, we reply: this is not a fault; for the object of cognition (meyam) is only the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). Pramāṇavārttika 2.53.
Therefore, because the accomplishment of purposeful action depends upon the investigation of existence and non-existence,
and because that [accomplishment] is apprehended through both its own form and the form of others, two types of objects of cognition are recognized.
The second type of error is held to be due to an incorrect adherence [to an object].
If there were movement by way of another's form, then error would not possess the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.55.
Even though there is error, there is validity because of the non-contradiction of the intended purpose;
furthermore, movement is seen to be otherwise, and this position has already been answered.

For two people who run toward a jewel and a lamp-light respectively, perceiving them both as jewels, although there is no difference in their false cognition, there is a difference with respect to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Pramāṇavārttika 2.57.

Just as it is, even though inference and its fallacy may lack correspondence with reality, their status as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or its semblance is established in accordance with their capacity for causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.58.
Wherever cognition follows the presence and absence [of an object] through the power of that object, its apprehension is independent; any other entity is beyond the senses. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.59)
Since its own nature is unperceived, another object must serve as its locus for that movement;
if it were connected with that locus, only then could it be a signifier.
At that time, there is comprehension only in the form of a generality that follows the suggester;
therefore, every remote object is not apprehended in its particularity. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.61.

And that manifestation of a property belonging to its correlate which is known in the subject is inference; it is exclusively the means of establishing things that are beyond the senses. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.62.
There is no possibility of another object of cognition (prameya) apart from [those established by] perception and inference;
therefore, the duality of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is asserted on account of the duality of the objects of cognition. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.63.
Alternatively, the exclusion of the number three [of objects of cognition] follows from the observation of only two types of objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
If it is held that there is only one [object], because the non-existent is not an object of knowledge, that is indeed our own view.
If non-existence were not an object of cognition, there would be no certainty regarding it;
