nor can that certainty be established by a second means of knowledge, for cognition born of the senses does not [apply to such an object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.65)

If the universal were produced by the force of the object in the absence [of a real entity], and if it did not depend on the power of the object, then sensory cognition would arise even when there is an intervention or other such obstacles. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.66)
If it is argued that the certainty regarding non-existence belongs to perception itself, that is contradictory;
or else, that very [non-perception] is the logical mark (liṅga) characterized by both positive and negative concomitance.

And the two means of valid cognition for the apprehension of another's consciousness are established; one who is engaged in practical activity and the like is established as having certainty regarding its existence. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.68)

If it is argued that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists because of its non-contradiction, but that there is no confidence in it due to occasional deviation—this is merely a case of misperceiving the logical mark (*liṅga*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.69)
Since its cognition is sometimes established regarding a certain object,
that [object] must necessarily be either produced from that [cognition] or possess its nature.
An object cannot come into existence without its own cause or its own nature;
and whatever form is observed in those two is itself the defining characteristic in other cases as well.

Whether it be in its own nature or its own cause, or in the visible objects that are the causes of perception, or when other [conditions] are present yet the object is not seen—how can there be existence for that which possesses such [a nature]? Pramāṇavārttika 2.72.
And since the cognition of a universal would lack validity, its exclusion [from the object] follows;
like the state after death, it is perceived by the senses through a successive process.
And that [non-existence] is not [perceived] through the capacity of the sense organs and so forth, because sensory cognition would be impossible;
rather, it would be the arising of a cognition [of non-existence] in the apprehension of absence. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.74)

And perception, being non-conceptual, occurs with respect to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); without conceptualization, there is no grasping of the universal (*sāmānya*), and therefore, inference operates upon that [universal].
If the objects of cognition are restricted [to the six categories], the impermanence of sounds is not perceived;
for there would have to be another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the cognition thereof, since it cannot occur without a logical mark (liṅga). Pramāṇavārttika 2.76.

In the case of inference based on perceived particulars (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), because the relationship of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not established [prior to the observation], it is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*); or else, there is a multiplicity [of means of cognition] due to the multiplicity of objects to be known (*meyabahutva*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.77)

Or likewise, because multiple means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) function toward a single object, and because no distinction [between them] is perceived, there would either be a negation of the numbers one and three, or else there would not. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.78)

Because there is no restriction on the objects [of inference] and because other objects of knowledge are possible, this fault does not apply, due to the application [of the reason] to the generality of color. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.79.
It is not the nature of a non-entity, because it is established as being exactly thus;
if you argue that one thing cannot be established by another, we say no, because it is established as that very thing itself.

For whatever entity exists in a certain way, it is the cause for a cognition possessing a corresponding mark; therefore, from that [entity], there arises a cognition of the inferential mark directed toward the object as it truly is.
Thus, because the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) are indirectly connected to the real object,
they are non-deceptive even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [object].

And because of the determination [of those two] as having that form, even though they are devoid of that form and do not actually deceive regarding that form, the status of being an error is established for them. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.83)

Therefore, when an object is to be cognized, the cause for the mind [to apprehend] the pervaded is either the pervader itself or its nature; and that [cause] is indeed the cause for the cognition of that [object].
But negation is established everywhere through non-apprehension; for those who assert establishment by means of valid cognitions, the opposite follows by implication. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.85.

When there is a statement contradicting [the proponent's] doctrine, whether it concerns that [doctrine] itself or its cause, even such a negation indicates the lack of validity of that very [proponent]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.86)

Otherwise, by the statement of the intrinsic nature of one phenomenon, how could the non-existence of another be understood? If it is argued that this is due to contradiction, then that [contradiction] must also [be established]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.87)
If it is argued that [the self] is established because of its non-coexistence with anything else, from what is that [non-coexistence] known?
If it is argued that it is because of the absence of perception of a perceptible object, then that [absence] lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.88)
Therefore, even though it is expressed by its own term, that [non-apprehension] establishes non-existence;
for one for whom it is not a means of valid cognition, negation is in every respect inexpressible.
By this, the statement of an effect that is contradictory to that [probandum] has been explained.
Only the formal application (prayoga) differs; in all cases, the underlying meaning does not differ. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.90.

Furthermore, that statement of a means of valid cognition regarding a negation—which neither provides nor indicates a remedy for what is contradictory—is not in accordance with the traditional doctrine. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.91)

Because there is no established proof of contradiction regarding supersensible matters, such as the denial of an omniscient being, rebirth, and so forth, [the same applies] to speech and other [means of knowledge]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.92)
If both reasoning and cognition were [equally] real, what relationship of sublated and sublator could there be?
If it is argued that such a relationship exists because one is not perceived, then let that very non-perception be the means of proof.
Such non-perception has been described as "non-ascertaining";
therefore, regarding things that are absolutely beyond the senses, there can be no certain determination of their existence or non-existence.

Whether a property be distinct or non-distinct [from its locus], it is applied as a contradictory [reason] when, for example, existence (*sattā*) or birth (*janman*) are employed to prove that fire is not cold, or to subvert [the notion of] birth. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.95)
Just as a real entity alone is considered the means of proving real entities, so too a real entity alone is the negator of real entities through its own cessation. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.96)

By this, the property (dharma) such as "being either the subject or one of its similar instances" (pakṣasapakṣānyataratva), which is superimposed by conceptual construction because it could occur anywhere, is refuted. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.97)
In that case as well, a pervading property is considered to be the indicator of the absence [of the probandum], provided that its own pervasion is somehow determined. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.98)
Whatever mark is stated for the very absence of being a means of valid cognition is intended only for those who are utterly deluded, for it is not hidden even from cowherds. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.99)
This much is the result of certainty: non-perception in the case of absence;
and that [non-perception] occurs when the cause or the essential nature is considered perceptible and is not perceived.

This sequence is held to apply to the apprehension of impermanence and so forth through inference; it is not considered that there is validity elsewhere, because [the object] has already been apprehended. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.101)

There is no impermanence other than the entity itself; if that [impermanence] were established prior to the object through the sense-faculties, it could not be said to have multiple forms. What is expressed is a property (dharma) born of conceptual construction.

When the substratum of a universal is established, that universal is indeed established. For when that [substratum] is not established, it is precisely through inference that its establishment proceeds.
In some cases, there is a lack of recognition of that [difference] due to the occurrence of another similar thing;
this is because one does not perceive the distinction from error, like the difference between a [real] ball and a magical illusion. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.104)

For indeed, even a child, observing that a lamp or similar object lacks a mark [of continuity] and arises unconnected with what follows, certainly determines it to be perishable. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.105)

Even though the capacity exists as the very nature of the entity, there is delusion regarding the perception of the result because of the lack of immediate succession and due to the observer's lack of proficiency in discernment.
In order to exclude that very [objection], inference is described; for those of great intelligence discern all aspects from perception alone. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.107.

When that [object] has been excluded from everything else, cognitions—bound by the very act of exclusion—operate upon the object as if they were distinct, even though they have a single basis. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.108.
And according to the instruction, that [consciousness], in the absence of a cause for error, naturally connects the designations and intuitions that correspond to itself. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.109.
Alternatively, destruction is established here as well through the mark of non-perception;
for a thing that, having previously existed, no longer exists, is designated as "impermanent."
For whomsoever the scriptural statement on impermanence expresses a relation with existence delimited by both ends, for him those two [ends] are recorded as such in the tradition.
If there is non-existence both before and after, why is that itself not impermanence?
If it is argued that this is because [terms like] the genitive case and so forth are inapplicable, then how could that [non-existence] exist at the two ends?
Since existence and its relation are permanent, they cannot be qualified by the two extremes;
if the two extremes were the cause and the effect, then [existence] would indeed remain unqualified.
Because there is no connection [between the entity and its prior non-existence], he does not accept the prior non-existence of an entity;
and when that [non-existence] is designated by means of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), neither that [adjunct] nor this [prior non-existence] is established. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.114)

It is said that existence (*sattā*) is the cause because it effects its connection with its own causes; yet both that existence and that relation are eternal. What, then, is the effect in this case? *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.115.
That whose non-existence would be produced is not an entity possessing prior non-existence;
consequently, because no relation [between them] is admitted, this entire universe would be eternal. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.116)

Therefore, even in the case of words intended to have non-different meanings, those which possess different denotata and consist of a mass of useless [elements] serve as the basis for cognitions that apprehend difference. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.117.
There is no recognition of specific qualities because of the difference between every moment;
nor does it have specific qualities as its object, since it grasps them through their similarity to what was previously seen. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.118)

If it is argued that the example itself is the [object of] non-apprehension of the universal because it is an example, then what further purpose is served by establishing it through a means of valid cognition?

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the object] has been forgotten, then for that very reason there is no illustrative example. If it is argued that its existence is established through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding another object that has been perceived, [then the same problem follows].
When there is a superimposition of reality, there is error; because that [superimposition] is established, it lacks the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since perception and its opposite are one and the same, the establishment of one is the establishment of both. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.121)

The wise know that determination which is being connected with another [cognition] is memory; for it depends on its own characteristic mark. If it were not memory, there would be no deviation [from the definition]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.122)
Perception, which is free from conceptual construction, is established by perception itself;
for everyone, conceptualization based on names is known through personal introspection.

Having withdrawn all discursive thoughts with a tranquil inner self, even while remaining [in that state], one perceives form with the eye; this is cognition born of direct perception (*sākṣātkṛta*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.124)

Furthermore, when one conceptualizes something, thinking "such was my previous conceptualization," one does not perceive it through the senses during the state previously described. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.125)
For a difference observed in one instance is not seen elsewhere;
therefore, there is no other distinct universal, because cognition is undifferentiated. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.126.
Therefore, every cognition born of the sense-faculties has particulars as its object; there is no possibility for words to function with respect to those particulars. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.127)

Because particulars lack positive concomitance (ananvaya), linguistic convention cannot apply to them; therefore, that alone which is the object of words can be associated with them. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.128)
In the relation expressed as "this belongs to that," the relation exists only between those two objects that appear [in cognition]; at that time, it is not within the range of the sense faculties.
Because at that time the object does not appear clearly, the distinction between objects is indeed determined by the difference in the appearance within consciousness. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.130)
Even when an object appears to the eye, it is that which another person designates as "this" that is connected with words; indeed, it is not the actual range of the sense faculty itself.

Because one whose sense faculties are not engaged does not perceive [an object] through mere words of another, and because it would follow that there would be knowledge spontaneously without a previously established relationship [between word and object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.132)

Due to the simultaneous occurrence of conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions of the mind, or because of its rapid functioning, the deluded person determines them to be one and the same. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.133)

If it is argued that perception becomes interrupted by the intervention of conceptual construction, then how could this be the case for another [perception] when there is a conceptual construction of a different kind? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.134)
If the position that [the object] exists is considered strong, like the perception of a whirling firebrand, then that same [reasoning] applies elsewhere as well;
or else, there would be a simultaneous hearing of two distinct phonemes.
Even though the sense-faculties here are in contact with all objects simultaneously,
that [cognition] which appears as if unobstructed despite being separated by the five [faculties], [is the object of inference].
That cognition appears as if interrupted because it is mixed with momentary cognitions that have no end; this is its diversity. Therefore, let there be simultaneous cognitions.
Furthermore, how could there be no distinction in appearance between those [cognitions] that are separated and those that are not?
And in the case of pure mental conceptualization, there would be no perception of succession. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.138)

When the mind of someone is attached to something else, there is a non-apprehension even when an object is present; because that attachment causes a deficiency in the arising of another [cognition], this objection applies equally to both [theories].
The rapid movement of a firebrand or similar object produces the illusion of a circle by obstructing the perception of its continuity;
it does not do so through the joining together of successive visual perceptions.
Some assert that because it arises from the sense faculties and so forth, cognition is non-conceptual like that of an infant;
they further claim that the cause for an infant’s lack of conceptualization is their dullness regarding linguistic conventions. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.141)
For those [who are not yet proficient], it would indeed be a matter of direct perception because they lack conceptual construction;
furthermore, that [perception] would not exist even later, due to the absence of the means of linguistic convention.

If it is argued that the mind exists because it possesses a well-established convention, then the same would apply to what is produced by the sense faculties; and this [argument] is similar to the remaining [points].

Whatever proof is applicable to the fool, let that very same one be stated here as well; by this, experience and so forth are explained on the grounds of the equality of the intellects of those with impaired senses.
Having grasped the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and the worldly convention, one synthesizes these and cognizes [the object] in that way, and not otherwise.

Just as, in the case of a person carrying a staff, there is no connection with that which possesses [the staff] because the universal and so forth cannot be determined through differentiation, therefore conceptual construction does not exist here either. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.146.
Even that pervasive cognition which appears as the manifestation of a word and its individual instance is described as "cowness" (gotva), for it is devoid of the forms of color, shape, and syllables.

Even though it is the same, there is no grasping of that very [object] within the range of the eye; because two appearances are absent, a distinction in cognition is difficult to establish. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.148)
Since inherence (samavāya) is not apprehended by the senses, the non-perception of a [real] relation is established;
furthermore, expressions such as "the cloth is here in the threads" are merely created by oneself.
In the world, it is said that "the horn is the cow," whereas "the cow is in the horn" is unworldly;
for no separation of the remaining parts from what is designated as the cow is perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.150)
"This cloth is made from these threads" is the subsequent effect that is spoken of;
it is produced by the processing of the threads and can never exist at the same time as them.

Due to the superimposition of the cause, someone might even apply the designation "thread" to the effect by means of a single abstraction, thereby demonstrating that the basis for the verbal expression is not [the effect itself]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.152)
The relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, or the perception [of a distinction] due to separation, is merely secondary;
that which is primary is the unerring cognition that constitutes the domain of the original linguistic convention.
Furthermore, there is no inference regarding a real entity that is differentiated by [accidental] properties such as genus;
for designations based on a staff and the like do not arise from anything merely conventional.
Words such as "building," "palace," and "row" do not depend on anything else;
for even if a "house" is a conjunction [of parts], how could its "row" be that same [conjunction]? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.155)
If the universal were the house, then even a single one would be called a "garland," just as [the term] is used for a tree.
If there is a plurality of garlands, how could that word apply to the universal, given that a universal is not itself a universal?

Furthermore, regarding garlands and the like, qualities such as "largeness" that are intended to be figurative are not actually figurative, because they are apprehended by a cognition that is indistinguishable from that which apprehends them in their primary sense. That state of having no other cause is equal even for those things accepted as being primary.
What other cause does the word "category" (padārtha) consider among the six [categories]? Pramāṇavārttika 2.158.

Whatever is established through conventional usage in a certain way, that which is spoken of in the same way due to its similarity to it—whether primary or secondary—is so designated even regarding non-existence by way of metaphorical application toward entities. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.159)
Conventional usage follows linguistic convention, and that [usage] follows the speaker’s intention;
it is established for the sake of practical communication, just like the names of parts of a meter. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.160)
By the very nature of things, objects are the cause of such a cognition;
even though there is a difference [between the object and its cognition], wherever that cognition occurs, it apprehends those [objects] in that way.

The same applies to cognitions: when there is a distinction and a reflective awareness of that distinction, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of a single entity with that exclusion of what does not produce such an effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.162)
Therefore, because [the capacity] exists in things, verbal testimony regarding them is based upon that [capacity];
even though it does not have as its object the exclusion of external capacities, such is the nature of that verbal testimony.
It is bound to the conceptual reflections that are based upon those [particulars];
therefore, because it is established in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the word is said to effect the exclusion of others. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.164)

That reflection of an object which appears in cognition as if it were distinct [from the word], even that is not the essence of the object; it is an error arising from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.165)

When that [universal] is denoted by the words, what part of the object is understood? And if it is not understood, the act of establishing a convention for its sake would be purposeless. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.166)
Regarding the question of which part of the object a word expresses, it is said there that it is "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha).
Yet, that mental image does not exist in the external object; how then can a word that expresses it be said to possess the object?
The effect of the recurring word is that which recurs with the object;
and that [word], though not recurring [with respect to its specific instances], is produced by the repeated practice of observation due to the non-difference of the cognition.

Furthermore, because there is the apprehension of an exclusion of others through the superimposition of that form [upon the object], it is not contradictory to state that "the meaning of a word is that very object. Pramāṇavārttika 2.169.
These cognitions produced by words have a false appearance;
nevertheless, the word functions as an exclusion (apoha) because it follows after this limit of the object. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.170.

Therefore, even at the time of convention, it is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) that is connected to the word in the hearing, conjoined with the indicated object and having its own cognition as the result. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.171.

Because it depends on the non-perception of others [i.e., other things] and because it depends on the perception of that [specific thing] in some instances, exclusion (*apoha*) is connected to the act of hearing; this is not tenable with respect to a real entity (*vastu*).
Therefore, universals and the like, as well as their connection [to objects], do not exist in the object, nor does the word apply to them;
rather, words are joined only for the purpose of excluding other things (*anyavyāvṛtti*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.173)

How can that [conceptual cognition], which has the recollection of conventions as its means and consists of the synthesis of what has been seen, exist in visual perception, which is devoid of reflection upon the prior and the subsequent? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.174)

Even when the mind is directed elsewhere, one perceives a form with the eye; the non-apprehension of its conventional designation therein is evident, as is the conceptual construction arising from it. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.175)

Conceptual constructions arise only where a word has been applied; therefore, they would proceed according to one's will and would not perceive external objects through the sense-born [cognitions]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.176)
One may perceive form as "form," but how can one perceive that cognition itself?
Since there is indeed an experience of it, how could that [experience] be non-conceptual?
By that very [cognition] experiencing itself, two conceptual constructions are not seen simultaneously;
by this, the experience of other cognitions existing at the same time is also refuted.
Furthermore, how could there be memory regarding a past object that was never apprehended?
Moreover, the cognition of one's own [past] cognition would have to be non-different in form from the cognition that discerned another [object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.179)
The cognition of an object that is past, unseen, and without a mark—by what means is that established? For in its case, there is neither perception nor inference. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.180)

If it were apprehended by a subsequent cognition that manifests its own nature—just as form and other objects are—then there would be no apprehension of the preceding cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.181)
Just as that non-conceptual experience of consciousness regarding its own object is impossible to associate with a linguistic convention, so too is any other [cognition] that is non-conceptual.
Words denote universals, and conceptual construction has that same object as its referent;
if non-conceptual [perception] were absent, how could there be the apprehension of particulars? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.183)

If there were anything non-conceptual, it would have causes identical [to those of other things]; for the difference among the natures of effects arises from the difference in their causes. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.184)
The association [of a word with its object] occurs through the recollection of convention without depending on an external object;
likewise, visual cognition functions by the power of the thing itself without depending on convention. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.185.
If form were dependent upon the recollection of convention for its appearance in sensory consciousness,
then, being unable to function without such dependence, it would be like a logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to memory alone.
Since that [cognition] arises from contact with that [object], it would be either a sensory perception or a memory;
therefore, even at a later time, it might occur in some cases due to the possibility of distraction. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.187)

If it is argued that [the cognition] is caused by both [the object and the sense organ] in succession, then [the cognition] would already exist [at the first moment], because there is no difference [between the two causes].
If it is argued that the cause of the sensory cognition is something else, then memory is likewise useless in that case as well.

Just as the recollection of a convention (*samaya-smṛti*) is accepted for the sake of establishing a similarity, a difference that is not similar must also be apprehended; what, then, would be the purpose of a recollection in that case?
When there is the apprehension of a mere generality, dependence upon particulars is not logical;
therefore, visual cognition arises in dependence upon both the eye and visible form.
Furthermore, an object is capable of producing cognition directly, just like a sense organ;
so why is it not called [a means of knowledge], since its arising depends upon both? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.191)
For a designation is applied only after observing its indicative power;
that [power] exists in the designation "sense-organ" (akṣa), and therefore its property [of being a sense-organ] should be applied.
Therefore, let the nature of the mark (*liṅga*) be applied here in this designation;
[the object] is excluded because of the exclusion of its pervading nature (*svabhāva*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.193)
That collection which is accumulated is the universal (sāmānya), and it is toward that [universal] that sensory cognition occurs;
moreover, a cognition of a universal is necessarily followed by conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Those other atoms which arise from the connection with different objects are called "aggregated" (sañcita), for they are indeed the cause for the production of cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.195)
That particularity of atoms does not exist without other atoms;
therefore, cognition that is not restricted to a single [atom] is said to have a universal as its object.
Furthermore, even though they belong to a single sense-base, multiple [atoms] are not perceived simultaneously;
for how could there be an appearance of simultaneous apprehension in the case of sesame seeds and the like when they are separated? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.197)

And here, lightness is attributed to those very [cognitions] occurring in succession; why is there no perception of non-succession? For all these cognitions are of equal duration. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.198)
Among those [cognitions], some appear to be non-sequential, while others appear to be sequential; why is this?
Therefore, it follows that this [perception] would be sequential in the apprehension of all objects. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.199)
Otherwise, how could a single form such as a variegated butterfly be perceived?
If it is argued that "that [single entity] is variegated," then this is even more variegated than that! Pramāṇavārttika 2.200.
For that which is variegated does not have a single nature, just like the form of a gem;
and the appearance of blue and other colors is the same in the case of a variegated cloth and so forth.

In that case, if only the form of the parts is seen in such a way, then you must perceive a variegated whole as something distinct from blue and the other colors, if indeed you see a variegated thing. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.202.

Of two [cognitions] characterized by having the same object, form, and time, why is one manifold in its objects and successive, while the other has a single object and is non-successive? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.203)
For it is through the very nature of cognitions that entities possess a manifold form;
if that [manifoldness] were not a factor, by what means could this establishment of distinctions be proven? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.204)
Because heterogeneous [atoms] do not initiate [a composite], there is no cognition of a "variegated" [whole] in paintings and the like;
because it lacks form, conjunction is not variegated, nor is it the locus [of variegation] due to figurative attribution. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.205)

Since each [object] is non-variegated, and since they are grasped sequentially, there is no synthesis of a variegated cognition, because multiple [objects] cannot be grasped by a single [cognition]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.206)
Therefore, [cognition] that has multiple objects would become one; thus, it is established that [perception] is free from conceptual construction.
For when one is conceptualizing one object, one perceives another as well.
If unity is not tenable for objects that appear as variegated, then how can that very cognition itself be a single entity appearing as variegated? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.208)
This is what the wise declare as established by the force of reality:
in whatever way objects are analyzed, they fall apart in that very same way. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.209.
Why would that variety not exist even in that single cognition?
If this [variety] is pleasing to objects by itself, then who are we in that matter? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.210)

Therefore, there is no appearance of grossness either in objects or in cognition, because such a nature [of grossness] has been refuted in the case of a single [atom]; it is likewise impossible even in the case of many [atoms]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.211)

This other internal portion of cognition appears as if it were external; though non-different from cognition, these two distinct appearances are a cognitive distortion (*upaplava*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.212.
In that case, through the absence of even one, both are lost.
Therefore, the reality of that [duality] is precisely its emptiness of duality.
And this establishment of the difference among entities depends upon that [conceptual differentiation];
and when that [differentiation] is a cognitive distortion, their difference is also a distortion. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.214)
There exists no characteristic that is external, consisting of the forms of the grasped and the grasper;
therefore, because they are empty of characteristics, they are revealed as being without intrinsic nature. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.215.
The specific characteristic of the aggregates and so forth is entirely conditioned by activity; and since that [activity] is not the reality, they are not distinct from it in their essential nature.

For those whose minds are overwhelmed by ignorance, a representation arises with a false aspect in dependence upon its respective conditions, just like [the perception of] a visual impairment. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.217.
And that [nature] is not cognized by any other philosophical systems, because for them it is impossible without the delusions of the grasped and the grasper. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.218)

Those who have neglected the true nature of reality, closing their eyes like an elephant, extend their investigation of external objects solely by means of worldly cognition alone. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.219)
In a variegated cognition, the blue and other [colors] are attributes of the cognition itself and do not belong to anything else;
they cannot be perceived [as external], for one who attempts to distinguish them falls back upon the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.220)
"In whatever manner a cognition appears, it manifests exactly in that way;
thus, there would indeed be a single nature for the variegated form within the mind. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.221)

If the form of a cloth and so forth were a single entity, it would likewise be non-discriminative; for one who has discarded discriminative objects does not perceive anything else that is discriminative. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.222)

What contradiction is there if many [causes], having each produced a specific excellence, could individually be the cause of a cognition, provided it is not like the case of the self, the sense-faculties, and so forth? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.223)
Apart from being a cause, there is no other such thing as "being an object of cognition. In that regard, whatever form the cognition takes, that is said to be its object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.224)
Furthermore, how could a whole (avayavin) be perceived simultaneously with its own parts?
For a cognition of a cow is never observed when the dewlap and other [parts] are not seen. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.225)
If it is also accepted that there is a comprehension of both the subordinate and the primary [aspects] simultaneously,
then neither would the object with all its parts be grasped at once, nor would it be grasped as possessing its qualities and so forth.

Because the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is dependent upon the speaker's intention, that which is presented as a subordinate element is indeed grasped by that very [intention]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.227)

Because it is not distinct from the thing itself, and because its differentiators—such as qualities—are not perceived, there would be a single cognition even for one who perceives both the prior and the subsequent. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.228)

If it is argued that the apprehension of multiplicity arises from the perception of differences in qualities and so forth, let it be so; nevertheless, there would still be a confusion of their related entities.

Since sound and the other [objects] are manifold, the simultaneous apprehension of many is established; for it is impossible to apprehend their arrangement if the arranged objects themselves are not apprehended. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.230)

When [the mind] has turned away from everything, that very multiplicity of the subject—which is inferred from the distinctions [of the objects] from which it has turned away—is its manifold nature. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.231)

These [appearances] are imagined due to the differentiation of forms within a non-conceptual mind; they are not the objects of a variegated cognition that appears variegated only occasionally. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.232.

Even though there exists whiteness and so forth, which is the object of the senses, it is not denoted by words because of the difference in their modes of cognition (*jñāna*) and forms (*rūpa*). Pramāṇavārttika 2.233.

Even if cognitions have the same object, if that [similarity] is due to their having different substrata, then how is it that the cognitions of the ear and other senses do not now have different objects? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.234)
Since the bases of the cognitions of that single object are indeed distinct, how can it have a single nature that appears with diverse forms? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.235)

Because verbal designation and conceptual construction involve the apprehension of the object of perception through the activity [of the mind], the recognition of cows and other such things is thereby precluded from being a direct perception. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.236)

Furthermore, the inference based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*) regarding the connection between a name and its conceptual construction with respect to a visible object such as a cow and so forth—concerning the universal (*jāti*) and other properties—is also refuted by this very [argument]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.237)
It has been described that even distinct perceptions, by their very nature, produce a single conceptual construction known as recognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.238)
If the mental [cognition] were to grasp what was previously experienced, it would lack the status of a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇatā*);
if it were to grasp what has not been seen, then even the blind and others would have vision of objects. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.239.
Because the past [moment] is momentary, the perception of it is not possible;
if it were non-momentary, its definition would have to include a qualification.
When the action has already been accomplished, why is another means—whether sensory or otherwise—sought, provided it does not produce any further distinction in the object? Pramāṇavārttika 2.241.

Furthermore, all cognitions produced by that [object] would arise simultaneously, because there is no difference in their being unproduced by other factors and because it is contradictory for them to depend upon that [object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.242)

Therefore, the mental consciousness (manas), which arises from the immediately preceding condition of sensory perception, apprehends a different object altogether; for that reason, it does not possess the vision of the blind.

Sensory cognition has as its cause precisely the dependence upon its own object and the object's connection [to it]; therefore, its status as having a restricted range of objects is considered to consist in its grasping only that which is other than those two. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.244.

If it is argued that an object, existing at the same time as its own cognition, could be a cooperative cause for the sensory consciousness because its activity is simultaneous with that [cognition], how could this be so? For [the object] does not have an activity at that same time. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.245)

Since that which is non-existent lacks causal capacity prior [to the effect], and since it is of no use afterward, all causes must exist prior [to their effects]; however, they do not exist simultaneously with their own cognition.

If it is asked how that which belongs to a different time can be an object of cognition, those who know logic understand its status as an object to be simply its causality, capable of imparting its form to the cognition. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.247.
For even though an effect may arise from multiple causes, that which arises imitating [one of them] is said to have "grasped" that form by means of it. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.248)
For the nature of passion and the like is impossible to conceptualize through linguistic convention, as it does not partake in anything else;
therefore, their self-awareness is not associated with verbal expression. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.249)
Since they do not themselves experience [the object], how can they know its own nature?
Some maintain that they are known by a consciousness residing in the same substratum as the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.250)
Entities possessing this or that form arise from causes possessing this or that form;
therefore, how could pleasure and the like—which arise from causes non-different from those of consciousness—not be cognition? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.251)

Just as the birth of pleasure and so forth is observed when the sense-faculties are present, suitable, and [functioning] in their respective minds, that same [condition] applies to mental cognitions as well. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.252.

Whether these [causes] exist or do not exist, neither birth nor non-birth is ever observed in the case of pleasure and the like, or of cognition; therefore, that [pleasure, etc. is not something other than those [causes].

Furthermore, the distinctions among pleasure, pain, and so forth belong specifically to those [sensations] themselves, just as the states of dullness or acuity belong to cognition itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.254)
How could that cognition, by the occurrence of which those [mental states] such as pleasure arise, abandon that object and apprehend only pleasure and the like? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.255)
If there were a perception of succession, that consciousness would not appear as uninterrupted;
if it is argued that this is due to its rapidity, then why is it not the case that there is no awareness at all, since that [rapid succession] is the same for both? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.256)
Furthermore, for one whose mind is sensory, there is no cognition of two [objects] by means of a single [sensation], because it is restricted [to its own object];
and because that capacity is not established, since [the sensation] arises from the object even in the absence of pleasure and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.257)

If the two [the cognition and the object] possessed their own distinct capacities, then pleasure would be perceived alone, just like blue and other objects, by one who does not perceive its cause. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.258)
For it is not logical that there be a cognition [of the mind] when [it] is apprehended together with the object itself;
what capacity do pleasure and so forth possess such that a cognition arising from them is not accepted? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.259)

If there were no object, then in the perception of pleasure and so forth by means of the eyes and other faculties, the distinctions such as form and the like, or woman and so forth, would never be grasped by the senses. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.260)
For when an internal object is present and capable [of producing cognition], the intellect does not perceive external things;
if it were to grasp that [external] object, there would be no awareness of pleasure and the like produced by it. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.261)

If two cognitions were to arise simultaneously, because their respective objects would be present at once, there would be the simultaneous experience of pleasure and pain when the object occurs. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.262)
Even when there is another truth as its material cause, suffering and the rest arise within cognition;
yet if it is thought that this [cognition] cannot be the material cause of what is contradictory to it, and that it is a single entity—*Pramāṇavārttika* 2.263.
By what means could there be cognition of that ignorance?
However, it is observed that [ignorance] may exercise a dominant influence even over its opposite. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.264)
Just as a single light from a lamp simultaneously effects both the impairment and the non-impairment of the visual perception of form for a night-prowler and for others. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.265)

Therefore, pleasure and the like are the perceivers of objects that appear as having been transferred into their own [form]; and for these, there is merely birth from the objects themselves. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.266)
For their very nature consists of the object, and it is experienced by them as being identical with themselves.
Therefore, there is the designation "experience of the object," while the objective support is merely its appearance as that [object]. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.267.
Someone else asserts that pleasure and so forth, which are non-conscious and external, are the objects of apprehension;
for him as well, the simultaneous apprehension of the two [the cognition and the object] is not logical.

If blue and so forth are apprehended simultaneously because they are not different in nature from pleasure and so forth, then what is it that is non-different between two cognitions that appear as distinct? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.269)
If there were no distinction in that [external object], then due to the gradations in cultivation, there would be gradations in the cognition, but not in pleasure and pain. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.270)

If it is argued that there is no contradiction even for cognition because it has pleasure and so forth as its nature, then how is it understood now that external objects have pleasure and so forth as their nature? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.271)

If [it is argued that the soul is not the perceiver] because the grasped and the grasper belong to different classes, then the person would be a non-perceiver of everything; consequently, its status as an enjoyer would be lost. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.272)
By this [argument], the relation of cause and effect is refuted;
for in the absence of the state of grasped and grasper, that [relation] would have to exist elsewhere as well, even where it is not [observed].
Therefore, those [mental factors] are indeed internal, and they are conscious because they are objects of experience.
That which does not have the nature of being experienced cannot be the experience of that [object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.274)

If it is argued that an experience which does not possess the nature of those [objects] cognizes them, then what kind of cognition could there be here other than a consciousness consisting of the forms of direct perception and memory? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.275)
Based on various objects, the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth is seen to manifest as a single [consciousness]; however, nothing else is seen in the interval between them.

If, due to contact, there were no distinction [between things], as in the case of a firebrand and the fire, then the established distinction between difference and non-difference would be destroyed for all entities. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.277)

The unity of that which has undivided sensation is established; that which is not so [i.e., lacks such unity] possesses division. If this [reason] were not a means of proof, then the proof for division would not be established. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.278)

If white, suffering, and so forth, which appear as distinct, were not distinct within cognition, then if those [cognitions] that appear non-distinct were themselves distinct, upon what would distinction and non-distinction depend? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.279)

Since even those [mental states] that are suppressed by a powerful [cognition] are seen not to be distinct at times, the establishment of the distinction between the various mental states is proven within the stream [of consciousness]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.280)
The knowledge of yogis previously mentioned is produced from meditative cultivation;
for them, it appears with perfect clarity, having shaken off the web of conceptual construction.
Those who are overwhelmed by desire, grief, fear, madness, dreams of thieves, and so forth, perceive even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.282)
For that which is bound up with conceptual construction, there is no appearance of a real object;
even in a dream, what is remembered is a memory, and it does not possess such [real] objectivity.

Even that which is unreal, such as the meditation on impurity or the totality of earth (*pṛthivī-kṛtsna*), is described as having a clear appearance and being free from conceptual construction, produced by the power of cultivation. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.284)
Therefore, whether it be real or unreal,
whatever is intensely meditated upon results, upon the completion of that meditation, in a clear and non-conceptual cognition.

In that regard, that which is consistent with reality, like an object previously determined, is accepted as direct perception (pratyakṣa) arising from the existence [of its object]; all others are distortions. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.286)
Whatever cognition apprehends a word-meaning with respect to an object, that cognition is conceptual with respect to that object.
Since its own nature (svarūpa) is not a word-meaning, it is therefore entirely direct perception (pratyakṣa) therein.
Cognition arising from a disturbance of the basis is threefold;
together with that which is non-conceptual, there are four kinds of what appear to be direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.288.
Two [types of cognition] were mentioned for the purpose of establishing that [perception] is not produced by the senses, because of the observation of error;
the statement regarding inference and so forth is for the sake of proving those two former [means of valid cognition].
In the conceptual construction that superimposes another object by relying on linguistic convention,
there is never a cause for error, because it does not follow from direct perception.
Just as this conceptualization of an imperceptible object, which consists of memory, depends upon convention and does not determine the object through direct perception; Pramāṇavārttika 2.291.
Likewise, without the recollection of what was previously experienced, there would be no cognition of jars and the like;
and that [recollection] is lost from direct perception.
The fourth [type of error] here is called "deficiency-born" (upaghātajam); therein, the term "timira" (eye-disease) is used merely as an illustration of such a deficiency. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.293)
Some maintain that even those [cognitions] are mental; however, their textual authority is contradicted by this [statement]:
"The sense faculties are also the cause of cognitions such as the perception of blue or a double moon. (294)

If it is argued that [the object] is the cause through a traditional succession, then while the domain of sensory cognition is being investigated, what relevance is there here for mental cognition? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.295)

If it is argued that the sense-organ is that which conforms to the presence or absence of the sense-faculties, then that [conformity] is the same as the case of transformation; if it is indeed this [conformity], why is it being denied?
Furthermore, like the error regarding a snake and the like, this [error] would cease even when there is a defect in the sense organs;
yet it would not cease even when the impairment of the sense organs has been removed. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.297)
Sometimes it might be projected in exactly the same way onto another mental continuum by means of expressive words;
in that case, it would depend upon the perception of what was seen and the memory [of the convention], and it would not appear with complete clarity.
Whether one is asleep or awake, whatever cognition appears clearly is non-conceptual in both cases; otherwise, it is conceptual. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.299)

Therefore, even though it is non-conceptual, its status as a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) is denied because it is deceptive; and for that reason, pseudo-perception (pratyakṣābhāsa) is said to be of two kinds.
Everything is indeed the means for accomplishing every action, for there is no means whatsoever that is not an action. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.301)
In that case, since cognition is of a uniform nature consisting merely of experience,
it must possess some internal property by which it is differentiated according to each respective object.
Even though a distinction exists within its causes, it does not belong to that [effect];
for a distinct cause cannot be the regulator of a non-distinct effect when the action is distinct. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.303)

Therefore, since the apprehension of this [object] occurs through a specific transformation of the self (*ātman*), this restriction of the object for an action is established; thus, that [apprehension] is proven by it. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.304)

It is by means of the object that cognition is made to correspond with it; for indeed, apart from the form of the object, there is no other way whatsoever for a distinction within cognition to be differentiated.
Therefore, the means for the cognition of the object of knowledge is its having the form of that object;
if the means were something else, its connection with that object would not be established. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.306)
And since that [cognition] is indeed its very self, the result is not a separate entity from it;
for it bears that [form] within itself by way of having the apprehension of the object as its nature. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.307)
Although it is itself devoid of causal agency, it appears as if active in its own operation because of that [cognition], since it is not established independently of it. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.308)

Just as in the world, because an effect arises with a nature similar to its causes, it is said that the cause "grasps" the form [of the effect], even though it is devoid of activity. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.309.

Therefore, the validity of these— namely, the observation, the contact of the sense-faculties, and the cognition of the qualifier— is not accepted with respect to the action, because they are separated from it by an interval.

Although all factors of action (kārakas) are employed with respect to an action, that which is the final differentiator of it is considered its most effective means (sādhakatama). *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.311.
Since non-moments are not the common cause of everything, such [a relation] does not exist for them.
For even when there is a difference between them, how could there be the notion "this belongs to that" for something that lacks that very nature? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.312)

By this, the rest is explained: for cognitions of qualifiers, there is no difference [between them] even when they lack that nature; or likewise, the same applies to other cognitions as well. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.313)

Even a difference in objects is not desired for both the action and its means when they have a single purpose; otherwise, the two would be redundant, and there could be no occurrence in succession. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.314)
When two parts of a cognition occur simultaneously, there is no actual relation of the proven and the means of proof;
rather, the establishment of the proven and the means of proof exists by virtue of their being the basis for that conventional determination.
Even if it were connected by its entire essence, it would be perceived only by some;
such a restriction regarding the properties [of the object] would not exist, because there is no distinction in the connection itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.316)
Even though there is no difference [between the cognition and the object], this distinction exists because that [cognition] possesses the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that this is due to mental cultivation (*saṃskāra*), [we reply] no, because even that cultivation is not established as having such a nature. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.317)
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between the action and the instrument being one and the same, this is incorrect;
for, while we admit a difference in properties, the entity itself is held to be non-different. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.318)

In this manner, the entire system of action and its factors (kriyākāraka) functions through the superimposition [of identity] upon entities, even when they are not intended to be distinct. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.319)
The cognition of an object is precisely this direct perception, this individual awareness;
by what means could that [perception] not be the cognition of the object, since it possesses the same form as it? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.320)
Now, where is that experience [of it]? This very point is being investigated:
by what means do those atoms produce a cognition that has the appearance of something gross? *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.321.
Therefore, its having the form of the object is not real; being fallible, it is incapable of establishing the existence of the cognition of that [object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.322)

If having the same form as that [object] and being produced from it were the defining characteristics of being cognized, then a subsequent cognition having the same object would be cognized [by the preceding one]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.323)

Where there is a determinative cognition such as "this was seen" or "this was heard," that [cognition] itself is not the direct experience; rather, it is the means of immediate proximity (*pratyāsatti*) that is being investigated. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.324.
That by which there is the seeing of the visible and the seer is considered to be that seeing;
this determination regarding the seer is based upon the relationship between those two. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.325)
That [self] is its experience, and it belongs to no one else;
even its being cognized through direct perception is its very nature as that [self]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.326)
There is nothing else to be experienced by it, nor is there any other experience of it;
because the same objection applies to that as well, it is that very [cognition] which shines forth by itself. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.327.
Its nature consists of blue and other such forms, and it is that very experience;
because it experiences blue and so forth, it is known as the experience of its own nature, even though it is [simply] the experience of itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.328)
Just as light is accepted as illuminating its own nature because it manifests through identity with that nature, so too is cognition the knower of itself. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.329.
And when that [consciousness] has another object as its cognizable, the roles of the cognized and the cognizer are difficult to establish;
it appears to the deluded as having the forms of both the cognized and the cognizer, even though it lacks such forms.

This [cognition] has been established as such because it is a distortion consisting of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender with distinct characteristics, just like the difference in cognitions of [illusory] hair and the like. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.331.
Whenever that [self-awareness] occurs, it is not characterized by the relationship of the object to be apprehended and the apprehending subject;
since at that time there is no other cognition, self-awareness is held to be the fruit. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.332.
If an external object were experienced, what fault would there be? None at all. Why then was it said: "That external object is experienced"? Pramāṇavārttika 2.333.
If cognition possesses that form, then it exists as something qualified by that form;
this deserves to be investigated whether [that form] comes from an external object or from something else. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.334.

Because that which is devoid of the adjunct of perception is not apprehended, whereas it is apprehended when perception is apprehended, it is perception itself that appears as blue; there is no external object whatsoever. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.335.
For someone, something specific serves as the awakener of an internal latent impression (*vāsanā*);
therefore, the restriction of cognitions is due to that, and not in dependence upon an external object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.336)
Therefore, there is a single [cognition] possessing two forms, which is thus experienced and remembered; the awareness of this [cognition] having a dual aspect is the result.
When another object, whether desired or undesired, is held to be the cause of a cognition, then there is likewise the experience of that [object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.338)

When cognition possesses an object because the object is established within a portion of the cognition itself, then that very experience of the self [of the cognition] is the determination of the object. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.339.
If the self were of the form of the desired [object], or if it were experienced otherwise, then the object—whether desired or undesired—would be known by that [self]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.340)

Even though an external object exists, it is determined by its very nature to be exactly as it is experienced; otherwise, there would be the fault of it having multiple natures. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.341)

If the external does not exist, of what could there be cognition? If, having no other recourse, it is the nature [of consciousness itself], why is it not considered to be the external itself? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.342)
Even if there were a means [of perception], there would be no experience of the two as distinct entities.
If it is argued that this is due to the obscuration by the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), then the cognition would not be subject to the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.343)

How indeed could that [cognition], which presents a manifold entity as having a single nature, be a perceiver of the object, since it does not perceive [the object] as it truly is? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.344)

If conceptual constructions, which manifest as desirable and undesirable objects, were not sensory cognitions, then one would not observe the non-connection of mental states even toward that which is undesirable. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.345)
Therefore, even when the object of cognition is external, it is logical that self-awareness is the result;
for the determination of the object occurs exactly according to its own nature.

The appearance of that object alone is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not even the cognizing self, although it exists, because it does not have another as its purpose; thus it depends upon external objects. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.347)
Because that object-nature, as it has been deposited in the cognition, is determined to be "thus deposited" by virtue of the self-awareness [of that cognition]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.348)

Thus, the cognition of the object is itself accepted [as the result], since the nature of the object is not perceived; therefore, the object as it is presented to the intellect is the means of cognition, and that [cognition] is its activity. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.349)

In whatever way that object is settled, in that same way it manifests; because the stability of the object consists in its identity with that [cognition], self-awareness is also considered to be awareness of the object. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.350.

Therefore, even when there is a difference in objects, self-awareness is not the result; for it has been stated in the investigation of intrinsic nature that the cognition of the object is identical with [the cognition] itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.351)

Even if an object appears in such a way [as it is], or even in a different way, since the object is still the cause of that cognition, the object's status as a cognizable (prameyatā) is accepted. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.352.

In whatever way it may be, how can there be a grasping of an object by that which appears while having abandoned the form of that object? Truly, I too do not understand such a thing. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.353)

Although it is undivided, the nature of cognition appears as if possessed of the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness, due to the distorted vision of those whose perception is inverted.

Just as for those whose senses are overwhelmed by mantras and the like, shards of clay and other such things appear in a completely different way, even though they are devoid of that [apparent] form. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.355)
For they are seen in that very way by one whose vision is unimpaired;
or just as even a small object is seen from afar in deserts.

And this establishment of the object of cognition, the means of cognition, and the result is performed according to how things appear, even though the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the consciousness [of them] do not exist [as distinct entities]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.357)
Otherwise, how could the aspects of a single entity that appears in various forms be real? For that would entail the loss of its unity. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.358)
Furthermore, because the distinctness of one thing from another would be lost, there is no non-difference [of the object] from the perception of its form;
for, perceiving the non-difference of the form, the intellect determines the non-difference [of the object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.359)
That form by which entities are characterized does not exist in reality, because neither a single nor a manifold form is found in them. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.360.
In the world, an error arises from the perception of similarity by means of determining identity in that which lacks that nature; but here, that is not the case. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.361)
Because not even a single person of that nature is seen in this world, there exists this [other kind of doubt] as well, which arises from an internal disturbance. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.362)
By its very nature, that [cognition] arises from a defect and appears erroneously,
independent of the perception of similarity and so forth, just like the vision of one suffering from cataracts and the like.
In that regard, the discernment of cognition is considered to be its subjective aspect;
because of their identity, it is the self-cognition of that [cognition], and therefore it is the means of establishing it.
In that regard, concerning the cognition whose object is the self, just as there is the experience of desire and so forth—
this establishment of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result should be applied everywhere.
In that case as well, because they consist of experience, they are capable of being cognized by their own self-awareness;
thus, that capacity is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the self is the object of cognition (*prameya*), and self-awareness is the result (*phala*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.366)

The nature of determination, which is reckoned as the aspect of the apprehender within itself, is called "capacity"; and this self-cognition is declared to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.367.
For every consciousness indeed arises from objects;
even when other causes are present, it somehow bears the form of the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.368)

Just as, when the birth of offspring occurs due to causes such as food and time, it takes on the form of one of the parents and not that of any other; so too [is the case with cognition]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.369)

Although it is equal [to other objects] by virtue of being their cause, the status of being an object is held to belong to that [specific] aspect among other objects; in the absence of that [aspect], it would not exist.

Even if the mind possesses an object, there might still be a suspicion that it has the form of a non-object, provided that the apprehension of a past object is established as having a dual nature and being self-cognizing. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.371)
Because it is differentiated by the appearance of blue and other qualities, the universal (*jāti*) would not be unitary;
furthermore, that [universal] would not be a universal if it were impermanent, and how could that which is eternal be something produced? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.372)
Names and so forth were refuted previously; this is not the sequence for those things that possess real referents.
Because they follow mere whim, the power of the referent is not established.

If memory is such a kind of cognition, and its arising occurs from experience, yet that [experience] is devoid of the form of the object, how can it [memory] now possess that [form]? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.374)

An entity does not arise from an object because that [object] is absent; even if there were such an experience, that form would not belong to the object, because it is distinct from the clear form [of the object].
If another were to perceive that form as distinct [from the cognition], then it would be perceived eternally within the self; and yet, it is not so perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.376)
If there were a connection with each [moment] individually, a mental synthesis (pratisandhi) would not be possible;
for such synthesis consists in the speaker’s and the listener’s minds being directed toward a single object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.377)

If it is argued that there is a single conventional usage for those two things—which do not appear as such [i.e., as identical]—due to their similarity, then how could an object whose nature is distinct be grasped? In that case, cognition would be devoid of its object.

And that [object] is subsequently connected by a cognition of it—a cognition which, through a single specific form, relies upon both parts by means of experiential awareness (*anubhavavijñāna*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.379)
Otherwise, how could that which is not of such a nature ascend into cognition? For it is logical that cognition possesses a single form; thus it has been stated. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.380)
For its form as an object and its own form as a self-nature are indeed distinguished by a third cognition from that second one. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.381)
If it is argued that the recollection of the object within the recollection of the cognition occurs through a confusion based on their being the effect of the same object,
then that same confusion would also occur in the case of the [recollection of] light and mental attention.
If all effects were apprehended in that same way as their causes, then a jar would not be remembered apart from the potter and other such factors. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.383)

Since it is due to this excellence that cognition becomes the locus of connection with the object, how could that [excellence] be anything other than similarity (sārūpya), given the observation of twins and the like? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.384)

For if the first [moment] were of neither nature and the second were established as having only one nature, then the second would not be distinguished by the reflective consciousness (*parāmarśacetas*). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.385)
The second [cognition], which consists of the synthesis of objects, then takes as its support the cognition appearing before it in the form of blue and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.386)
Otherwise, only the first [cognition] would be connected [to the object], because the object exists;
for subsequent cognitions have no perceived relationship with the preceding object.

Since an object being perceived at one and the same time is necessarily [perceived] together with the cognition, by what characteristic could its distinctness from that [cognition] be established? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.388)

And difference would be perceived by erroneous cognitions, just as [multiplicity] is seen in the non-dual moon; there is no rule of simultaneous perception for two distinct things, such as blue and yellow. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.389)

Nothing is observed that does not cognize an object, nor is there any cognition of what is not an object; since that which is being cognized is seen [in both cases], there is no distinction between the two. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.390)

Therefore, since an object appearing at the time of cognition cannot be avoided [from being so], its non-difference from the cognition would follow; thus, there would be an inference based on a difference in causes. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.391.

If one were not to state the restriction [of sensory cognitions] based on the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), then sensory cognitions would not arise even when other causes are present. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.392)

The production of a sprout from a seed, and the establishment of fire from smoke—such is the status of causal and indicative relations, even though they rely upon external objects. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.393)

If it is argued that those [universals], appearing as the form of that [particular] and having a fixed association with it, are postulated by relying upon cognitions, then what contradiction is there? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.394)

Smoke might be something not produced by fire; thus, there would be no cognition of the cause from its effect. Or, even if it were a cause, how could there be a certain cognition [of that specific cause]? Pramāṇavārttika 2.395.

Even in that case, a cognition appearing as smoke leads only to another cognition appearing as fire—due to a latent impression (vāsanā) potent enough to awaken it—not to actual fire itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.396)

Therefore, smoke, which contains within it the latent impressions (vāsanā) suitable for that [cognition], manifests a cognition appearing as smoke within the mental continuum; thus, smoke is not non-causal.
There is this doctrine of the learned, which is described by relying on external objects:
duality of form is established because of the rule of simultaneous cognition. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.398.

Cognition is observed to exhibit a variety of appearances—such as being sharp, dull, or blurred—with respect to a single object, depending on the differences among the sense faculties. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.399)
Since the object has an undifferentiated nature, the mind would have to be of a single form;
if it were [to perceive] that object through all [its aspects], then it would not possess the appearance of that object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.400)
For that [cognition], which arises based on an object and imitates its form,
there may be differentiation from another [object] through some particular aspect.
For in this way, although a son resembles his father by depending upon him,
he nevertheless maintains a distinction from his father in certain respects.
Those with dull vision perceive the halo of a lamp or similar object as having the form of a peacock’s eye, shimmering with blue and red. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.403)
If that [cognition] does not have an external form, what is the objection regarding one with clear vision?
And how could a perceiver who sees a real object have impaired sense faculties? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.404)

When his eye, which transcends the senses, has been purified of darkness and clearly perceives an object visible to other eyes, how could that same object again be unclear to him? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.405)

It is understood that, apart from the mental attention toward light and the eye, there is the power of one [specific factor] as the cause; therefore, nothing else is the cause, and how could that which is not a cause be the object? *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.406.
If that very [object] were the cause of cognition, why would it depend on a lamp?
Since cognition occurs by means of the lamp alone, neither [the object nor the lamp] is the cause.
It is not logical for a thing to be both manifest and unmanifest based on distinctions such as distance and proximity;
if it were so due to differences in illumination, that would apply equally to the opening and closing of the eyes.

Whether it be a perception or a non-perception, the view is the same; there is no subtle part whatsoever of it that is not seen by one who is dull-sighted. Therefore, if there were any distinction [between them], it would not be perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.409)
If the external object were a single unity, how could there be a distinction between its being seen and not being seen?
If it were manifold, being divided into atoms, how could there be a distinction between its being seen and not being seen? *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.410.

If the difference in the appearance [of cognition] due to the distinction between dullness and clarity constitutes a difference in the cognitions, then how can that which is undifferentiated appear as differentiated when another thing is different? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.411)
Even that [faint] light is dull; why then is it not obscured here?
This attenuation of light exists elsewhere as well, yet there is no lack of attenuation [in the case of the sun]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.412)
And if that light were extremely close, it would be very clearly and distinctly perceived;
even in that case, if another form were to arise depending on the unseen [karmic force], [it would still be perceived]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.413)
Because they would mutually obstruct one another, there would consequently be a destruction of their luminosity;
thus, only a single [light] would be seen, provided it were not obstructed by the others. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.414)

If a single person were to perceive a form clearly or unclearly due to the unseen [force of karma], then what could that unseen force accomplish, since it is not by means of it that benefit or harm exist? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.415)
Therefore, consciousness, arising according to its causes and depending upon the object, bears a diversity of appearances; all other views are the fallacious arguments of the dull-witted.
Because knowledge, words, and lamps—whether perceptible or otherwise—are momentary, they perish as soon as they have acted as the producers of their subsequent effects. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.417)

How can there be manifestation of that which is non-existent, since it provides no assistance to anything other than cognition? If it is argued that all objects would be manifested upon the manifestation of one, provided there were a restriction based on their cause; Pramāṇavārttika 2.418.

This conceptual construction also [occurs] in cognition; however, because cognition has the appearance of the object, it may be said that "it manifests that [object]," even in the absence of that [external object], since it is produced by it.
Furthermore, another object does not produce a form [in cognition] because it does not assist [it], since they arise simultaneously.
If it is manifested without producing a cognition through its own form, how could it exist?
