Even an object such as a diamond or a crystal, being stable and independent of anything else, would produce cognitions of itself for the entire world simultaneously and equally. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.421)
"Those [causes] become its auxiliary and supportive conditions in succession;
they say there is a difference [in the entity] at every moment. That same fault applies here as well, just as before. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.422)
No one disputes that cognition possesses the nature of identity [with its object];
its having the form of the object is established, and that too is proven by recollection. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.423)

When this [object] has not been experienced through differentiation and remains undivided by its own objective domains, the cognition "it is thus" and not "it is not thus" would not be differentiated. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.424)
Nor does mere experience distinguish any difference;
for a cognition that lacks clarity regarding the difference cannot be discerning, just as in the case of [the perception of] *yama* and other such [identical twins]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.425)

Self-awareness is also established for the most part by the proof of its dual nature, because at that time, the appearance which constitutes its own form is perceived as being aware. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.426)

If cognition is ceased by a mental state (*dhi*) possessing that same form, how can there be experience? And since that [mental state] does not know its own form, all experience would be utterly destroyed. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.427)
And that cognition appears as if directed outward, manifesting as the appearance of an object;
whereas the awareness that apprehends the intellect is always inwardly directed toward the self.

That which appears as an object to someone does not know even that [object]; otherwise, the cognition of all similar things would mutually reach one another. If it is argued that the intellect knows the object because it possesses its form, then in that case, cognition is not something that possesses a form. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.430)
That experience itself does not have similarity as its cause;
rather, it would be the basis for the established distinction between action and object in the world. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.431)

The designation "experienced" applies to blue and so forth due to the cognitive distortion of superimposing the awareness of its own nature and its qualities; it does not apply to an experience that has a separate essence from the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.432)
If cognition possesses a form such as blue and so forth, what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) could there be for an external object?
If cognition does not possess a form such as blue and so forth, how could that [object] be its experience? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.433)

When its nature as consciousness is established by itself alone and is not dependent upon similarity [to the object], for what purpose is it brought forward [by another means]? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.434)
Nor is there equality in every respect, because that would entail the consequence of [all] being ignorance;
nor is everything known by everyone through some part [of it]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.435)
Just as the experience of blue and so forth is considered [to occur] because of its having the nature of blue and so forth,
so too there would be an experience of that [cognition] because it has the nature of experience.

If it is argued that the determination "experience has not been experienced" is meaningful and therefore free from fault, [we reply] that this is not the case, for such a determination does not always exist even with respect to an object.
Or why would it not exist in the experience itself, given that existence is tied to being present?
Furthermore, this [cognition] appears even when something white or the like is being perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.438)

That cognition which has the form of the manifestation of white and so forth is clearly a male [subject]. Is that [cognition] of a nature other than the manifestation of white and so forth, or is it of its own nature? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.439)
If the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) does not manifest its own form, how can it manifest the white [color]?
Manifestation is cognition; if that is not manifested, the entire world remains unmanifested. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.440)

Because the same fault would follow even if one individual were manifested by another individual, how could that [individual] distinguish [the object] through perception when its relation [to the word] is unknown? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.441)
Because when one of two things is perceived, there is no perception of the second;
for the certainty that "this has been seen" occurs only when both are seen in conjunction.

If it is argued that when a cognition possessing a form is perceived by another cognition, the term "seen" applies there because of their similarity of form, then self-awareness is established for that which possesses such similarity of form.
Furthermore, how can that which does not know its own nature know the nature of another?
Moreover, the claim that cognition [occurs] due to similarity has already been refuted.

If there is a grasping of similarity only between two things that have been seen, and one has not previously seen the object, how can he determine its similarity with the perception? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.445)
For one who does not even desire similarity [between object and cognition], there is no perception of both;
thus, the discussion regarding whether the object is known or the cognition is known has come to an end.
Now, if it is its own nature [that is cognized], then that [nature] must manifest by itself; for if it were not manifest, the object would remain unmanifested. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.447)
By this, those who— on the view of one who does not know the self— assert that cognition is imperceptible because no object whatsoever is perceived, have also had their position refuted.

Due to differences in their basis, object, and practice, these cognitions function differently; they are nothing other than cognitions distinguished by pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.449.
These [objects] are directly perceived, and nothing else distinct from them is discerned;
if that cognition were known by another means, then even a stranger would experience these [objects].
If cognition knows only that which arises from it and appears as such, and nothing else,
then for anyone who perceives an object, these two [the object and its appearance] must necessarily exist.
If, however, it does not arise, then that cognition appearing as such would be without an object; and if it is not apprehended, the universal [would likewise be non-existent]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.452)
It is said that it is not apprehended, yet it is not some kind of real entity.
Therefore, this appearance of an object is nothing other than that very cognition.
If it is argued that once those who know the nature of direct perception have attained [this knowledge], they nevertheless grasp those [objects] again,
yet this is not direct perception— then from what source does this distinction between two things that have the same object arise?

If it is argued that the restriction of cognition arises from its connection with an unseen factor (adṛṣṭa) or a single object, then no one else would ever perceive that object; furthermore, the distinction between cognitions has already been refuted.

Furthermore, those yogins who perceive the pleasure and so forth of another through direct perception would themselves become afflicted in that same way, since their experience would be identical. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.456)

If it is argued that suffering does not arise for them because of the absence of contact between the objects and the sense faculties—and thus suffering born from those [faculties] does not occur—it is not the case that there is no arising of suffering at all. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.457)
It is indeed the sensation of suffering that gives rise to the cognition of suffering;
for it is not the case that suffering and so forth, when not being sensed, can be the cause of affliction or benefit. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.458)
When pain itself, appearing in its own nature, is suffering, then the cognition that takes it as its object is not [itself] suffering; thus it is not applied in that way. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.459)
Because of that [distinction], for all cognition, there is a distinction between the objective support and the experience;
the objective support consists in the conformity with the object, while the self-experience is itself manifest.

Moreover, in the absence of direct perception, the cognition of [the object] would have to arise from a logical mark (liṅga); and that [mark] could be either the sense organ, the object, the cognition itself, or even the preceding mental attention (manaskāra). (Pramāṇavārttika 2.461)
In this causal complex, there is no other related entity;
for no capacity is observed therein, and the sense organ is not [the cause] because of its deviation. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.462)
Likewise, the object, the cognition, and the mental attention—these and the resulting knowledge are not established.
That which is unestablished cannot function as a logical mark (liṅga), nor is the manifestation of the object considered to be mere consciousness.

Surely that very [manifestation] is the sign (liṅga), for it is knowledge; by this, the manifested object has been described. For if the manifestation itself were not experienced, there could be no ascertainment of the object's being manifested. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.464)

Alternatively, if it is claimed that manifestation is some specific quality of the object itself, there is no such quality whatsoever belonging to an object that is devoid of arising and perishing. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.465)
Alternatively, if that [momentariness] is desired as the probandum, it follows that momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) must be established.
And that [destruction] would have to be either known or unknown; for only what is known can serve as a logical mark (liṅga).
If cognition is not itself determined, how can it be known that "this object has been cognized"?
Furthermore, how can that [object] be a means of knowledge if it is not determined as having been cognized? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.467)
For things whose seeing has not been witnessed are never seen by another seer;
since that distinction exists even when there is seeing by another, there would be the realization of one's own cognition.
Therefore, inferential cognition does not arise from an object-property alone that is independent of its own property;
for what property of the object could there be other than the property of its own cognition?
The cause is apprehended through direct perception as producing [an effect] similar to its own kind;
from what source, then, could there be a distinction in that cognition? Moreover, that which is born from something else would be inconstant.
Apart from the five objects such as form, the sense faculties, and the act of apprehension, no other effect of that [cognition] is perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.471)
In that regard, among the five objects, not even one of the two [types of] imperceptible [objects] is observed;
for that which arises from the perception of form could not otherwise occur as a distinct possibility.
To say that what is thus unperceived is the "logical mark" (liṅga) is utterly contrary to common experience;
for even when the mark exists, one does not see it together with that [object] which is to be inferred. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.473)
For how can a cognition be a logical mark (*liṅga*), since a mark does not reveal that which has not been perceived?
Therefore, it must be described as being already established prior to that very mark. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.474)
If that [second cognition] is also to be established by another example, there would be an infinite regress;
thus, the establishment of the object is from the cognition, and not from the object of that [cognition] in any way whatsoever. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.475)
If that [inference] is not established, the object itself remains unestablished;
for one perceives the cognition directly and [subsequently observes] its effects, such as purposeful action and speech. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.476)
Furthermore, there would be no inference of another's mind, because [the relationship] is not perceived in oneself;
for the connection [between the sign and the object] is not established, as the mental cognition and the object serving as the logical mark (liṅga) are unproven.
Or how could cognition be manifested by another cognition for you?
Since both are of an unmanifest nature, they are equal; how then can there be the relationship of the manifestor and the manifested? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.478)
How is there a manifestation of the object? Through the transfer of its form into the illumination.
And that illumination, possessing that very form, manifests by itself. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.479.
If it is accepted in that way, then cognition is established as self-cognizing when it is cognized by another cognition;
otherwise, the object would also possess properties identical to those of the cognition.
Thus, our own intellect, being of the nature of luminosity, shines forth by itself;
another object, however, shines forth as luminous within it through the transference of its form.
For even when there is similarity, another cognition is not considered to be manifested by that [first cognition];
rather, the object, being self-luminous, manifests itself in its own form.
Just as in the case of two lamps, or a lamp and a jar, the conventional usage based upon them is extended through the distinction between the manifested and the manifestor. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.483.

The certainty that "it was not seen" does not arise from the mere presence of the object and the sense faculty; therefore, one must state the perception of something else [the mind] as the cause of this [certainty]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.484)
If cognition were perceived by another [cognition], the self-cognition of memory would also be established;
otherwise, there would be no apprehension of long [sounds] and so forth, because many moments do not persist.

If the cognition were to appear all at once while the sequence remains untraversed, then the phoneme would be without sequence and not long; how, then, could that which possesses a sequence be non-sequential? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.486)
The constituent parts of the phonemes, though not merging with one another, would assist [the cognition];
thus, the sound would arise as it increases from its initial state up to the final moment. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.487)
If [cognition] were apprehended out of sequence, there would be no sequential cognition at the end;
nor could cognition itself persist, because it would not remain once its subsequent object has been established. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.488)
If it does not perish by itself in its own place, it would likewise not perish later;
this same fault applies even to the persistence of phonemes that arise simultaneously and without succession.
Since it arises from a single effort, subsequent efforts would be useless;
this same fault applies even to the manifestation of phonemes.

If that [long object] were grasped by multiple cognitions, then the cognition undergoing that process would itself be experienced; yet that [cognition] does not grasp the long [object], and thus there would be no memory of the cognition of length. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.491)

Furthermore, if there were a distinct cognition for each [sound], then upon hearing those sounds, there would be no appearance of continuity, and the synthesis [of them] has already been refuted. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.492)
If one who hears [the sounds] as discrete still experiences an uninterrupted delusion,
then there would also be an uninterrupted delusion even when two short vowels are uttered.
When the visual perception [of the object] has ceased, there can be no uninterrupted superimposition by means of the sense organ;
for otherwise, it would follow that all sensory cognitions are false. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.494)
For even the final phoneme, whose duration is equal to a blink of an eye, comes to rest through a successive connection with multiple atoms. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.495)
The time required for the displacement of a single atom is considered the smallest unit of time, a moment (kṣaṇa);
and since cognition is momentary, it apprehends the phonemes in succession.

Thus, even regarding color and so forth, every cognition—even one that appears as uninterrupted—would otherwise be false with respect to its object, even if it appears as interrupted. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.497)
And that [cognition] which combines entities elsewhere due to a sensory aberration, being confused regarding their distinct characteristics, is conceptual memory. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.498)
How could that [cognition] which is associated with verbal expression have a clear manifestation?
It has been analyzed that there is no application of words to what is grasped by the senses. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.499)

Even for one who perceives with the senses that [the object] is interrupted, if conceptual construction were to join together the object and its cognition as they appear continuously, [there would be no contradiction]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.500)
If there is a subverting factor (bādhaka), then how can it be said that [the cognition] is interrupted when there is a valid reason?
If you say it is because of the restriction of the capacities of cognitions, from what does that [restriction] arise? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.501)
If it is argued that [simultaneity is not perceived] because cognitions are not seen simultaneously, then this very point is what is being investigated:
there would be a restriction of the capacity of those [cognitions] toward objects of the same class. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.502)

For indeed, conceptual constructions (vikalpas) arising in succession are correctly perceived; by this [it is refuted] that one who imagines recognition (pratyabhijñāna) regarding an object present before the eyes [is valid]. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.503.
One might also imagine that [an object] has a clear manifestation as if it were directly perceived, but that too is refuted;
for even in the case of [illusions such as] hair-nets, eye-diseases, lamps, and the like, there is a clear manifestation. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.504)
Even when a difference is perceived, how could the perceptual cognition be of such a nature [as to perceive identity]?
Therefore, the determination of the oneness of phonemes and so forth does not arise from recognition.

Without the recollection of what was previously experienced and the superimposition of its properties, the cognition "this is that very same thing" does not exist; how then could it arise from that [sense-faculty]?

Furthermore, the simultaneous occurrence of the cognition of an object and the awareness [of that cognition] is impossible, because the two appearances of the object and the cognition of the object are not perceived as distinct. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.507)
For cognition does not consist of the appearance of an object, nor is there merely an external object;
because if the object of apprehension were of a single form, it would follow that there is no distinction [between them]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.508)

How could those two—the object and the cognition of the object—which were not distinguished by a clearly perceived difference at the time of their awareness, be remembered separately later on? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.509)
Even if experience arises sequentially, this fault of questioning how there can be a diversity of appearances for the object and the mind remains difficult to remove. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.510.
First, there is the cognition of the object, and from that follows the cognition of the non-existence of the object;
for a cognition that is purely [self-referential] could not be a cognition of an object. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.511)
For indeed, the form of blue and so forth is perceived as one, and the cognition as another;
however, within the cognition that has the appearance of blue, no further cognition is perceived.

If there were an experience by means of another cognition, then there would likewise be a memory of that; by what, then, is the awareness of that [second cognition] known? If it is by yet another, then this same [infinite regress] follows.
Who produces this continuous chain of those who possess knowledge?
If it were the preceding cognition itself, there would be no transition to another object.

Without having grasped that preceding cognition—which has attained the status of being an object of apprehension, which is proximate, and which is the producer—how could a subsequent cognition grasp another [object]? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.515)

And since that [cognition] is fixed in its own nature for the production of knowledge within itself, what other external factor indeed could obstruct it, which is internal by nature? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.516)

For even when an external object is present, it is not capable of obstructing that [cognition]; otherwise, no one would experience cognition while an object is in its proximity. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.517)
Since there is no state whatsoever in which an object is not present [to consciousness], memory—whose root has been uprooted—is also utterly destroyed; such is the brilliant doctrine.

For those conceptual constructions regarding the past and so forth, in which there is no presence of an object, reflection upon that object would vanish due to the absence of any means of transition [to it]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.519)

If the transition to another object occurs gradually due to the exhaustion of the capacity to produce self-cognition, then how can that [subsequent cognition] be a cognition of an object? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.520)
When the capacity [of the preceding cognition] has perished, there is no subsequent cognition without the preceding cognition;
for when the knowledge is impaired by its attachment to another object, the arising of further knowledge does not occur. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.521)

Even when there is the simultaneous arising of a different type [of cognition], another [cognition] does not arise because of the impairment caused by a single, more powerful mind that has been produced. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.522)
Otherwise, one would not expect the equality of one mental state with another;
even the sequential arising of mental cognitions must be established as being dependent [on such a cause]. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.523.

If, because the mind is unitary, another [cognition] does not arise when it is attached to one [object] due to the non-arrival of the other, then no other cognition would ever arise, since they arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, since they would be equal in their constant state of equilibrium, there would either always be no further arising [of cognition], or birth [of cognition] would occur all at once for those things produced merely by the conjunction of the self and the mind. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.525)

If the action were one and the same, how could a lamp be perceived by many? Even if it occurred successively, it would not be capable [of producing multiple perceptions], since there is no difference in its state even later on. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.526)

If it is argued that the body and the person are thus expressed through their formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*), from what source does that restriction arise? If it is said to be from cognition, let it be as you agree. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.527)
There is no apprehensibility other than [the capacity for] producing [cognition]; production is the defining characteristic of the apprehensible.
For there is no light that is unapprehensible, nor is there [such a thing] in the partless due to its subtlety and so forth.
There would be a loss of the capacity for being an object of cognition, but not of that which consists in the nature of producing [a cognition];
for indeed, in the definition of being an object of cognition, there is no other production than this. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.529)
For the form and so forth cannot otherwise be the cause of the cognition directly;
what other restriction could there be for its existence apart from the characteristic of being an object of apprehension? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.530)
Since that [object] also exists for the intellect, it too is established as being existent;
the perception of the object and its appropriation is the defining characteristic of the grasping mind.

Thus, for one of purified intellect, the consideration of the characteristic of the apprehended object regarding form and so forth, as well as the mind itself, is the inconceivable state of the yogis. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.532.

In that case, by becoming subtle and so forth, the object of apprehension would reach a state of non-apprehensibility; what has arisen in the cognition subsequently that was not present before? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.533)

Therefore, when there is the apprehension of its own cognition, that very state of being the immediate cause of the mind is itself the state of being the object; hence, there is no cognition of anything other than that.

Even in the absence of multiple powers, an entity does not produce multiple effects by its very nature; this has been stated [previously], for it would not follow that [the effect] arises from more than one [cause]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.535)
Nothing arises from a single cause; rather, everything arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
It has been stated that a single [effect] may belong to two complexes, and thus it is produced by many.
If a subsequent cognition were to apprehend the object only after the preceding one,
then two expressions would always occur simultaneously, despite being observed to follow a sequence.

Because the preceding and succeeding objects appear within a single moment of thought, each [object] would appear twice, and the self as well as its cognition would each appear once, due to their being manifest. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.538)
If the final [moment of consciousness] is not experienced when shifting to another object,
it follows that there would be no experience of any [objects], just as in the case of what is experienced by another.

If that which is directly perceived by one's own experience has not been experienced by others, from what source is that self-experience established, by virtue of which it is stated thus? Pramāṇavārttika 2.540.
For one who desires the manifestation of a manifestation, there would be the non-establishment of the cause of manifestation;
yet if this world were manifest even when the manifestation itself is unestablished, then everything would be manifest. *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.541.
The third chapter, on inference for oneself, together with the author’s own commentary:
"The logical reason is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) that is pervaded by a part of it; it is of exactly three kinds."
Other than those [valid reasons], the rest are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) because they lack the necessity of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).
A cause is [established] by as many essential natures of the effect as are inseparably connected to it;
likewise, in the case of an essential nature, an existent thing is a reason when that nature follows upon the mere existence [of the subject].
The non-operation of the means of valid cognition has non-existence as its result;
however, in some cases, depending on a distinction of causes, it has the cognition of non-existence as its result. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.3)

The non-apprehension of an object is fourfold: the establishment and non-establishment of two contradictory effects, and the establishment and non-establishment of the states of being a cause for two things whose natures are perceptible. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.4)
When an apprehension of a cause that is contradictory to that [effect] is employed, it is inconclusive if there is an absence of contradiction between the two causes. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.5)
Even in the case of an effect that is contrary [to what is expected], dependence on place, time, and so forth is required;
otherwise, it would be inconclusive, like ashes used as a means to prove the absence of cold.
When a foot is inferred from the body by means of a complete causal complex,
that [inference] is described as an inference of essential nature (svabhāva), because it does not depend on any other distinct entity.

In a case where there is a continuous transformation of the potencies of the causal complex toward its fruit, there is uncertainty regarding the effect, because the possibility of an obstruction exists. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.8.

The cognition of color and so forth, which depend on a single causal complex, occurs through the inference of the properties of the cause, just as [the presence of] fuel is inferred from smoke. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.9)
Without the activity of a capacity, there is no essence; that [activity] itself is the cause of others.
Thus, the cognition of things belonging to a single past time arises from the mark of their effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.10)

When the production of an effect is inferred from a cause that is incomplete, that inference is like the "residual" (śeṣavat) type because of its lack of necessity, just like the inference of passion from the body. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.11)

Knowledge of a cause based merely on not seeing it in the absence [of the effect], due to observing a general similarity of the effect, is a fallacy of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), just like [inferring] passion from speech. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.12)
Nor is there non-deviation from the counter-example (vipakṣa) by mere non-perception, because deviation is possible—just as in the case of rice being cooked in a pot. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.13)

When the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is demonstrated merely by the non-perception [of the probans] in that [subject], it is illustrated as "the remainder" (śeṣavat), because that [non-perception] is a cause for doubt. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.14)
Therefore, he has described the ascertainment of the reason in all three aspects by way of its opposition to the unestablished, the contrary, and the deviant. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.15)

Furthermore, that statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) which [is made] by way of a counter-example where the deviant [reason] is absent—if its purpose is merely the non-observation [of the reason in the counter-example], then that is understood even without it being stated. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.16)

And it is not the case that something does not exist simply because of the statement "it does not exist"; rather, if that logical principle by which its non-existence is made known is absent, then it is understood that it does not exist.
If cessation [of doubt] were to occur through mere non-perception, would the "remainder" (śeṣavat) inference not be fallacious?
Even a negative-only (vyatirekin) reason would exist; thus, the application of the charge of "unestablished" (asiddhi) need not be stated.
The exclusion of a particular [object] would be the cause [of its non-existence] because it is not perceived.
If it is argued that there is sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then such a non-existence does not exist at present.

Likewise, in other cases as well, sublation by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) may be possible; for the non-perception of what is not seen would contradict the perceived logical connection with touch. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.20)

The potencies of substances are seen to differ due to differences in place and other factors. Therefore, it is not logical to determine the presence of a potency in one case based on its observation in another. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.21)

Is that very same non-apprehension, which does not establish the non-existence of the self, clay, consciousness, and so forth, capable of establishing the non-existence of the reason? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.22)
Therefore, a nature connected with that alone would either negate the entity itself, or the cause would negate the effect, because of their non-deviation [from one another]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.23)
How could the exclusion of one thing result in the exclusion of another?
Just because a mortal does not possess horses, does it follow that he must not possess cows either? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.24)
Just as there is proximity for one [entity], how can there be proximity for another? Would a mortal necessarily possess horses simply because he possesses cows? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.25)
Therefore, in the case of a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), a substratum is not necessarily required here;
for even in its absence, the [logical] understanding [of the probandum] occurs through the statement: "In the absence of that, this is not. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.26)
For those who do not understand it, the presence [of the probandum] and the causal relationship [between the reason and the probandum] are demonstrated by means of an example;
however, for the learned, only the reason itself need be stated. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.27)

When the relationship has been known by that very means, through the utterance of either one of the two [terms], a recollection of the second also arises by way of presumptive implication (arthāpatti). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.28)

Therefore, when there is the negation of something, the absence of the nature of its cause is the reason; and that [absence] consists in the non-perception of that [cause], which would otherwise be perceived under appropriate conditions. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.29)

Thus, although this non-apprehension has been described as threefold, it is of many kinds through the application of various distinctions, such as the apprehension of that which is contradictory to it and so forth.

The restriction of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva) arises either from the relation of cause and effect or from an essential nature (svabhāva) as the regulator; it is not established by non-observation, nor by observation alone. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.31)
Otherwise, what necessity is there for another [cause] to ensure the certainty of occurrence?
Or, if it were caused by something else, it would be like the color on a cloth. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.32)
For a property (dharma) caused by a different object would indeed be something else entirely;
since one observes [the property] even when the entity is absent, there is no causality, so how could there be any certainty regarding the result? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.33)
Smoke is the effect of fire because it follows the properties of its cause;
if it were to exist in the absence of that [fire], it would transcend the principle of those things that possess causes.
A thing must be either eternally existent or non-existent, because it does not depend on anything else;
whereas the occasional occurrence of entities is possible only through dependence.
If the summit of Mount Śakra has the nature of fire, then it is simply fire;
but if it does not have the nature of fire, how could smoke exist there? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.36)
For fire has the nature of having smoke as its cause and possesses a specific causal capacity for it; if smoke were to exist from a cause that is not the cause of smoke, it would be without a cause.

Whatever nature is observed through positive and negative concomitance to follow another, that [nature] has the latter as its cause; therefore, it cannot arise from something different. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.38)
Intrinsic nature also possesses inseparable concomitance, as it follows upon mere existence;
for if that [nature] were absent, the thing itself would be non-existent, since there is no difference between them.
All things, by virtue of their own nature, are established in their respective natures; for they partake in exclusion from both their own nature and the nature of others. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.40)
Therefore, from whatever [object] things are excluded, based on that,
various conceptual distinctions (jātibheda) are constructed which penetrate those specific differences.
Therefore, whatever specific property is perceived by means of a particular dharma cannot be [perceived] by anything other than that; thus, their establishment is distinct. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.42.
When a single object-entity is itself directly perceived, what other part of it could there be that is not seen and thus requires investigation by means of valid cognitions? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.43)

If another quality were not associated with it by means of a cause of error—just as the form of silver [is superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a similarity in appearance—[then there would be no error]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.44)
Therefore, every quality of an observed entity is indeed observed;
it is not that it is determined [as such] due to error. Thus, the means of proof proceeds.
When a single property is ascertained through inference upon grasping an object, there would indeed be a grasping of everything; however, this fault does not apply in the case of *apoha*.
Therefore, the logical mark (liṅga) is proclaimed to have exclusion (apoha) as its object;
otherwise, since the subject (dharmin) is already established, what more remains to be proven? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.47)
In some cases, a cognition produced by perception regarding a universal is not born of a logical mark;
how can that [cognition] have the exclusion of others as its object, when its scope is the exclusion of only that [particular]? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.48)

Because there exists a relationship of the sublated and the sublator between the mind that apprehends certainty and the mind that imposes [superimposition], it is understood that the function of this [mind apprehending certainty] is the removal of superimposition. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.49)
As many as there are superimpositions of parts, so many are the determinations for their removal;
and there are just as many words, for that reason they have distinct domains.

Otherwise, since a single object would be pervaded by one word or by a single cognition, there would be no other object [for further words or cognitions], and thus they would be synonyms. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.51)

Even for one who holds that the cognition grasps an object possessing various attributes which are distinct [from one another], [it must be admitted that] when there is the apprehension of the self which is non-different from the capacities that constitute the factors for the assistance of those various attributes, [the object is grasped as a whole]. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.52.
For that which is to be assisted by its very essence, how could there be any undetermined distinction?
Because of the connection between those two within the self, both are apprehended in the cognition of one. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.53)

If there is a difference between the capacities for assisting [the object] and the [entity] itself, then what is it to that [entity]? If there is no assistance from those capacities, then there would be an infinite regress.
When a single beneficiary is the object to be apprehended, there are no other benefits [to be apprehended] beyond it;
since that [beneficiary] is seen, those not yet seen are also seen, and upon its apprehension, there is the apprehension of the whole.
If, even when [an object] has been apprehended for the sake of removing error, another [exclusion] is still desired,
then it is established that the latter, like the former, has as its object the exclusion of that [other].
Furthermore, how can that form which is not ascertained by determinate cognitions—even though they operate within a domain free from superimposition—be their object? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.57)
Even when a particular object devoid of parts has been grasped by perception,
that cognition which exists as a determination of a specific feature is what is cognized.
In that case as well, both words and determinate cognitions—such as "exclusion of others" and "excluded from others"—depend upon a causal basis (*nimitta*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.59.

Even when two [words] are expressed by a single [term], the case-ending, though distinct, follows as if it had a different meaning, due to a slight difference in the expressed object. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.60)

The exclusion of other differences and the non-exclusion [of them]—these two are the basis for the distinction of linguistic convention, which conforms to the desire of the cognizer. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.61)
This very distinction exists everywhere between two words denoting a substance and a state; however, there is no difference whatsoever in their referent. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.62)

Whether one wishes to make that meaning known by means of a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita), or by means of a primary derivative suffix (kṛt), or by means of a nominal ending (sup), there is no difference beyond that. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.63)

Therefore, the description of the "possessor of that" (tadvat) regarding the object of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) has been rejected; for if there were a difference [between them], there would be the fault [of a real relation] between the universal (jāti) and its possessor.

The objection regarding the genitive case, number distinctions, and so forth, is appropriate only against those for whom words are governed by the nature of things and do not depend on the speaker's intention. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.65)
In whatever way a word is employed by speakers as a signifier,
that speech is a signifier for them in that very way, regardless of any external object.

In cases such as "the wife" (*dārāḥ*) or "the six cities" (*ṣaṇṇagarī*), where both difference and non-difference are established, what is the basis for [the usage] in such instances as "the nature of space is spaciality" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ khatvam*)? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.67)
By means of that cognition which, relying upon distinct entities, manifests them as a single object, the other form is concealed by its own form. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.68)

By that [conventional reality], the variousness [of things] is concealed; thus, through convention, entities which are themselves distinct appear as if they were non-distinct by virtue of some particular form. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.69.
By virtue of her intention, the universal is proclaimed as existent;
yet it is non-existent in the ultimate sense, just as she had conceived it.
Individual instances do not follow after one another, nor does anything that follows them appear;
or else, if it were not distinct from cognition, how could it become a different object? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.71)
Therefore, this false conceptual construction which grasps at a single nature in objects has the mutual exclusion [of those objects] as its seed; such is the purpose of its designation.

Even though they are distinct, certain things are determined by their own nature to produce a single unifying reflective awareness, a cognition of an object, or a single effect, just like the sense organs and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.73)
Just as certain medicinal herbs are observed to alleviate fever and other ailments either together or individually, while others are not, despite their diversity. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.74)
Because there is no distinction, it is not a universal; for otherwise, the consequence would be that there are no distinctions at all.
Furthermore, even when there is a difference in their fields and so forth, [the universal] remains constant and thus provides no assistance. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.75)
The cognition that arises from grasping the intrinsic nature of that [object], or even one that does not seek its actual object, is conceptual;
it is produced as being fixed upon a distinction between that object and its effects. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.76)
In that [cognition], whatever form appears as if it were external, unitary, and distinct from others—
as if excluded [from others]— is devoid of reality, because it does not withstand critical examination.
Objects are established within cognition; thus, while they possess excluded forms, they appear as if non-different from one another, yet are nonetheless excluded from others. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.78)
It is precisely through cognitions and designations whose objects are common and share a common substratum that their erroneous conventional usage is extended. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.79)
And all that [conceptual content] is based on the mutual non-existence of things;
therefore, it has the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) as its object and is the basis for what merely appears to be a real entity.
Where there is a connection with a real entity, as in the aforementioned inference, [the cognition is valid];
not elsewhere, even if there is an equality of error, as in the case of the light of a lamp [mistaken for] a jewel.
In that case, although many things have a single effect, they are based on their difference from those that do not produce that effect;
thus, through designations and cognitions, linguistic usage is induced by treating them as one.

Therefore, although it is a single entity that performs many functions, when its nature is fully elucidated, it is perceived as possessing various properties through the differentiation of objects that do not produce those effects. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.83.
This meaning of words is stated according to how it is perceived, even though it does not exist [ultimately];
furthermore, co-referentiality (samānādhikaraṇya) is not possible for this [meaning] in a real entity (vastu).

The distinction between property and its locus, as well as their non-distinction, are of such a nature that they are perceived in the world by those who have not investigated the true meaning of reality. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.85)

Relying upon that very [conventional reality] in such a manner, the establishment of the means and the goal of proof is devised by the wise for the sake of entering into the ultimate truth. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.86.
Ultimately real objects are neither conjoined nor divided by themselves;
that they appear as both unitary and manifold is a cognitive distortion regarding them. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.87)
Therefore, this distinction— namely, that within a conceptual object there is both a universal and a particular—
is merely a postulated differentiation of attributes for that very same entity through the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*).

Because the perception of the real thing is lost when there is a conceptual construction of the probandum and the probans, it is a particular conjoined with a universal that is apprehended here, not the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.89.

That [object] cannot be apprehended in any way through forms such as "identical" or "different," because it is impossible for multiple distinctions and their many subdivisions to reside within that single [entity]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.90)

That form [of the object] is distinct from everything else; likewise, there exists neither scripture nor conceptual construction that establishes it as such, because they function only by way of a universal.

Words express that which is conventionalized for the sake of practical usage; since that [particular] does not exist at that time, there is no conventionality with respect to it. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.92)
A person might act only after having recognized things as capable of purposeful action;
thus, linguistic expressions are applied to objects for the sake of accomplishing that [action]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.93)

In that case, neither the universal (jāti) capable of performing a purposeful action nor its possessor is directly applied [to the object]. If it is argued that this is because of infinity, then this objection applies equally [to both].

If [it is argued that] the distinction between those who perform that [action] and those who do not is the same [for both], why has it not been established? If [you say] it is because the defect is likewise equal, then let there be no need for a further universal (jāti). Pramāṇavārttika 3.95.
And it is said that the implication (dhvani) is that [the word] should function by excluding those other [things];
therefore, if this [word] were not excluded from them, how could that [implication] exist? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.96)
If there is indeed this exclusion [of others] for it, then surely this much alone is the purpose of words; what need have you there for another, additional universal?

Having observed various purposeful activities such as cognition and so forth, even though there is difference [between objects], one acts toward those objects together with verbal expressions whose scope is the exclusion of what is other than them. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.98)
Even when seeing another [object], one might perform recognition by connecting [it with the previous];
yet that cognition does not arise from the universal alone. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.99)
If there were constant cognition of that [universal] alone, it would follow that the individual is never cognized;
for at that time, the possessor of that [universal], though connected to it, would remain ungrasped. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.100)
In that case, there would be no ascertainment of the possession of that [universal]; how then could there be linguistic usage?
If it is argued that the individuals, aided by a single entity [the universal], are the cause of cognition—*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.101.
Does that single entity remove their multiplicity? And because of their multiplicity, they are not accepted as being the cause of a single cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.102)

Even if many [things] were to produce a single cognition by depending on one another, they would nonetheless produce that cognition individually, even in the absence of those [other things]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.103)

Even by that single [cause], they lack such capacity; thus there is no grasping by the cognition [of them as distinct], because a separate capacity for blue and so forth is observed in visual consciousness.
Even in the case of a collection, there is no such capacity for the individual [atoms] in any way;
if that [collection] is capable by depending on their mutual difference, then it is not the individual [atoms] alone that are so.

If those [atoms] could assist that single [cognition], why would they not assist a single cognition? For that which is called "assistance" is nothing other than the production of their effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.106)
If it is thought that cognition does not have an undifferentiated appearance regarding distinct things, [we reply:
the appearance is indeed differentiated by the cognition, because they are grasped as being "the same. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.107)
How can those [particulars] be grasped by distinct cognitions if they are identical, given that they have a single effect?
Surely their similarity is the effect of those [cognitions], yet that [similarity] is itself differentiated.

Because it is the cause of a single unifying cognition, the intellect is non-different; and by virtue of being the cause of that single cognition, the individuals themselves are also non-different. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.109)

And that [exclusion] is the exclusion of what does not have that effect; it is the basis for convention regarding an object possessing that [effect], because of the non-perception and the negation of anything else that persists [in its absence]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.110)

The scripture, for the purpose of prompting activity through the exclusion of what does not produce that [result], presents as having a form identical to that which produces it an entity that does not actually perform that action. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.111)

Even though they produce a cognition whose seed is merely the distinctness of objects and which is itself devoid of purpose, [they do so] because it serves as a factor for the exclusion of what does not perform that function. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.112)
And because it relies on a distinction between real entities, it is considered non-erroneous with respect to the object;
therefore, its object is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), since its existence depends upon that which produces it.
When the object "tree" is apprehended as distinct from non-trees, there is a twofold [dependence]:
they are mutually dependent; thus, in the absence of the apprehension of one, there is no apprehension of both. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.114)
"Therefore, some declare that convention is impossible; for them, are non-trees excluded from the convention or not? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.115)

How can exclusions (vyavacchinna) be known prior to the apprehension of the tree? For if they were not excluded [from non-trees], there could be no conventional usage by those engaged in linguistic practice regarding the convention. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.116)
There would be no activity directed toward that [specific object] by way of exclusion, as in the case of a particular tree;
for one does not exclude others without first prescribing [the object], nor can one demonstrate a single thing standing before one without [first] excluding the rest. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.117)

If it is argued that the convention "this is a tree" is established and that one apprehends that [tree], and therefore there is no fault in this [usage] even in conventional practice, [the response is: "the tree. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.118)
The undesirable consequence that "this too is just this" does not cease;
for [the universal] resides in a single cognition known as the unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.119)
The person who has attained [this state] distinguishes for themselves the objects that are causes of that [cognition] and those that are not;
these entities, which reside within that cognition, appear as the causes of the intellect.
"The statement 'one should perceive multiple forms as distinct, even though they lack a cause for such distinction' is intended to establish difference. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.121)

The intellect, striving toward that [object], perceives it as a single entity through error, having turned away from something else in order to settle upon a particular object. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.122)
A word is employed because it determines its own object;
otherwise, its employment would be useless. This applies even to words such as "that which is to be known" (*tajjñeya*) and so forth.

Among those things brought forward in linguistic convention, there is something to be excluded; and that which is to be established is that which is distinguished by excluding whatever it differs from. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.124)
When that [universal] is differentiated according to the differences among the things that appear with a common form,
it is understood through the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti) as belonging to that entity.

It is said that there is some "portion" [of reality], yet it has no form whatsoever; nevertheless, through words directed toward that [portion], the exclusion of others is understood. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.126)
In that case, no one is understood to be superior or distinct from another by anyone else;
nor does the word "mutual non-existence" (anyonyābhāva) establish duality. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.127)
The perception of the formless as having the nature of form is a derangement of the intellect;
for that very reason, this [perception] is not the ultimate reality, since a thing cannot exist otherwise than it truly is.
Exclusion becomes a real entity; it is a distinction [of one thing] from another through differentiation.
A single sound operates to effect the connection and separation of a single referent. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.129.
In that case, either a logical mark (*liṅga*) must be stated, or no object at all;
for it is through the expression of [the mark] that there is comprehension of the entire [object] by the power of the thing itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.130)
Therefore, a single sound may have various effects; thus, while indicating a distinction, it functions without rejecting its own unity. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.131.
When one thing is pervaded by that [other] and appears as identical with it, then there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), in accordance with the cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.132)

The contact with the property of a real entity would truly belong to a sound that effects a separation; for that [contact] exists therein, but not in a word denoting a single entity. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.133)

Because there is a determination of the non-existence of the visible object when it is illuminated by the cognition of a Buddha, it is said that [conceptual cognitions] have the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) as their domain and the universal (sāmānya) as their range. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.134.

Since words and cognitions cannot possibly exist with respect to a single entity, because the nature of that entity is unitary, how could there be a cognition of diverse forms? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.135)

Furthermore, positive and negative concomitance cannot both pertain to a single object for a single [entity]; moreover, if there were actual difference, the linguistic usage of non-difference would be without basis. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.136)
Because [the term] is excluded from all things that are not [the cause], these faults do not follow;
for when one is inquiring about the effect of certain entities that produce a single effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.137)

Due to the considerations of respect, incapacity, and futility in expressing the difference [between individuals], the learned have established a common verbal designation based on the exclusion of what does not produce that effect (*atatkāryavyāvṛtti*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.138)
Since all entities are established according to their own intrinsic natures, that which is the form of a brindled cow does not exist in a black cow. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.139)
The exclusion of what does not produce that effect exists for both [the word and the object];
moreover, without non-difference in meaning, non-difference in the word is not tenable.
Therefore, even its status as an effect [of that cause] is accepted only because it is distinct from that which is its effect,
just as in certain cases the eye and so forth are distinct from the single result of visual consciousness.
When it is possible to enjoin that effect without distinction, someone [employs] a conventional expression for the sake of cognizing all [the particulars] at once. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.142)
One may apply [the term] even without a universal distinct from those forms;
for if that which occurs in many were to possess a single denotation, it could be so even if it is manifold. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.143)
In that case, it is not tenable that its occurrence consists in being located or being manifested;
for since an eternal entity cannot be assisted, there can be no substratum for that which does not spread out. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.144)

The capacity [of a pit or similar object] to produce its effect, such as a jujube fruit, does not exist in this case [of a permanent entity], because even in the absence of that [capacity], the entity remains present. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.145)

That persistence as well is untenable when one analyzes its difference or non-difference [from the self], because that which conforms to another within the self is for the sake of the capacity for the arising of cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.146)
That [manifestor] is considered the cause that brings about the manifestation and the causal agent of the capacity;
however, since its capacity already exists beforehand, dependence upon it is not tenable.

Since the universal is unchangeable, how could there be a refinement of that which possesses the universal? It is not a refinement of the sense faculty either, as in the case of the application of collyrium to the eyes. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.148)

If it is maintained that universals possess the state of being universal because the manifestor is non-different during both the time when it exists and the time when it does not exist, due to the non-difference of its manifestation; *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.149.

For those who maintain that a universal (jāti) exists—whether it is different from the individual manifestation or not—the lamp and so forth, which are illuminators, would be apprehended as possessing that [universal] by way of "lamp-ness" and so on. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.150)
How can there be cognitions of a universal regarding those individuals which are unprecedented?
For that which exists in one place cannot possibly be perceived elsewhere as existing. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.151)
If there were non-difference, there would be no persistence; if there were difference, there would be no dependence.
It does not go [to another state], nor was it there before, nor does it exist afterwards, nor does it possess parts. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.152)
Alas, the continuous succession of calamities abandons its former substratum when that which exists elsewhere gives rise to birth in another location. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.153)
"It is highly illogical to claim that there is activity [of a thing] without it moving from its own place;
for even when that entity exists [in one location], it is not connected with [another]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.154)
And it pervades that which possesses that location; this is something truly wonderful.
If [the universal] were omnipresent because it is non-different from the individual, then it would be manifested everywhere simply by being manifested in one instance. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.155)
Because it is non-different, it would be perceived everywhere; furthermore, that [manifestation] does not depend upon a particular individual.
For as long as the manifestor is not perceived, the manifested object is not correctly perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.156)
Furthermore, why is the reverse [i.e., that the universal and its possessor are identical] not accepted?
For in the case of "cook" and the like, [the word] is expressive even without an undifferentiated object [in the form of a universal]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.157)
Action is not the cause of this [cognition] because of its diversity; nor is genus [the cause], since it depends upon action;
for another scriptural authority is the cause, and because there is no persistence of action. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.158)

Because there is no connection, the universal [is not the cause]; nor is it illogical for it to be the cause of the word, because that would lead to over-extension. Furthermore, an action that is non-existent cannot be the cause of cognition and verbal designation. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.159)
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of [the action] being causeless; nor can there be a capacity, because it lacks connection [to the individual].
If the universal such as "cook-ness" were to exist even prior [to the action], [it would be permanent]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.160)
If it is argued that the entity is manifest on that day but not on others, this is not so, because there is no difference [in the conditions] afterwards;
for if an unchanging thing were a manifestor while depending on the assistance of an action, it would be contradictory.
Even if there were an excellence in its dependence, how could there be activity, given its momentariness?
Since the difference is equal, by what proximity does the universal proceed [to some and not others]?

If there is no other positive concomitance (anvaya) among entities apart from their exclusion (nivṛtti), then let that very exclusion alone be the basis for the cognition of words in some cases and not others. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.163)
Because of their absolute difference, the effect of one would not belong to another;
if, however, the manifold were of a single nature, it could be the producer of a single effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.164)
Or, if that [nature] exists even in isolation, then the auxiliary causes would be useless;
for that non-different nature does not depart, while the specific qualities are indeed subject to disappearance. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.165)
Because there is an absence of the effect when even one [of the causes] is missing, its arising must be from the specific [causes].
That alone is an ultimately real entity which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
And that which does not persist [through change] cannot produce an effect;
therefore, even though there is a difference in their essential nature, one thing is a cause and another is not. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.167)
If this were their intrinsic nature, then non-differentiation would imply that the destruction and arising [of the two] would occur simultaneously.
If it is argued that there is nevertheless a difference [between them], then it is not so; for when one among those that are identical perishes, [the other must perish as well].
The self does not persist; therefore, there could be no cognition of generality or difference [regarding it].
Since cessation is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva), there can be no conceptualization of its staying or not staying.
And since the "affliction" (upaplava) is common to all cognitions, it does not constitute a refutation [of the validity of cognition].
For how could that which is a producer [of a cognition] be other than its own nature as a producer? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.170)

If it is argued that the distinct particulars are the producers [of cognition] and that there is also some non-difference among them, then for that reason they are said to be non-producers; for even the appearance [of identity] is a differentiator.
That object alone possesses no other [properties]; the others are its exclusions (vyāvṛtti).
That which is described as cause and effect is held to be the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
All human activities have as their fruit the abandonment of that [suffering] and its attainment;
for although there is no difference in their distinctness, not everything is the means for achieving everything. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.173)

Likewise, even though there is no difference in their being distinct, not everything is the means for producing everything; for, due to the nature of things, only a specific cause can be the producer of a specific effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.174)
But if there is no difference [between the cause and its states], then for that single entity, both activity and non-activity are contradictory.
If it is argued that even though there is a difference, it exists due to non-activity [of other factors], then the auxiliary causes would not produce anything.
Or is agency [alternating] by way of succession? Would that [agency] belong to that very same entity?
However, absolute difference and non-difference would both apply to that entity which possesses them.
Or else, there would be a mutual distinction between those two, whose natures are respectively similar and dissimilar;
for even between those two, there would be a distinction by virtue of that nature which [distinguishes] them.
If it is argued that "particularity is the universal," then if it exists as that very essence, it would be merely a particular;
and thus there would be no distinction between the universal and the particular.
Just as there is mutual distinction and generality among jars and other such things, so too is this person who acts by placing a certain self (ātman) at the forefront. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.179)

One who desires the fruit to be accomplished by that [means] considers both difference and non-difference as residing therein: difference by its own nature, and similarity through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.180)
The entity certainly exists, yet it does not persist [as a single thing], because that would entail the consequence of [constant] activity and so forth.
By this very [argument], whatever indecent and confused [claims] the shameless ones have made— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.181.

They prattle on [that it is not so], but that too is rejected because it is possible only in one way; for if everything possessed both natures, the distinction between them would be abolished. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.182)
When urged, does a person who eats curd run toward a camel? Or is there some excellence by which he behaves according to the distinction [between them]? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.183)
"That very thing is curd; it does not exist elsewhere"—this is the ultimate non-duality.
Furthermore, if all things possessed the nature of everything, then cognition and verbal expression would not be distinct. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.184)
Because there is no difference [between the word and its referent], the theory of the synthesis of distinctions is impossible;
since non-existence lacks form, words are designators of form. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.185.
Since they are established as being incapable of being doubted, they therefore express exclusion;
[the object] is either an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) dependent on a distinction of conditions (upādhi), or it is the intrinsic nature alone. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.186)
It is said: For the sake of establishing the probandum, [the reason] is like "being an effect" or "existence" in the case of destruction.
If the reason has existence as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how can that very existence be established? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.187)
For the lack of positive concomitance (ananvaya) among particulars contradicts [the requirement of] the reason and the probandum;
however, when the probandum consists merely in the affirmation of existence, it resides in a subject that is a universal. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.188.

No object whatsoever would be established, and such [a thing] would be unrefuted; if this probandum were to consist in a difference that has been specifically assumed, the reason would be one lacking positive concomitance (*ananvaya*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.189.
If existence were the property to be proven by that [reason], then a specific quality would be established;
however, when the object in its mere generality, without reference to its particular differences, is what is being proven, [the reason is inconclusive]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.190)
The positive concomitance (anvaya) of the probandum, which pervades that [subject] alone, is not obstructed.
A property of existence does not exist in what is unestablished; that which relies on both [existence and non-existence] is inconclusive (vyabhicārin). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.191)
How can that existence (sattā), which is a property (dharma) contradictory to non-existence, be established?
A proven essential nature (svabhāva) is the indicator [of another], provided it is ascertained to be its pervader (vyāpaka). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.192)
This nature of that [cause] is either accessible [to perception], or it is the cause of cessation upon the cessation [of the effect];
just as in the case of impermanence, there is either an effect or a non-effect in relation to that which is indestructible.
Since destruction is without cause, it follows from the very nature [of things];
for among those entities that depend on other conditions, necessary occurrence is not observed.
For even if that cause is abundant, there may be non-occurrence [of the effect] in some cases;
by this, the fallibility [of the reason] is stated, because the effect is not invariably established. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.195)
For those who maintain that destruction is caused by a cause for all things, [destruction] occurs by its very nature because that cause is incapable [of producing it]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.196)
Even where [an inference] occurs from this [logical mark], it likewise exists by way of its own nature;
whatever inference has an existent thing as its object is of only two kinds. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.197)

Because their relation is restricted by the presence or absence of the effect in its own probandum, and because activity is preceded by cognition, [the object] is not perceived when that [cognition] is absent. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.198)
It has been stated that there should not be [such] activity; thus, non-apprehension is established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Within the scope of a treatise (*śāstra*), many objects beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*) would be irrelevant. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.199)
And how can there be an absence of those [entities] which lack any characteristic mark, based on non-perception?
If it does not result in the certainty of existence or non-existence, then it would follow that [non-perception] is not a means of valid cognition.

There may also be some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arising from a specific excellence of the logical mark (*liṅga*); this principle has been illustrated in the context of the non-cognition of an indicator of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.201)
In the case of an effect, however, the non-cognition of the causal factor is the means of proving the absence [of that effect];
and the non-perception of the essential nature [serves as the proof] when the essential nature itself is the inferential mark (liṅga) of the object. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.202.
Its absence would be cognized by some means of knowledge if, while the object is perceptible, there were no possible cause for its non-perception. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.203)
The absence of an entity that has not been perceived is cognized;
likewise, when a contradictory entity exists, [the absence of the first] is understood because its existence is sublated. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.204)
Upon the perception of that which is contradictory to it, there would be the ascertainment of non-existence;
[this non-existence] is established by conceptual construction arising from beginningless predispositions.
The referent of a word is a threefold subject (dharmin) based on existence, non-existence, or both.
When that [subject] is to be proven as not being the basis for existence, its non-perception [serves as the reason]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.206)
Thus, there is no absence of a cause for that [usage], because of the employment of words; for if words were restricted solely to the ultimate reality, they would have no basis.

There would be no engagement with objects that differ according to various philosophical systems, nor with those that are past or yet to be born; furthermore, there would be no falsity regarding their referents.
The phrase "of some speech" is considered to have as its object a meaning established by valid cognition;
for if one were to deny the existence of the word's referent, the locus of the property would be negated. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.209)

For those who do not deny the referents of words, the composite whole cannot be the object of proof, nor can the property alone be so, regardless of the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.210)
Only that entity is piled up [in the ritual] upon which the arising of the fruit is dependent;
what is the use of investigations or examinations regarding that which is incapable of causal efficiency? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.211)
What is the use of examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch for a woman in love?
The referent of a word is constructed as an object of conceptual cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.212)
The proponent of logic has stated that for this [inference], the basis of the entity is unestablished, because words lack an invariable concomitance with real entities. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.213)
Therefore, there is no establishment of the object [from the words themselves], for they indicate the intention of the speaker;
their status as inference arises from the commonality of being non-deceptive, like the speech of a reliable person.

A statement that is coherent, possesses appropriate means [to its goal], expresses a human purpose, and is subject to critical examination is authoritative; anything other than this is not so. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.215)
Non-sublation by both types of valid cognition—perception and inference—and the non-contradiction of its two objects, whether visible or invisible, constitute its reliability. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.216)

Because of the commonality of non-contradiction with the speech of a reliable person, the cognition [of such speech] is said to be inference due to the lack of any other way; yet it is also denied in the case of its own specific object.

Or rather, because the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with its means, is established, inference [is valid] regarding other matters due to its non-contradiction with the primary object. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.218)

Others maintain that [the scripture] is true in accordance with reality by depending on a superior person (puruṣātiśaya). This point is accepted, provided that such a superiority can be recognized. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.219)

Others, however, maintain that whether this [person] is thus [faultless] or not, or whether they possess faults or are faultless, is difficult to understand because of the scarcity of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.220)
Since all [defilements] possess opposites and depend upon decrease and increase,
the outflows (āsravas) might perhaps cease through the cultivation of those opposites once they have become naturalized.

Because it has as its object a nature that is free from affliction and is real, the intellect cannot be subverted by errors even when effort is applied, due to its partiality toward that [true nature]. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.222.
The origin of all classes of defects arises from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
That [view] is ignorance; attachment to it therein gives rise to hatred and the other afflictions. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.223)
Therefore, delusion alone is designated as the primary cause of the defects;
elsewhere, however, it is identified as the view of a self-identity, because [all defects] are abandoned through its abandonment.
Some declare that because the defects which cause the falsity of words reside in persons, that which is non-personal (apauruṣeya) must have true meaning. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.225.

Others declare: "Since qualities that are the causes of the truth of words depend upon a person, how could that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya) be false in its meaning? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.226)
For convention, which depends on persons, is the cause for abandoning the ignorance of meaning;
therefore, even if words were not of human origin, the possibility of falsity remains. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.227)
If the relationship were not of human origin, there would be cognition even for one who lacks awareness [of it];
if it were manifested through convention, the postulation of anything else would be useless. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.228)
If words were restricted to a single meaning, there would be no comprehension of other meanings;
if they were connected to multiple meanings, there would arise the possibility of contradictory manifestations. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.229)
Furthermore, the postulation of its being authorless would be futile;
and a reason must be stated for the establishment of a relationship between distinct entities. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.230)

If it were not subject to refinement by persons, it would be entirely useless; if, however, one admits its refinement, this would be like the "bathing of an elephant" in its primary sense. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.231.
Because the related entities are impermanent, there is no permanence in the relation;
and since that which is permanent cannot be assisted, it cannot be a substratum for something that provides no assistance. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.232)
That [word] is to be refined by persons through their intellect according to the objects [it signifies];
since it arises together with the objects themselves, there is no change in its intrinsic nature.

If it is argued that this fault does not apply when the relationship between words is conceptualized as eternal—just like a genus (jāti)—such that it does not perish even when its substratum perishes; Pramāṇavārttika 3.234.
