In the case of eternal entities, what is the efficacy of the substratum by virtue of which it is accepted as such a substratum?
[It is] due to its connection with auxiliary causes that are the reasons for the production of cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.235)

The arising of things that are unchanging, even in the case of jars and the like, is held by those who know the reasoning to be "manifestation" (vyakti), insofar as it is an arising characterized by the capacity to produce a cognition [of the object]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.236)
What purpose is served by the manifestors, since it is held that those [universals] are manifested by them?
Furthermore, if the relation were a real entity, there would be a diversity of cognitions due to its differentiation. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.237)
If there were no difference between those two, they would be identical; therefore, there is no other possibility for the nature of a real entity.
Since the form of a real entity is distinct, any connection between them is a product of conceptual construction.
How could a real entity be dependent on another, or how could it be the relation of another?
Since the phonemes are themselves devoid of meaning, [the categories such as] words and so forth are merely conceptual constructs.
How can there be the operation of this relation, which is itself a real entity, with respect to that which is not a real entity?
Furthermore, its lack of human authorship is asserted on the grounds that no authors are remembered. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.240)
"There are those who repeat this as well"—fie on that all-pervading darkness, such that he could not have learned this sequence of syllables and words from anyone else! (Pramāṇavārttika 3.241)

Some [claim] that another person is likewise capable of composing such a work, or that some other treatise has been composed by others apart from traditional transmission (*sampradāya*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.242)
Who has been observed to have been so designated that he too could not be inferred in this way?
For one who is established as belonging to a certain class is indistinguishable [from others of that class], just like fire and wood.

Even another cause that has not been perceived is understood to produce that [effect], when people do not point out its distinction there because of the observation of a commonality in the effect. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.244)
All those reasons that are set forth are fallacious;
in this way, only beginninglessness would be established, not a lack of dependence on a person.

Therefore, if [the Veda] were not of human origin, there would be another [source] that does not depend on humans for the linguistic conventions of barbarians as well as for the words of atheists. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.246)

Because the continuum of prior formative predispositions is beginningless, it exists in such a manner; even if such authorlessness were established, what benefit would there be? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.247)
Since one observes differences in meaning and mental impressions, doubt arises once again;
for if phonemes were established as being non-distinct from one another, what would be the result? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.248)
A sentence distinct from its phonemes does not exist, because it is not perceived;
if it were composed of multiple parts, those parts would be individually meaningless. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.249)
And the attribution of that nature to what lacks it is a conceptual construction, like [the attribution of] "lion-ness" and so forth;
even though each [individual] possesses its own meaning, the conceptualization of multiplicity is false. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.250)

Furthermore, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence would occur through the apprehension of even a single constituent part; moreover, if all parts were heard simultaneously, a temporal sequence [of their apprehension] would be untenable. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.251)
For even if it were a single, undivided entity, gradual movement would be impossible;
how then could that which is impermanent, produced through effort, and human-made not be [considered] such? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.252)
Even if [the self] were eternal, there would be constant perception because there is no possibility of its being obscured;
if it is argued that there is no hearing [of sound] due to the deficiency of some auxiliary cause, [that is not so]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.253)
If they were not all-pervasive, there would be non-perception of them everywhere, and their restriction [to specific locations] would be contradicted. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.254)
If there were pervasiveness, there would be the simultaneous perception of all things.
Furthermore, when that which is conditioned is perceived, who could be the conditioner of that which is unchanging? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.255)

If it were argued that there would be a refinement (saṃskāra) of the sense faculty, and thus one would hear all of that [sound], because the restriction to a single object is due to the distinction between different refinements; Pramāṇavārttika 3.256.
How can there be auditory perception of a cacophony consisting of a multitude of words?
If it is argued that in such a case only sounds (dhvani) are heard and not the expressive [words], [then... Pramāṇavārttika 3.257.
That there exists something distinct from the sounds (dhvani) is something very difficult to believe.
While other sounds persist, how could that which is expressive (vācaka) be heard? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.258)

Or how could the perception of distinct sounds arise from a restriction of capacity, given that those who hold that sounds are non-expressive due to certain defects [of the theory] accept them as such? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.259)
If this [word] is manifested by sounds, why do those [same] phonemes not also manifest the expressive word?
If you say it is because the sequence of phonemes constitutes the sentence, that is not so, because there is no difference between the phonemes [in either case]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.260)
And there can be no fixed order among them, because that would contradict other sequences;
for they are described as being all-pervasive and eternal, and thus lack any sequence of space or time. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.261)
Furthermore, the fault regarding impermanence and non-pervasiveness has already been stated previously.
Nor can the sequence of manifestations constitute the sentence, because the theory of eternal manifestation has been refuted. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.262)
Since that [cognition] is established through its own activity, the causal status of causes is also established.
When an object is already established, that which is the cause of another's cognition is considered a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) by means of its own cognition.
Whether it be like a lamp or otherwise, what distinction is there for this [cognition] from its producer?
For it is perceived through the operation of the complete collection of causal factors (*karaṇa*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.264)
Furthermore, being an effect is necessarily absent in that which merely manifests [an existing thing], because manifestation would be impossible for it;
for if manifestation were simply the removal of the obscurations of its form, [it would still be an effect]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.265)
In the absence [of a real universal], what indeed could that capacity of the collection of sense organs be?
Furthermore, it would follow that other things as well would be manifested by means of specific words.

If that were accepted, all causes would be rendered purposeless, including the means of proof such as recognition, the application of existing things, and so forth, which are held [to be necessary]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.267)
Because all entities undergo momentary destruction, there is no example [to support] them;
furthermore, any other fallacious reason would be refuted if cognition were not based on a person.

The difference between the sphoṭa and the sequence [of sounds] from the phonemes has been examined by means of perception, inference, and what is accepted as sublated, respectively. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.269)
How could that [impermanence] be something superimposed by conceptual construction, or how could it be independent of a person?
Since destruction is necessarily concomitant with mere existence, sound is impermanent.

If a different entity [the destruction] were to arise from the fire, the wood would still be perceived, since it has not perished. If it is argued that "this very [new entity] is its destruction," how could that be so? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.271)
Let it be that one thing is destroyed by another; why then is the wood not seen?
If you say it is because of its grasping [by the fire], no, for by that [grasping] there is no obstruction.

If destruction were itself destructible, then there would be a further arising from it; just as one sees the wood [again] when the killer is slain, so there would be no non-rebirth for Caitra. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.273)
If it is argued that "it is the same here as well," [we reply]: because the killer does not die;
for if destruction were non-different [from the wood], then the wood itself would be the destruction. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.274)
Because that [destruction] is its very nature, it lacks a cause; there is no other possible way [for it to exist].
Even if destruction were causeless, because it is eternal, there would be no distinction between the entity and its destruction.
If it follows that [the cause and effect] exist simultaneously, how can there be permanence for that which is non-existent?
Furthermore, if it is non-existent, the consequence that it is destroyed by non-existence is also not tenable.

Since the destruction of an entity is not desired [to occur] through another destruction, that [statement] is for the purpose of making known that the perishing entity is independent of anything else. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.277)
The cause of this [non-existence] has been stated by the mind through the superimposition of its distinctions;
even if non-existence exists inherently, this conceptualization is the same.
For that [non-existence], nothing at all comes into being; it simply does not exist.
For this conceptual construction regarding existence would occur only if there were an object corresponding to it. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.279)
It has been stated that an existent does not come into being; nor does it follow that a non-existent comes into being.
A subsequent cause would be required only if some effect were to exist [independently].
What object that is incapable of performing any function would be expected by anyone?
For by this same reasoning, even if destruction were causeless, it could not occur because it would not have previously existed. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.281)
The objection regarding the fault of [the self] being a consumer of existence has been refuted;
just as for some, aversion toward living beings is accepted only in certain cases.

If destruction is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities, yet it does not belong to those that are unproduced, then because the cause has a restricted intrinsic nature, the effect must also have a restricted intrinsic nature. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.283)
In that which is impermanent, there is no differentiation of form, because there is an absence of differentiators;
for this very reason, their relation must also be rejected as being permanent. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.284.
The capacity of words has already been undermined by the previously mentioned defects regarding their relationship [to objects];
thus, it is not the case that what is non-human (apauruṣeya) is a means for producing knowledge of reality as it is. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.285)
Fire and other such things are seen to be otherwise even when not defective due to human fault;
therefore, if that [fire] were considered uncreated, it could not even be the cause of cognition.
Because of the inherent capacity of eternal entities, nothing whatsoever has an origin;
[these cognitions] arise from the latencies of conceptual construction and have superimposed objects as their domain. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.287.
In that case, cognitions arise that have no real object as their domain;
for falsity is observed only in things that are produced, and thus the Word is unproduced (*akṛta*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.288)

If, because the exclusion of the object of truth is pervaded by its opposite, one suspects the existence of that [opposite] even when the impossibility [of it in the locus] has not been stated regarding the reason, *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.289.

It has been stated that even for contradictory entities, non-existence is not established merely by the observation of their pervader, because [the pervader] is not perceived in all cases. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.290)

If non-existence is unestablished, then the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful; likewise, the positive concomitance (anvaya), the negative concomitance, or existence [of the reason] in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) is doubtful. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.291)

If the means of proof are established by cognitions that have the result of ascertaining that [reason], then the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the opposite of the probandum is described therein. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.292)
That alone would be its similar instance (sapakṣa); therefore, every reason would be positive (anvayin).
For if mantras were conventional, then the accomplishment of some effect would belong to anyone [who knows them]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.293)
Furthermore, even if there were an inherent power in the entity, it would remain the same regardless of other circumstances;
moreover, the claim that sequence is a distinct entity has already been refuted.

The accomplishment of that purpose would be constant; there would be no dependence on [auxiliary causes] if there were incapacity. If such were the nature of the power of entities, then everything would be the means of accomplishing it. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.295)
Furthermore, dependence on a difference among the agents is not tenable for that which cannot be refined;
for even in the case of a thing that can be refined, it is indeed a difference in the entity itself that constitutes the differentiator. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.296)
The restriction [of meaning] would apply to the capacity [of words] due to the difference among the users, but not to the convention;
for what could a user effect regarding those things to which no specific quality can be imparted? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.297)

If the application [of the means] is manifestation, that has already been refuted. Furthermore, since manifestation is cognition, if that [cognition] is connected with the results [of the action], then... [Pramāṇavārttika 3.298]

There may indeed be a connection with the fruit for the listener, for the speaker is the cause of manifestation; [otherwise] there would be no purpose for the employment of the organs of speech, whose sounds remain unmanifested. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.299)
Or else, mental recitation would be useless, for sound is within the range of the ear;
if it is argued that even that cognition is its manifestation because it is produced from it through a causal series, [then the same applies].
If those [universals] were likewise [non-existent], then for that purpose [of denoting them], [the reason] would be unestablished because of its connection with conceptual construction;
for there is a desire to express a single entity among things that possess the natures of both the particular and the universal.

In the case of the assertions of those who establish conventions, there is no contradiction regarding the object itself; however, if there were no sequential order, the words "sara" and "rasa" would be heard as identical. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.302)
If it is argued that there is no difference in the effect [of the sound], [we reply: that [difference] exists based on the person;
for the sound arises from a cognition produced by the cognition that initiates the articulation of a particular phoneme.
That which arises as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) is determined by scripture;
it is that whose cognition is produced by the knowledge thereof, yet whose hearing is unskilled regarding that scripture. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.304)
"Subsequently, depending upon that memory, one produces a memory within oneself;
thus, this [memory] belongs solely to the person, as it arises from the cognitions that grasped its causes. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.305)
The causal relationship among phonemes is said to be their sequential order;
however, the form of those phonemes in each word is something entirely different from that.
Distinct from the refinement of the agent, that sequence—which, when combined, produces a difference in the effect—is established for phonemes by virtue of their arrangement. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.307)

Because the establishment of the causal relationship between people and the sequence of phonemes is contradicted by the fact that the accomplishment of things contrary to one's will would violate the established order [of causality]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.308)

Just as the sequence of letters [is established] from the phonemes according to the principle of fire and fuel, the uniqueness of those who perform the sequence known as mantra is proven. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.309)
For men, [the success of mantras] is due to their knowledge and power, whereas for others it is due to the absence of these;
even those who are experts in the tantras and perform certain mantras [do so through these means].
Their power over the Lord arises from their following the principles taught by Him;
therefore, the mantras, which are produced and composed by persons, should be recited by one who desires a result. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.311.
By this very [argument], the proof for the incapacity of persons has been refuted;
as for the proof that is described—such as the existence of intellect, sense organs, speech, and personhood—it is likewise [refuted]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.312)

That which appears as a means of valid cognition does not exist as it truly is; for there is no inference from what remains [of the object]. Words do not declare, "This is the object" or "This is not the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.313)
This matter must be conceptualized by persons who are themselves possessed of passion and other defects;
in that case, what is the basis for the distinction that one among them knows reality while others do not? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.314)
In that case, how could there not be some knower among you who possesses masculinity?
For if he whose word is non-contradictory is one who knows the object, then [he is a valid authority]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.315)
For there is no possibility of [independent] validity regarding things that are absolutely beyond the senses;
rather, the word of one whose speech is consistent with valid cognition is what constitutes valid testimony. *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.316.
It follows that scripture is purposeless and lacks human authorship, if it were possible to have knowledge of an absolutely imperceptible object without recourse to scripture. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.317)
It might be intended that there exists someone who knows objects beyond the senses;
yet one who is himself possessed of passion and other defects does not know the meaning of the Veda, nor can he know it from another.
Even a speaker does not perceive [the meaning]; how, then, can there be an understanding of the meaning of the Veda?
Therefore, regarding the Vedic revelation (śruti) "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," [the meaning is not established by the words themselves]. Pramāṇavārttika 3.319.
Regarding the statement "one should eat dog-meat," what is the proof that this is not the intended meaning?
If you claim it is a well-known worldly saying, then who among them perceives supersensible objects? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.320)
By him, among words with multiple meanings, this specific meaning has been distinguished;
and it is observed that words such as "svarga" (heaven) and "urvaśī" (a celestial nymph) denote meanings that are not conventional.
Let such a conceptual construction apply to other similar words as well;
yet, while the consensus of people is a form of discourse that serves as a means of valid cognition, that [consensus] is not accepted [as a final authority here].
Furthermore, regarding the comprehension of the meaning once again: is this [meaning] something desired by both parties?
Or, if it transcends common consensus, there would be no basis for such a conceptual construction. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.323)

Since common consensus (prasiddhi) is not a valid means of knowledge, what would be the basis for grasping it? Indeed, doubt regarding the determination of the meaning of words has already been produced by that very consensus. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.324)
Because it is observed therein that words function with multiple meanings, since there is no impossibility otherwise, the sound itself possesses manifold capacities. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.325)
For those who perceive no regulating factor, doubt must necessarily arise:
"Someone says, 'This is a post; this is the path. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.326)
The distinction between these two—[the one who says "another" and the one who says "I myself speak"]—should be examined:
why should there be a restriction [on the speaker] when it is equally possible for anyone to illuminate a single object? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.327)
By what means can those things that transcend the senses be known, other than through speech intended for expression?
Convention is the cause for restricting the intention to express, and it serves to manifest that [intention]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.328)
In that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya), such [intention] does not exist; how then could it have a single meaning?
Furthermore, if there were a restriction by intrinsic nature (svabhāvaniyama), it could not be applied again to something else. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.329)
Furthermore, the convention would be meaningless, and how could there be any restriction regarding the individual instance?
Where the will is independent, what indeed can be called a restriction? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.330)
By that [conventional usage], the convention would merely manifest its own intended fitness;
for it is said that such is the truth, just as fire is the dispeller of cold. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.331)
Another [opponent] asserts that even other [texts] are the word [of the Buddha], because they are a part of the Veda;
or else, because they possess a similar form, like a flavorful [sauce], or because they were cooked in the same vessel, like a [single] dish. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.332)
Logicians have rejected such [analogical reasoning] as being fallacious because it is subject to deviation;
for instance, [the claim that] an eternal person is an agent, or that there are eternal entities beyond the senses. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.333)

The person who perceives through the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) a discordant cause for entities, their discordant state, their cessation, or anything else that falls outside the scope [of those two], [is mistaken]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.334)

Whether he speaks by means of an inference that relies on scripture or one that contradicts it, he does so without resolving the contradiction and without demonstrating the meaning of the treatise. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.335)
One who asserts the truth of his meaning might, through audacity, win over a harlot;
if validity were established in this way, what then would be invalid? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.336)
For it is not the case that there is no single true meaning among the many words spoken by a person;
nor is sound the intrinsic nature or the effect of things residing in the speaker. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.337)
And there exists no non-deviation for anything other than that;
if it is argued that the activity of denoters is caused by the perception of the denoted. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.338)

How could that [scripture] which contains mutually contradictory meanings exist in one place? Therefore, the scriptures are not in any way inseparable from real entities (*vastu*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.339)
For those who are traveling, [the means of knowledge] do not succeed; how then could there be a determination of the object from them?
Therefore, even by their cessation, neither existence nor non-existence is established.
Therefore, the non-apprehension of the result of a non-existent certainty is not established.
This is the fourth chapter, titled "Inference for Others."
Some say that because it is to be established for another, even if it is not seen by oneself, it is nonetheless a "means of proof seen by others";
the statement regarding "seeing by oneself" is intended to reject that view. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.1)

In the domain of inference, the authority of verbal testimony is not accepted because it consists of the acceptance of what has already been examined; for once that [object] has been established, inference does not proceed with respect to it. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.2)

Since the proponent states the means of proof for the sake of refuting [the opponent's position], that [scripture] is not a valid means of cognition (apramāṇa) for him; therefore, it is unestablished for him, while everything established by it is established for the opponent. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.3)
If [an opponent argues that] "it is established for one who possesses that scripture," then for whom is which scripture?
How can that which is sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) be established as a scripture? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.4)
How could there be an acceptance of that which is contradictory to it by means of that very same [cognition]?
If one accepts something other than that, then the abandonment of the former would result in its lack of validity. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.5)

Why then has that proof not been stated, from which one’s own realization arises? Why is that reasoning, by which scripture is to be accepted, not [also] used for another person as well? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.6)

Those very means by which the perception of an ordinary person was previously established are sufficient for this [person] to know the capacity of the object regarding the means of proof. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.7.
Even for those things whose continuity is severed and which are not within the range of even a general [conceptualization],
there is no consideration whatsoever of a probandum or a probans regarding those objects.
When the determination of reality and unreality depends on the subjective intention of persons,
the distinction between a valid reason and a fallacious reason is lost, because that [intention] does not rely upon the actual state of things.
An existent object depends upon cognition [for its manifestation], whereas a non-existent one cannot be established by cognition.
Even for that which exists, a cognition that is not connected with the actual thing is equivalent to a non-cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.10)

The logical mark (liṅga) is either an essential nature (svabhāva), an effect (kārya), or simply the non-perception of the perceptible; it is established as being connected with the object in reality. How could that be unestablished for oneself? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.11)

It is also improper for one to proceed elsewhere by means of another's conceptual constructs; a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) functions through the connection of two factors, such that when one is removed, the other is eliminated. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.12)

The mention of "that object" (tad-artha) is for the purpose of establishing that things whose nature is superimposed by the conceptualization of words are not logical reasons (aliṅga), because an object is established from an object [directly], not through such conceptual constructs. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.13)

Because conceptual construction and scripture follow merely the desire of their author, and because the nature of things is otherwise, those [cognitions] produced by them are fallacious. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.14.
Since the understanding of the object follows from the object itself, there is no capacity in the statements of the thesis and the reason regarding that object;
therefore, those two do not possess an inherent status as means of proof.
That statement of the thesis is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for communicating the speaker’s intention; however, because it gives rise to doubt, it is not a direct proof (*sādhana*).
By the mere statement of the probandum itself, even indirectly, it is not sufficient;
for the statement of the reason, though itself incapable, indicates that which is capable. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.17)
It is said that its statement is incapable [of proving the thesis] because it has as its object only the meaning of the reason;
yet, if it too possesses efficacy, it is because it prompts the utterance of the reason. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.18)

For one who desires to know due to doubt regarding that [object], there would be reliance on a treatise (*prakaraṇa*); yet, since this [doubt] would likewise arise upon encountering a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.19)
Internal capacity, however, resides in the three forms [of the means of knowledge];
therein, the application of mindfulness is established as belonging to that very [capacity]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.20)

For if the object has not been made known, the operation of a reason is impossible; if it is argued that the reason possesses the capacity [to prove the conclusion] simply because the object is made known, [then the reason is redundant]. Pramāṇavārttika 4.21.

It has been stated here that even without this [explicit statement], when it is said, "All such produced things as sound are impermanent," the cognition of its destruction would arise by implication. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.22)

Even if the thesis is not explicitly stated, because it is established through logical necessity, the failure to state any one of the three [characteristics of the reason] alone is declared to be "deficiency" (nyūnatā). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.23)

When stating the proposition (pratijñā) as the expression of what is to be proven, one is not subject to faults; for it is precisely because the [proposition] is not authorized as a means of proof that fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) do not apply to it. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.24)
Even a statement made without qualification brings about doubt regarding that which belongs to a single class;
otherwise, it would follow that every statement of a probandum would constitute a thesis (*pratijñā*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.25)

Since it is stated by the Siddhas and because it serves as a means of proof, there is no fault even for another [school]. But now, how can the statement of the probandum (sādhya) be a member of the proof (sādhanāvayava)? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.26)

The mockery consisting of the introduction of objections such as "the statement is fallacious" and so forth, along with their refutations, is irrelevant; for it has been described that this [objection] is not logical. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.27)
Even though the meaning is already implied, the definition of the thesis is stated for the sake of avoiding confusion;

that [definition] consists of four characteristics, [determined] by the words "itself" (*svayam*) and so forth, occurring in connection with the verbal suffixes (*rūpa*) and particles (*nipāta*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.28.
The thesis is held to be that which is not unestablished, not a means of proof, is stated in its proper sense, and is accepted by the proponent;
even if not explicitly stated, it is pervaded by [the proponent's] intention, like the self in the argument for the existence of the self. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.29)
Even when all other desired [means of proof] have ceased, there remains the warding off of grounds for doubt;
this was stated by the author himself through his own words, and it was composed for that very purpose. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.30)
The distinction between the property and the property-bearer is stated because it depends upon that [intention].
Even if it is not explicitly mentioned, its understanding occurs through the context when there is a desire [to express it]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.31)
The absence of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) in the example is also a fault for that [reason], as has been stated:
"If the self were other [than the body], it would be unestablished (*asiddha*); thus, in that case, it would subvert what is intended. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.32)

If that which was not presented as a probans (*sādhana*) in the debate is not established, then what is being proven? Otherwise, it would either result in something undesired or be utterly futile. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.33)

In arguments involving a second [term], there is the fallacy of non-concomitance (*niranvaya*) and contradiction (*viruddha*); by this, both are explained. Alternatively, the probandum (*sādhya*) may be accepted in its general form. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.34)
"Because there is no other object [to be denoted], that very [denotative capacity] is not established when the body is not attained;
this is merely the description of the dullness of those who prattle on while devoid of anything to be expressed. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.35)
If it is argued that [the case] is the same even regarding destruction, provided there is a conceptual distinction between sound and a jar, [we reply]:
no, because sound is established as possessing that [destruction] by means of a destruction that is already proven. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.36)

Likewise, if there were a separate entity [of impermanence], then the jar would possess that [impermanence]; furthermore, [impermanence] would not be connected with sound as a qualified attribute. If you say this is not so because it excludes non-connection, [we reply: no. Pramāṇavārttika 4.37.
For exclusion is of two kinds: that of dissociation and that of non-connection.
When exclusion is intended to preclude non-connection, there is no occurrence of non-concomitance. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.38.
That which is to be proven is indeed the universal, and it is not the proving of what is already established;
and that [universal] is qualified by the subject (dharmin), so it does not suffer from the fault of being "without a logical connection" (niranvaya).

By this, [the opponent's position] that the property and the subject are distinguished by the subject and the property respectively is refuted; for, in this way, one cannot negate [the property] while remaining within the subject itself, since there is no means of proof. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.40.

For the removal of the aggregate is not contradictory with respect to the subject (*dharmin*), since the probandum (*sādhya*) is not intended in that way; here, only the property (*dharma*) is the probandum. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.41)

Even though many properties may reside in a single subject according to various treatises, that which is to be proven must be intended by [the proponent] himself; thus, the word "himself" (svayam) is employed. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.42)

Since one accepts the treatise itself by undertaking it in its entirety, if a contradiction were to occur therein, there would be a fault even for a single instance regarding either the reason or the thesis. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.43)

If the non-destruction of sound is what is to be proven, then [the reason] would be contradictory because the quality of smell being a property of earth remains unimpaired; if it is argued that this is not so because [smell] does not belong to the subject [of the argument], then that same [objection] applies elsewhere as well.

Now, if the subject (dharmin) under discussion here were invalidated by the meaning of the treatise, then the proponent would have to state its status as intended [by the treatise] through the proof of its properties and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.45)

If this desire were to exist through certain circumstances and be understood by them, then [the claim] "this desire of yours exists by force" is clearly the work of a Lord (Īśvara). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.46)
One who asserts that [the mark] has as its logical reason something that ought not to be the case is sublated by deviation;
and when a thing that is not invariably concomitant is sublated, what harm is done to the other? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.47)

And it has been said: "Inference regarding its own object does not depend on scripture; since that [object] is established by it [inference], the treatise is not consulted at that time. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.48)
If it is argued that there would then be an abandonment of the debate, that is not so, because [the thesis] has not been accepted as a means.
For this [thesis] is a means only when it is accepted; even if it exists at that time, it is not a constituent part [of the proof].

Then, when the two objects [of perception and inference] have been purified, that would be the time for one who desires to undertake the study of the treatise; at that time, there may be sublation by the treatise. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.50)

Because reflection that contradicts that [scripture] is impossible for the sake of establishing its objects, the adoption of scripture is justified when one has transitioned to a third position. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.51)
In that case as well, the sublation of what is invariably concomitant with the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) must be avoided;
however, this does not apply to other [properties], because it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress.

By whom was this rule established that a treatise must be accepted in all matters of inquiry? Now, one cannot infer fire from smoke if the underlying principles are not established. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.53)
For a person born empty [of wisdom] and unable to discern quality from defect, alas, by whom have these treacherous houses of philosophical tenets been bestowed? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.54)
If one were to show the entire treatise as an illustration for a single proof in a given instance, that would constitute a proof; such is this extraordinary principle. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.55.

For a property that is unrelated [to the subject], why would it not be established even if unestablished? Why would a reason stated to prove it be defective when it is established therein? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.56)
Without even bringing forward all the subjects (dharmin) in the example, people infer from the smoke of speech and so forth the fire of consciousness and the like. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.57)

When an object establishes its own nature (svabhāva) or its cause through deviation [from what is not that], it does not cease to be its own nature even when there is a contradiction of someone's thesis. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.58)
And another person who resorts to that [reason], which is invariably concomitant with the desired objects to be proven—how could he not be understood by means of that reason? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.59)
Whether stated or unstated by him, how could it not be established?

Whether the reason has been stated or not, what does it matter to the proponent here if it is contradictory? For it is not by virtue of a defect in his statement that the reason becomes a subverter of the treatise. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.60)
If it is argued that there is a fault because a sublation has been stated, [we reply: if he were not to state it, why would he not sublate?
By doing nothing improper, how can he be at fault? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.61)

In other fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), one would be censured for stating something futile because one's own intended point is not established; but this is not the case here, because that very point is established.

If something established by scripture is refuted somewhere on the grounds that it is illogical, while another thing [established by scripture] is asserted as being logical, this is the established practice of the royal court. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.63)

If one were to treat all things as equivalent and thus claim that no means of proof can be stated, then the established distinction between the probandum and the means of proof would have to be abandoned everywhere. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.64)
"Let there be sublation [of one reason by another] because two contradictory [reasons] cannot coexist in a single locus;
however, in the case of the 'contradictory-exclusive' (viruddhaikāntika), there is no such contradiction here. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.65)

Even if there is no relationship of sublated and sublater between those two, if there were sublation even when [the object] is not connected [to the scripture], because it would result in the subversion of the meaning of the treatise, then everything would be sublated by everything. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.66)
If it is argued that there is a connection because [the reason] is sublated in that very [context], that is not so;
for one must consider the merits and defects of every reason with respect to its own probandum. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.67)
The necessary connection with the probandum is what constitutes a valid relation here, and that is not observed.
The fault of contradicting the treatise applies equally to one who has committed the act as to another.

If everything seen in the treatise were to be proven simply because of the acceptance of that treatise, it would follow that one is asserting a thesis, a proven example, and a reason [simultaneously]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.69)

If it is argued that the two [the thesis and the example] have been stated as means of proof, we reply: since the word "intended" (īpsita) is used, the status of being the probandum (sādhyatva), which is established by logic, does not cease merely because of a verbal statement. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.70)

If that which is unintended by the proponent and unprovable were [the subject], then any other property not intended by him would also be unprovable; in that case, how could something that subverts the unprovable be contradictory? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.71)
If the word "himself" (svayam) is intended to exclude [the proponent] from the definition of the thesis, it is redundant;
if its purpose in the treatises is to indicate that [the proof] proceeds by way of the [proponent's] own desire, then from where does this doubt arise? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.72)
If it is not prohibited by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), who can prevent one from grasping it?
If it is prohibited by a means of valid cognition, who can urge one toward it by mere words? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.73)
Previously, too, he adopted this doctrine solely according to his own will; why then should he not be able to adopt yet another? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.74)

In this regard, [the author] himself has formulated the scriptural testimony (*svayaṃśruti*) concerning the various misconceptions regarding perception, demonstrating the undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), the lack of provability (*asādhyatva*), and infinite regress (*anavasthā*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.75)

Another [teacher] himself stated the word "itself" (svayam) for the purpose of grasping a subject that is well-known, by way of excluding any distinction based on convention (*samaya*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.76)

The locus (*āśraya*) is established as proven simply by the commencement of the investigation, since there is no dispute regarding categories whose distinctions are imagined according to one's own will. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.77)

Now, [the opponent] asserts that the subject (*dharmin*) is unestablished with respect to its locus of proof; however, this is already covered by the very statement that "it must be indicated by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇaiva nirdeśya*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.78)
For if a statement were possible in the form of something already established, then the rule that "only that which is to be proven should be stated" would be fruitful. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.79)
And it has been described that inference has the universal as its object;
yet here, even if [the universal] is not explicitly stated, nothing is contradicted regarding the subject (pakṣa). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.80)

If one were to make the subject itself the probandum, what would follow from that? It is not possible [to prove it]. Why? Because of the absence of the reason's positive concomitance (anvaya); nor is there any fault in those two [the reason and the concomitance] themselves. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.81)
It is not accepted that a defect depending on the stated members [of the proof] constitutes a defect of the thesis;
likewise, it would follow as an absurd consequence that a defect of the reason and so forth would also be a defect of the thesis. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.82)

Because the entire thesis is sublated [by such defects], therefore only those that adhere to the mere [thesis] are considered defects of the thesis, and no others, just like contradictions with perception and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.83)

Setting aside the sublation [of the thesis] by means of the definitions of the reason and so forth, the definition of the thesis is stated for the purpose of avoiding under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*vyatireka*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.84)
Terms expressing an inherent form or a specific occurrence are subverters of exclusion;
likewise, the mention of a desired [term] together with what is not excluded subverts the charge of over-extension (*avyāpti*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.85)

The definition of a thesis (pakṣa) is the acceptance of what is to be proven; among those [cases], there is no status as a thesis: in the case of the sublated, because of the presence of contradiction; and in the remaining cases, because they do not function according to the definition.

Although the restriction [of the word "only"] is already understood by its own preferred designation, it is stated here because of its connection with a word ending in a kṛtya suffix, in order to exclude other times. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.87)
In this context, the term *iṣi* (to desire) has its finality in that which is desired;
however, by that [term], it is only the "limb" (*aṅga*)—such as an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*) and so forth—that is negated. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.88)

And because it is not expressive [of its own nature], it is illogical for that which is desired by the proponent himself to be the probandum (sādhya) independently of the entire treatise; such is the view of the proponent. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.89)

Therefore, even when that which is desired is sublated by something mixed with what is undesired, the thesis and the reason are not defective, because there is no sublation of the probandum as it was intended. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.90.
And that acceptance is held to be one which is not refuted by the two means of valid cognition;
because the statement of a reason occurs when there is doubt, what is excluded [by those means] cannot be the locus for a reason. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.91.

That sublation is said to be fourfold through the divisions of inference. Among these, [sublation by] what is accepted is a member of the effect-reason; the member of the essential nature is the established order of the world. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.92.
One who is considered free from self-interest and whose speech is endowed with certainty regarding reality is an authoritative person (*āpta*);
his own word and a treatise are said to be one and the same because of their equality. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.93.

Just as speech does not proceed when one lacks valid cognition regarding oneself, so too there can be no investigation into a matter established by a treatise if that treatise is not accepted as a basis. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.94)

For, since the treatise is an authority when it serves as the basis for that [introduction], this statement is made alongside its own words in order to show their equivalence regarding the point to be expressed. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.95)

An illustrative example similar to that has also been described by him, because in the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the words of the treatise would be untenable. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.96)

In the case of contradiction with one's own words, there is a clear example in scripture: "In that regard, the dharma after death does not bestow happiness. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.97) This serves merely as an illustration of the direction.
Even for a teacher, when there is a contradictory statement regarding a real entity that does not depend on [the authority of scripture],
there would be neither sublation nor obstruction, because those two [statements] possess equal status.
Just as it is in the case of one's own words, so too at that time, this [contradiction] consists of one's own statement;
whichever of those two possesses a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) shall subvert the other. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.99)
Otherwise, how could a thesis or an inference—whether devoid of reasoning or consistent with reality—not contradict [the opponent's position]? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.100)
The validity of scriptures has already been refuted previously;
therefore, this fault is intended [to apply] specifically within the investigations of accepted means of knowledge (*abhyupāya*).

Therefore, although it is not external to inference, this means of knowledge is treated separately for the sake of showing its distinct object, because it subverts [the opponent's position]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.102)

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), or the separate mention [of the two] would be purposeless; for if difference were expressed by mere words, there would be a contradiction even with respect to one's own [stated] meaning. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.103)
Because he has accepted it, the treatise is an authoritative means of knowledge regarding all things;
if he does not wish for it to be sublated, what indeed could possibly sublate it? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.104)

In the case of contradiction with one's own words, there would be non-distinction between contradiction with one's own words and contradiction with a treatise; furthermore, its status as a valid means of knowledge is established by human intention and is fully complete. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.105)

Therefore, regarding well-established objects, there is no harm even in disregarding the treatises; however, regarding supersensible objects, no inquiry proceeds at all unless it is established by scripture.
In this context, even the investigation consists primarily in pointing out contradictions, as follows:
"Passion and the like are the root of unrighteousness, yet bathing is the destroyer of unrighteousness. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.107)

A treatise that is not contradicted by established facts, by reasoning, or by its own words—whether regarding the perceptible or the imperceptible—is to be accepted; thus the investigation is set in motion. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.108)

Since it is not prohibited with respect to objects and conforms to human desire, the person whose speech is unimpaired is the authoritative source (āpta) for that which is intended by the word "desired. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.109)

Dharma arising from worldly convention has been described by the term "well-known" (prasiddha); those things cognized through perception and other means are indicated by the superimposition of the term "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa). *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.110.

By virtue of conforming to the desire of those [beings] who have arisen based upon that [mind], the universe—whether already produced or yet to be produced—is, by its very nature, fit for them, provided it does not contradict [their intent]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.111)
One who opposes [a word] is sublated by that word's fitness, whether it be past, future, or conforming to the mere object. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.112)
By the very power of its fitness, sound is in fact produced;
therefore, even when that [fitness] is not explicitly perceived, all [sound] is established as such through it. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.113)
Otherwise, there would be no unique character for the subverting reason here;
its negation would have to occur through inference, because the word's referent does not function within the domain of the senses. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.114)
Where there is no positive concomitance (anvaya), the reasons are uncommon;
how then can the statement "existence" also be considered an example of a reason in such a case? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.115)

Words depend upon convention, and that [convention] depends solely upon desire; therefore, there is no lack of proof for those things established by words—this is the statement regarding what is established by verbal testimony (*śābdaprasiddhi*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.116)

In this way, he demonstrates the non-existence of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) among those [reasons] established by inference, because such cognition possesses the nature of inference. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.117)
Alternatively, it might be argued that for people who speak, there is an absence of inference; but what does that matter? For perception has a different object from inference. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.118)

Therefore, it is indicated that because [cognition] conforms to the existence or non-existence of things through inference, its occurrence is distinct from those [things] and does not depend upon them; thus, it is said to be "dependent on that [person's] will. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.119)

"If one does not accept the moon-ness of the moon, what cognition does he desire?"—in response to him, that [reason] is considered non-common (asādhāraṇa) because there is no similar instance (adṛṣṭānta). Pramāṇavārttika 4.120.
This is not stated with reference to a single example alone;
for it is a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and because [the definition] would be contradicted if one were to say that a *dhātrī* tree is a tree. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.121)

In this case as well, because it is observed in the world—as in the case of camphor, silver, and so forth—there is either the occurrence [of a term] due to convention, or even its non-commonality [to other objects]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.122)
If that [property] were established for him anywhere, it would be established by the force of the thing itself (*vastubala*).
However, if one accepts what is established by mere cognition (*pratīti*), then there is no way to prevent it even in the case of a non-hare (the moon).
When that entity is established, there is no prevention even regarding the moon;
when that entity is absent, there is no fault even if there is a prevention regarding the moon. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.124)
Therefore, because desire is not obstructed, objects are capable of possessing properties that arise through the power of conventions fixed upon non-existent things. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.125)

The inference called "dependent origination" (pratītya), arising from the non-denial of convention, strikes down that [opponent] who obstructs such fitness regarding the object of fitness. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.126)
"The restriction of the meaning of words that follow convention is not [inherent]," by this it was stated; therefore, a negation of these [words] here would be contradictory. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.127)
For it has been explained that one who denies the meaning of a scriptural statement based on specific causes, or the ultimate meaning of words, is not subject to refutation. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.128)
Therefore, in order to demonstrate the difference in their objects, even cognition—which is not external to inference—is treated separately, as before. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.129)

Demonstrating the purpose for explaining the two types of valid cognitions separately, [the author] states that these two— namely inference and perception— are accompanied by their respective causes, but not so in the case of sublation.
In this case as well, when there is sublation by perception, since sound possesses a manifold nature, whatever form appears in the hearing of what is well-known [as sound]— [Pramāṇavārttika 4.131]

Because no non-dual [object] is seen when a variegated appearance arises as cognition, the statement that it has that [variegation] as its object is like [the claim] regarding this very [cognition]; thus, there is sublation by perception when it is negated. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.132)
That very form is the object there; the remainder is characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
Being a non-entity, the universal is therefore not within the range of the senses.

Because the non-perceptibility of general properties (sāmānyadharma) is thereby established, it is demonstrated by the mention of "audibility" that there is no sublation even when [the property] is rejected. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.134.

Because its nature is in every way inexpressible, because it is established by relying upon that [inexpressibility], and because [the auditory cognition] is sublated by the force of that [nature], the object of the senses is said to be "audible. Pramāṇavārttika 4.135.

In all cases, that property which the proponent intends as his own probandum—sublation would apply to that property when it resides in the subject, but not to another property in the subject. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.136)
Otherwise, what obstruction would there be if [the property] were sublated in another locus?
Since the meaning is already understood by this definition, the mention of "one's own locus" (svadharmin) is repeated. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.137)

In order to establish that there would be a sublation of the subject (*dharmin*) itself when there is a sublation [of the property], [the opponent argues] that because the substratum is contradicted, that which depends upon it is not contradicted. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.138)

Otherwise, because of the statement that "such a property (dharma) is to be proven," one would consider that very [property] to be sublated; therefore, the mention of "one's own subject" (svadharmin) follows.
But is this not already established by the facts? True; however, some have arrived at the conclusion that there is a fault even when there is a negation of the subject alone. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.140)

Just as space and so forth do not possess a previously non-existent form produced by others, because they are not the cause of sound and the like all at once—when this has been stated, the opponent replies: (Pramāṇavārttika 4.141)

In the same way, even if the subject (dharmin) such as space were non-existent by its own nature, there would still be no sublation whatsoever of the intended probandum (sādhya). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.142)

For when both [the property and the locus] are to be proven, that sublation which contradicts the property to be proven by means of the locus is described here as "sublation" (bādhā). *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.143.
In the same way, since the subject (dharmin) here is also the object of proof, it is not [the object of proof] in its isolation.
If this were so, there would be a sublation (bādhā) here: [the subject] would not possess a capacity that is not produced by another.
"Because it is not the cause of sound and so forth simultaneously, pleasure and the like [are momentary]," as before;
this would be a conclusive reason here if there were a contradiction [in the contrary case]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.145)
Because there is no contradiction between succession, action, and permanence,
and because there is doubt regarding its exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa), this [reason] is not accepted as a variety of inference "from the remainder" (śeṣavat).

Since the dharma that is desired by oneself is what is to be proven, it has been indicated that its basis must not be sublated; neither can that which is unrelated to it, nor that which rests upon something else, be sublated. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.147)

The sublation of the properties of others by one's own direct perception (śruti) is called "sublation" (bādha); likewise, the sublation of those belonging to another locus by one's own locus is also so called. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.148)

Although every defect of the means of proof (sādhana) obstructs the thesis (pakṣa) itself, nevertheless, the status of being a "defect of the thesis" belongs only to those [defects] that arise from the mere statement of the proposition (pratijñā). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.149)
The fault that depends upon a subsequent member [of the syllogism] is what is being discussed by the word "thereby" (tena);
therefore, it is said that the fault of the thesis consists in such things as an unestablished locus (asiddhāśraya). Pramāṇavārttika 4.150.

By this very [means], the sublation of the specific properties of the subject, of the nature of the subject itself, and of those factors that constitute the probandum has been demonstrated. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.151)
In this regard, a mere direction is stated as an illustration for the sake of seeing the meaning:
there is another object associated with the characteristic of a substance which, in the case of conjunction, possesses visibility. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.152)
A thesis concerning a specific, imperceptible [whole] is purposeless;
for the whole is accepted as the effect [of its parts], which is impossible among those [parts] that are imperceptible. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.153)
And if another [entity] that is not distinct [from the subject] is being proven, it is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).
If it were to possess weight, there would be downward motion and a bending of the scale.
Therefore, being devoid of qualities and activity, it is not an inherent cause;
for that very reason, it is not perceptible, since its effect and its form are themselves unperceived.

Because the specific property that arises as an inseparable concomitant of that [substance] is subject to sublation, the series of substances must be weighed down to its subtlest limit, just like a beam of light. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.156)

Another has said that there is no motion of the gravity of a distinct substance; for when a heap of dust is joined to [a scale] all at once, it is so even when joined gradually. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.157)
Therefore, there would be a difference in weight when weighed separately and together; thus, it is not logical for gold *māṣakas* and the like to have an equality of number. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.158.
If weight were not perceived even in a great heap of mustard seeds that increases more and more, [then] it would have to be produced by the garland. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.159)
The weight [of the mountain], even starting from a mustard seed, is immense and difficult to perceive;
yet it can be weighed because its cause is perceptible, whereas the weight of the effect itself is not perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.160)
Surely that object is not perceived like a part [of it], nor is its effect observed; for, just as with the non-falling of a heavy object, none of its qualities are perceived. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.161)

The absence of excess or deficiency in [weights such as] a *māṣaka* and so forth is merely an illustration; for, when form and other [objects] are perceived by their respective sense-faculties, there is no [perception of] further increase or decrease. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.162)

However, because it is possible for one's own words and so forth not to be contradicted, the example may be understood through another direction according to what has been stated. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.163.

However, because verbal suffixes (kṛtya) pertain to all three times, even then that which is not of such a nature but is presented as such to another is not accepted as the [true] probandum. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.164)
But in the context of establishing cognition, [the term "probandum"] excludes everything that is unestablished;
for the mention of the "probandum" does not depend upon a specific [unestablished] quality that is not intended. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.165)
Therefore, he has provided an example and a reason that are unestablished;
otherwise, even in the case of a hare’s horn and the like, which are entirely unestablished, they would be subject to proof.

Since everything is unestablished [for the opponent], it is in no way possible for him to engage in the analysis of the presentation and refutation of distinctions such as action and so forth. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.167)
"It is incorrect to say that a member [of a syllogism] is the thesis because its nature is not previously established;
for they are all equally *siddhāntas* (established tenets), since they are characterized by being accepted. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.168)

Even if the collection [of the two] is what is to be proven, each is a qualifier of the other; thus, both would be unestablished as the probandum, and the definitions of the reason and the example would fail. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.169)

If it is claimed that, because [the property] cannot exist [elsewhere], the word "probandum" (sādhya) refers to the locus (dharmin), then enough with the treatise; let it proceed according to common usage in the world itself. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.170.
By the force of the statement of the proof, the status of being the probandum is understood to reside in its object;
and because of the pervasion [of the reason] by means of the statements of the logical reason and so forth, the proof is beyond doubt. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.171)
Since the restriction applies to the preceding [term], the statement of the definition of the thesis would be redundant;
therefore, that statement results in pervasion, as it is understood through the force of the context.

Contradiction, [the thesis being] unestablished, lack of connection, lack of assistance, and non-coexistence—thus all defects of the members [of the syllogism] would constitute defects of the proposition (*pratijñā*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.173)

It has been established that the fault of the thesis does not depend on another [reason]. Furthermore, that very same [fault] would be refuted as being "unestablished" (asiddha) because it is impossible for it to be intended [by the proponent]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.174)

If impermanence and its cause were [already established], then sound alone would proclaim them; for apart from the presentation of an example, what other demonstration of the meaning is there here? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.175)

Having designated [an object] as distinguished by its specific qualities, if one then applies a general term, what is the result of that application? Is it the pervasion of that generality, or something else? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.176)

"It might be argued that the refutation occurs while [the word] remains [in its own domain]; therefore, he said: 'By speaking of another object which is contradictory, one expresses the non-identity of the heard word. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.177)
And because it does not reject particularity, that [exclusion] does not exist for universals, as in some context where one says, "A tree is not necessarily a *śiṃśapā*. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.178)

If it were not so, there would be a prohibition against the occurrence of all auditory cognitions in a single [object]; yet that is not the case, because such [a single occurrence] is impossible if those various differences are not unreal. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.179)

Because there is a distinction between the object to be known and the means of making it known, the probans—which is to become the property of the subject—is unestablished; thus, the indicator lacks proof because its own subject is unestablished in its own demonstration. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.180)

If it is argued that the fault is equal everywhere because the distinction between property and property-bearer is unestablished in all entities, we say no; for there is a distinction by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.181)
In investigations into the ultimate truth, since such things are not established as they appear, identity and difference are denied in respect to conventional entities. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.182)

This establishment of the conventional usage of inference and the object to be inferred is conceived by relying upon a distinction that is thoroughly established through cognition. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.183)

When, for a discerning person, the substratum (dharmin) and its properties (dharmas) appear within cognitions that are established according to their respective distinctions, conventional usage (vyavahāra) then relies upon them.
In this context, that very same [entity], when brought forward in common practice and devoid of the cognition of difference, is the probandum;
since it is then led to the status of a means of proof, it is shown to be unestablished [as a separate entity]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.185)
From the difference between the property and the general property, there arises the relationship of part and whole;
for example: "Sound is impermanent because it arises from effort, due to its being produced by effort. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.186)

Even though it is a part of the [opponent's] position, there is no "unestablished" (asiddha) fallacy regarding a different subject because it is not contradicted; for example: "This object is not a horse because it has horns," or "This object possesses horns. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.187.
Alternatively, one might observe that the exclusion [of the reason] is a subordinate member of the time of the probandum;
however, even a specific [reason] cannot be the object of the thesis because of the difference in its property (dharma). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.188)

In order to facilitate easy comprehension through the classification of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), a summary of the meaning of the section on the reason (*hetu*) is stated in the form of a verse. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.189.
The particle [eva], which functions as an exclusion, excludes non-connection with the property, connection with others, and absolute non-connection. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.190)

Whether expressed together with the qualifier, the qualified, or the action, every such meaning is understood through the speaker’s intention, even when not explicitly employed. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.191)
A statement has exclusion as its result, as for example: "Caitra is an archer," "Pārtha is an archer," or "The lotus is blue. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.192)

In that case as well, the exclusion of the counter-correlate is understood regarding the objects, due to established usage, the capacity [of the words], and the conformity of the speaker’s intention with the sound. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.193)

Because that [property] excludes non-connection, the subject (dharmin) is a qualifier of the property (dharma); since the property is thus qualified by it, it does not incur the fault of being without a substratum (niranvaya). *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.194.

For the sake of establishing [an effect] through its own nature or its effect, there are two types of reasons and their two contraries each; because of the dispute regarding particularity and generality, the remaining [reasons] are those that establish exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.195.

For there is no pervasion of the object to be known by anything other than its own nature when it resides in its cause, because of the possibility of deviation; therefore, the result is a twofold exclusion.

Knowledge that follows immediately after an effort does not necessarily pertain to something already existent, because such effort is in no way applicable to its [the object's] concealment or to the sense organs or words. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.197)
Since it is contradictory for that which is independent of thought to produce an effect with a specific form, the fact that its fruit is occasional is established; such knowledge is its logical mark.
Although this much alone would suffice for the proof, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is treated separately;
[this is done] so that when it is taught alongside the effect, one should not think that everything is of such a kind.
The statement of the reason was made for the sake of etymological derivation when the stated object was already inferred;
here, the classification has been explained, but the definition does not differ.
Therefore, in this case, even a nature that resides in only one part [of the whole] serves as an effect-reason (*kāryaliṅga*);
hence, there is a similar example [for the inference of the cause] because the manifestation arises from effort. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.201)

The meaning is that whatever entity is invariably concomitant [with another], or whatever possesses non-differentiation from itself, must be non-deviant from that; therefore, there is a differentiation of those [entities]. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.202.

It has been stated that those [reasons] such as "conjunction" (saṃyoga) and so forth, which lack such a necessary connection, are not valid reasons, because of the possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra). *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.203.
Or, if there is an obstacle [to inference], let that very obstacle be the means for understanding [the object].
For invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is a restriction (*niyama*), and what is restricted cannot be the means of proof (*sādhana*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.204)

The state of being exclusive regarding exclusion is called inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); and that [concomitance] does not exist in things that lack a necessary connection. For that very reason, the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) [is possible].
For it is only when identity with the self or the state of being a cause is established that negative concomitance (vyatireka) can be established;
therefore, in the absence of such distinction, there is neither negative nor positive concomitance.
By taking up mere non-perception alone, the reason is stated as being purely negative;
therefore, it would be inconclusive, whereas otherwise it would be a means of proof.

If the absence of breath and so forth were pervaded by selflessness, then upon the exclusion [of selflessness], breath and so forth would be excluded; but that is not the case. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.208)
Because it is illogical for the cessation of one thing to result from the cessation of another;

if [it is argued that] it has that as its nature or is produced from it, [then we reply: this is not so, because [the effect] is not perceived when that [nature or cause] is being perceived. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.209.
The perception and non-perception of that [object] are established only when there is perception and non-perception [of the cognition];
however, for something that is absolutely beyond the senses, such seeing and not seeing are not established.
Otherwise, how could one say "not" regarding a jar or the like for that whose form has not been seen elsewhere?
And how could there be pervasion of an exclusion whose negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unknown? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.211)

And since the existence or non-existence of the vital breaths and so forth is perceived through their being observed in some instances [and not others], if the self were likewise observed, its existence or non-existence would be perceived in the same way. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.212)

Since it is due to the absence of that [vitality] as a cause that breath is observed in a jar, if that were not present in the body as well, its occurrence in the body would not be logical. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.213)

If reality were perceived even when things are distinct due to some slight similarity, then why is the possession of a self not inferred for jars and the like on account of their being objects of cognition? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.214)
If it is argued that [the Veda] is not desired [as a source], then valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed the basis for all things desired;
for who, without it, would be capable of establishing the distinction between existence and non-existence? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.215)
Memory, desire, and effort give rise to respiration, the blinking of eyes, and so forth;
these arise from objects, the senses, and the mind, and they themselves originate from their own respective classes. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.216)

Mutually dependent upon one another and partaking of positive and negative concomitance, this non-existence extends only this far; any further postulation would lead to an infinite regress. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.217)
That [reason] is equivalent to "being audible" because of its deviation, as in the case of "vital breath" (prāṇa) and so forth.
If it is argued that this is not so because of its deviation even when there is a negative concomitance (vyatireka), then how [can it be a valid reason]? Pramāṇavārttika 4.218.
"Surely it is said that its dissociation occurs only from what is impossible to accomplish;
however, the absence of persistence in the case of what is possible follows by implication, and this [absence] is the same for other things as well. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.219)
The existence [of the cause] is stated in the case of the probandum (sādhya) because the cessation [of the effect] occurs precisely from that which is incapable [of producing it].
For this very reason, it has been said through presumptive reasoning (arthāpatti) that both [the presence and absence of the effect] are seen by means of a single [instance]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.220)
Therefore, such non-deviation is not established in cases where there is no positive concomitance;
and what other kind of negation of a negation could there be than through affirmation? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.221)

The cessation of what is non-existent cannot be established as something to be accomplished; therefore, it does not apply to things that are impossible to achieve. [Objection: Is it not the case that "it is not" is itself that very cessation? [Response: What is considered to be the cessation of a non-existent thing? *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.222.
"The absence of cessation is indeed a positive injunction; even though it is a non-entity, it exists as a real thing.
But the absence of a real thing is 'non-existent'—behold this display of sheer stupidity! (Pramāṇavārttika 4.223)

If there is no activity of the reason with respect to that [object], why is its cessation (nivṛtti) desired? Even that [cessation] is not a negation; why then is this cessation being negated? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.224)

Apart from affirmation and negation, there is no other verbal usage; and since that [usage] does not exist regarding non-existent things, it follows that one must remain silent in this matter. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.225)
There is no negation of existent things, nor does it exist for non-existent things; by this logic, the meaning of the negative particle has vanished from the world. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.226)
If there is a negation of place and time, it is negated exactly as it exists; if it does not exist in such a way, then even so, it is not negated. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.227)

Therefore, relying upon the meaning of words, all affirmation and negation is accepted here as resting upon the existence or non-existence [of that meaning], without any external basis. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.228)
Connected with those two properties, that non-existent [object] appears as if it were such [an existent];
because verbal usage occurs toward it, it too is accepted as participating in conventional discourse. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.229.
Otherwise, in the affirmation and negation of things, there would be the affirmation and negation of the entire nature of a single property. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.230)

Because they are not non-distinct, when there is a difference [between properties], there is no coexistence of affirmation and negation within a single substratum, just as with various types of affirmation and negation. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.231)

With reference to a single subject that serves as the locus for various properties, [the inference] prescribes one property while remaining indifferent toward other properties that likewise possess that subject. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.232)

Just as the intellect, when there is a negation, constructs a conventional usage that is devoid of that [negated object] and dependent upon other things, even though its object is unreal; (Pramāṇavārttika 4.233)
