Those who have resorted to that very [cognition], which is based on the distinction of non-conceptual objects and arises from beginningless predispositions, do not subvert the worldly object. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.234)

An object, though single, appears as distinct in various ways—both as having that result and as not having that result—when it is led by various disturbances, as if by accumulations and depletions. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.235)

Even one who does not possess that [property] is brought before the vision [of the mind] through some connection; for they too rely on distinctions. Therefore, they are unaware of their own cognitive distortion (*viplava*).
And because it functions to establish existence, that [non-existent thing] would be doubtful;
moreover, since its non-existence is accepted, it is not logical for it to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.237)

Even if there is exclusion from what is non-existent, its exclusion from the similar class (sapakṣa) is doubtful; and its exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is doubtful because of that very doubt. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.238)
When one restriction is established, the exclusion of others is established;
for if two classes were observed among those seen, there would be doubt even regarding what is seen. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.239)

There are objects that, although not pervading all individuals, belong to that same class; there is no necessity [of their presence] everywhere simply because they are not observed in some places, just as with the property of being earthen or being scratchable by iron. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.240)
When a contradiction is not observed even in the presence [of the cause], who could dispel doubt?
Since there is a restriction in some cases, what else could that be than its being the nature of that effect? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.241)
Therefore, its cessation even through selflessness is doubtful for him;
let it be so, yet the self is not established by means of selflessness. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.242)
By this [reasoning], he does not accept the non-existence of exclusion as being a positive entity;
just as, even though there is no exclusion [from it], the vital breaths and so forth are not considered members of the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

If a reason lacks exclusion from the similar class (sapakṣa), then that reason is one possessing positive concomitance (anvayin); if it lacks both positive and negative concomitance, then [the argument] "that which is not selfless is not possessed of a self" [would fail]. Pramāṇavārttika 4.244.

That whose own nature is established as being inseparable from [certain] activities is, for that reason, the very thing that causes one to desist from them; yet it is also the instigator toward those [other] activities. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.245)
And that invariable concomitance (nāntarīyakatā) depends upon a means of proof;
for it consists in the observation of the effect and the non-observation [of the cause], which is indeed the nature of causality.
Because there is no necessary rule that another thing must exist when that [cause] exists, it cannot be inferred;
for those things that exist eternally cannot possibly be absent when that [cause] is absent.

Since the various specific natures of effects arise from their causes, how could that which arises from them possess a nature produced by something else in the absence of those very causes? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.248)
For it is due to the diversity of the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that things possess a manifold nature;
if that [power] were not differentiating, this world would necessarily be of a single form. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.249)
If there were both differentiation and non-differentiation, the nature of being distinct would be contradicted;
for if a single entity possessed multiple forms, it would have two forms: that of fire and that of what is other than fire. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.250)
If that which is its form as a producer were itself another [entity], then it would not be its form as a producer; how could that [form] possibly belong to it? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.251)
Therefore, the natures of cause and effect are necessarily related to one another;
consequently, when that [cause] is perceived, it is understood even through its effect, just as it is in the perception of the [cause] itself.
How can one [effect], such as moistening, arise from many [causes], such as milk and water?
It arises from the power of liquidity; for that moisture exists as a single [power] in both of them. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.253)

Is its nature both different and non-different? Or, if it is different, how can fluidity be said to be non-different? It is said to be non-different because of the non-difference of the cognition that takes that as its form. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.254)
Similarly, even though there is a difference [between fire and its effect], fire is the basis for the cognition "fire";
by that aspect through which it produces smoke, it is apprehended in that same way.

Because smoke arises from a cause that is a part of the conditions for burning and depends on other factors, it does not deviate from that [fire]; likewise, other effects are similar to that. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.256.
Since fire exists in that which possesses smoke, fuel, transformation, and parts as its conditions, if it were not fire, this would not be smoke; if it is smoke, then it is fire.

The state of being inseparable (nāntarīyakatā) should be understood with respect to their respective causes, just as was previously stated regarding the [inseparability] of destruction and the quality of being produced. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.258.
This entire logic regarding the consequence of being causeless applies to every positive instance (*vyatirekin*);
it should be inferred from the statement of "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) that was made for the sake of demonstrating parity. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.259.

Because the non-existence of an object is described as following precisely from the nature of its cause, it is indicated that this [non-apprehension] serves as a cause for doubt regarding a perceptible object. *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.261.
By this [negation], a negation that does not acknowledge any part of a real entity is established;
however, by the two preceding [types of negation], there is an exclusion (paryudāsa) from a real entity by way of affirmation.

In that regard, existence is nothing other than the perception of those things which are perceivable; thus, for the sake of making this known, the example of the "indescribable" (anupākhyam) is considered [to be cited]. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.263)

Because the object does not exist, the subject is negated—namely, cognition, its designation, and doubt—just as [the term] "non-fire" [is used] because of the absence of burning. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.264)
Likewise, non-existence is not perceived among things that are themselves unperceivable, because there is no perception [of it].
Therefore, the words for that knowledge are established as being based upon it, because they exist when that [object] exists.
For this conventional usage is established: that [an object] is non-existent when it is not perceived despite being perceptible.
When that [non-existence] is established, the cognition and the verbal expression are also established as being its effects, even though they are free from doubt.

Even though the object is present, one who, out of delusion, does not acknowledge it here is merely reminded of the convention by means of its similarity to what has been established. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.267)
Just as the relationship of cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception,
for it is by means of these two that terms such as "effect" and so forth are conceptually constructed for the sake of conventional usage.

Since the accomplishment of an effect from its cause occurs through its inclusion within the [cause's] own nature, no separate example has been shown for the explanation of the subdivisions of the reason (*hetu*). (Pramāṇavārttika 4.269)
From the experience of perceiving one thing, there arises the conceptual cognition that thinks, "I do not perceive this," or "I do perceive it. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.270)
The distinction among objects is understood only from a specific cognition;
likewise, the attainment of such a nature [by that cognition] is the cause for the awareness of its difference. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.271)
Therefore, the distinction between cognitions is established by themselves, and from those [cognitions], the distinction between their objects [is established];
otherwise, due to infinite regress, the distinction of anything whatsoever would not be established. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.272)
The exclusion of one thing from another occurs through the experience of its specific form;
therefore, the perception of that specific [form] is itself the non-perception of the other. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.273)

Therefore, this non-apprehension, being itself established through direct perception, is the means of cognition for the determination of that absence, because it functions solely with respect to its own [perceptual] occurrence.
Otherwise, the non-existence of an object is understood through its non-perception;
the non-existence of that perception itself would be understood by another [perception], leading to an infinite regress. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.275)
Because certainty is impossible regarding that which is imperceptible, its existence elsewhere is sublated;
just as, among other beings, conceptual construction and the like cannot be established without a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For this [reason] has as its result uncertainty; it is not capable of establishing exclusion.
Only a reason that establishes through certainty is employed at the outset. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.277)
In its own applications, that [inference] functions either in its own form,
or in the form of a sublation of the object, because [the effect] exists when [the cause] exists and is absent when it is absent.
Or [the non-existence of the other] is established through mutual exclusion, like the destruction of an eternal entity;
or it is due to sublation by another means of valid cognition, like an eternal entity that is dependent on something else. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.279)
How could there be a fixed presence of that which has arisen from another cause when [the primary cause] is present?
If it exists by virtue of its own causal nature, what is the point of such laborious recourse to a causal chain?
If that cause, having produced another destruction, were the destroyer of that [entity], what would happen if it were to produce that very entity as something perishable? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.281)
When that [cognition] exists as an established self, who could be its benefactor? And who, being depended upon by it, could be its benefactor? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.282)
And how could an entity that is independent [of causes for destruction] ever become otherwise?
For it is not accepted that the very same thing which does not admit of delay can subsequently possess a destroyer. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.283)
If it is argued that "if there is no dependence even for a single moment, one entity cannot be the cause of another entity," [we reply:
Indeed, such an entity is an existent; how then could a non-existent be an existent in that way? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.284)
For those things whose existence does not depend on anything else are indeed restricted to that very existence;
and when all the causal conditions are complete, there can be no obstruction to the production of the effect.
